News.title: Baby hauled alive from rubble & pool cleaner praying for his life… more jaw-dropping footage from Colombia quake emerges
News.content:
A BABY has been pulled alive from the rubble as dramatic new footage emerges of the devastating earthquake in Colombia.

The footage shows rescue workers digging beneath a collapsed building before carefully clearing debris to reveal a man cradling a baby in his arms.



The rescuers painstakingly freed the tiny infant from the man’s grasp and carried him to safety.

Moments earlier, Brian Osorio Zuluaga had left his office in Cali and was making his way home when he was forced to stop near the remains of a five-storey apartment complex.



As he approached the rubble, he heard sounds coming from beneath the wreckage and called out to see if anyone was trapped inside.

“Yes, I’m here. I’m with a baby,” a man replied.



Zuluaga and a group of men immediately began clearing the debris, but their efforts were hampered when they encountered a huge concrete slab.

“On the first attempt, we couldn’t lift it,” he told CNN.



After coordinating their movements, the men managed to clear a safe path to the trapped man and baby.

“You can see the baby’s little head there, which, at the time, looked sort of purplish because he couldn’t breathe,” Osorio said.

“Once we started removing the rubble, the baby began to … breathe, and his colour started to come back.”

The baby boy was quickly handed to a police officer, who whisked him to safety while the rescuers continued working to free the man.

Elsewhere, emergency workers continued searching through the rubble for signs of life.



Fire Chief Camilo Cano said more than 20 people had been rescued from a collapsed apartment complex at Torres del Limonar in the first 12 hours after the quake.

Three more survivors were later pulled from the wreckage, he said, but large crowds of volunteers initially made the search more difficult.

“We cannot concentrate and hear the calls of people under the structure,” Cano said.



Police have since imposed tighter controls, directing volunteers to specific tasks so rescuers can work more effectively.

Among those anxiously waiting for news was Marcela Perez, who said her partner’s 11-year-old daughter was trapped with her grandparents when the building collapsed.

“We have been here since Monday waiting for the girl to be rescued, and for her grandparents too,” Perez said.

“We are just waiting and trusting in God.”

Hundreds of buildings collapsed as the South American country was hit by a huge 7.4-magnitude earthquake on Monday morning – one of its largest in years.



So far, 254 people have been confirmed dead and nearly 2,600 left injured, officials said.

The death toll is likely to rise, with many feared trapped under collapsed buildings.

Striking at a depth of 64 miles in Chocó province, the quake was felt across a huge area – stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia, as far as Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, 750 miles away, and in Ecuador and Panama.



Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said 1,000 members of the security forces have been deployed to Cali following reports of looting.

The natural disaster is proving to be an early test for the president who was only inaugurated on Friday.

On Tuesday, he flew to Pereira, accompanied by his wife, the first lady Ana Lucía Pineda, to inspect one of the worst-hit areas.

“My commitment is to each and every one of the affected families,” the president wrote on X.

“We remain on the ground, working for our people.”



US secretary of state Marco Rubio said America “stands ready to support” the country.

The US Department of State described the disaster as “devastating” and pledged £11.5million to help provide emergency shelter and supplies.

The EU is also providing funding and supporting rescue operations, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Colombian government announced an immediate emergency rent subsidy for all those who had lost their homes.

The quake follows two back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes in Venezuela in late June.

News.title: Moment huge blaze burns next to rail tracks as trains cancelled and black plume of smoke floats into sky
News.content:
SHOCKING footage shows the moment a huge blaze burned next to a railway station, sparking travel chaos with trains cancelled.

The Royal Berkshire Fire and Rescue service scrambled to the scene on Brunel Way in Slough, and started tackling the blaze just after 4pm today.



Trains running to and from Slough and Windsor & Eton Central have been cancelled, sparking rush hour chaos for commuters.

There will be no train services between the stations until approximately 8pm due to the blaze, according to National Rail.



Footage from the scene showed thick smoke billowing into the sky with the fire service warning people to avoid the area if possible.

Multiple fire crews swooped on the area to tackle the blaze with eyewitnesses claiming at least twelve fire engines were on the scene.



Residents who live nearby were also warned to close doors and windows for their safety by the fire service.

Travellers planning a train journey on lines running through Slough have been warned to check for “potential delays”.



Local bus routes can be used instead by train passengers who can show their ticket to the driver.

A GWR spokesperson said: “Due to a fire on property near the railway between Slough and Windsor & Eton Central the line is blocked.

“Disruption is expected until 20:00.”

A spokesperson for Royal Berkshire Fire and Rescue said in a full statement: “At 4:02pm on Wednesday, 12 August, we received reports of a fire on Brunel Way in Slough.

“Royal Berkshire Fire and Rescue Service crews from Slough, Langley, Maidenhead and Windsor fire stations have been sent to the scene.



“A crew from Buckinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service has also been sent to the scene.

“Crews remain at the scene at this time. Please avoid the area while our crews respond to this incident.

“If you live locally, please keep doors and windows closed.”

It comes after a huge fire broke out at an industrial estate sending clouds of black smoke into the sky and causing a major A-road out of London to close.

Around 100 firefighters and 15 fire engines raced to the scene to battle the blaze on Ripple Road, Barking.



A section of the A13 from London to the M25 and Essex was closed following the fire.

News.title: Bus driver, 25, shot dead outside pub is pictured after being in ‘wrong place at wrong time’ as man, 22, arrested
News.content:
A BUS driver who was gunned down outside a London pub had a “gentle heart” and “wouldn’t hurt a soul”, his heartbroken pals said.

Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa, 25, known in the area as “Billy”, was arriving back home from work at Stockwell bus garage before he was killed on Monday night.



Cops and paramedics scrambled to the Landor Pub in Clapham, just before 10pm after receiving reports of gunfire.

Despite paramedics arriving within three minutes, he was pronounced dead at the scene and a 22-year-old was arrested on suspicion of murder.



Auguste was tragically in the “wrong place at the wrong time”, according to friends.

Speaking today at the scene, a close pal who grew up with Auguste said: “He was coming back from work to see his mum.

“He wasn’t dropping off his girlfriend. He lived just opposite with his mum.

“He lived opposite on the estate with her and was just parking up to get home. We think he was either followed or targeted by mistake.



“He was sitting in his car and was just about to get out to walk home.

“It happened right outside where he lives so I immediately messaged him on Snapchat to find out if he was okay.

“He didn’t reply for a few minutes which is unusual and I thought something had happened.

“I fell to my knees when I found out it was him. He didn’t deserve any of this.”

A police forensics tent remained in place across the road yesterday, while several bouquets of flowers were laid and a candle lit outside the pub.



Detective Chief Inspector Claire Guiver, who is leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts remain with Bile-aka’s family as they come to terms with this tragic incident.

“We continue to appeal for anyone with information to come forward.

“If you were in the area at the time of the shooting, witnessed anything suspicious or have any CCTV, dashcam or doorbell footage that could assist our investigation, we urge you to get in touch.



“Any piece of information could prove vital in helping us piece together the full circumstances.”

Staff from The Landor are understood to have rushed to Auguste’s aid after the shooting.

Auguste’s pal added: “He had an incredibly kind and gentle heart and wouldn’t hurt a soul. He would never hurt anyone.

“He was proud of his job and who he became as a person. He had only started his life. He was an amazing man who was just very hardworking.

“He was always there for his friends and family who always put other first.”



Auguste, from Clapham, South London, had been a bus driver for about a year, friends said.

Today, a forensics team were seen trawling the floor just by the shooting step by step.

The Sun has seen CCTV footage showing a male wearing a moped helmet limping with “blood pouring out his mouth.”



It shows the man walking down a high road about a minute from the scene of the shooting.

A witness said: “The man shouted out: ‘I’ve been shot, I’ve been shot. I’ve been shot.

“He was walking away from the scene with a limp. He was holding his leg and there was blood pouring out his mouth.

“He looked very dazzled and out of it. He was on the phone grunting, calling for his friends to pick him up.”

The man, who did not want to be named, said he saw the man jump into a car which drove away before police arrived.



The male limping is understood to be the 22-year-old male who presented himself to hospital with a gunshot wound.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He was arrested on suspicion of murder.

This man remains in hospital under police guard.

News.title: Labour’s £3bn contract crackdown will hit pubs, care homes and youth jobs, bosses warn
News.content:
LABOUR’S crackdown on zero-hours contracts could cost business up to £3 billion, a damning government assessment reveals.

The party came to power with a pledge to ban “exploitative” zero-hours contracts as part of a new workers’ rights package.



But top bosses last night slammed the rising cost of taking on workers and said it will do further damage to the youth inactivity crisis.

The workers’ rights package has been spearheaded by former deputy PM and now Communities Secretary Angela Rayner.



The impact is set to be most concentrated in industries where demand is more variable including hospitality, the arts along with health and social care, government documents show.

Andrew Griffith, Shadow Business Secretary, said: “Labour’s jobs tax and employment red tape have been so damaging already, but this goes further and once again, it will be young people who will pay the price, during a growing crisis of young Brits out of work.”

Firms have had to deal with hikes to national insurance hikes and minimum wage increases adding to the burden on business since Labour came to power.

Kate Shoesmith, from the British Chamber of Commerce, said: “The increased cost to businesses of the proposed changes to zero hours contracts will be a further hammer blow for many firms struggling to keep their heads above water.

“The government had previously claimed that the cost of the entire Employment Rights Act for business would be £1bn but this research clearly blows that out of the water.

“Businesses have seen their costs due to government policy increase by 70 per cent in the last decade, and their ability to absorb more is extremely limited.



“We are already facing a youth unemployment crisis – now is not the time to make it even more costly for employers to hire.

Kate Nicholls, Chair of UKHospitality, said: “The eyewatering cost of these reforms comes at the worst possible time for hospitality businesses, arriving on the heels of more than £5 billion in additional employment costs in the past two years.

“More than 100,000 jobs have already been lost in hospitality as a result and the extraordinarily high cost of employment continues to restrict job opportunities, particularly for young people.”

Workers on zero-hours and low-hours contracts will get the right to guaranteed working hours from next year if they want them.

The government is consulting on whether to apply the policy to anyone working 48 hours a week, but its preference is for the threshold to be between eight and 20 hours.



Firms will also have to fork out if shifts have been cancelled or moved at short notice in a huge financial blow.

In a worst-case scenario, the right to guaranteed hours could cost firms £450 million.

Then the right to reasonable notice of shifts could cost £1.2 billion and the then £1.3 billion for the right to payments for shifts cancelled or moved.

In a best-case scenario, the overall direct cost to business could be £350 million.

No final decisions on what is deemed an exploitative zero hours contract or what reasonable notice should be given. The consultation runs until next week.



The planned reforms will still “support growth” by improving conditions for workers, an impact assessment said.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A government spokesperson last night said: “We are absolutely committed to ending exploitative zero hours contracts, where workers bear all the financial risk when hours, shifts and earnings are unpredictable.

“These reforms will give workers in every postcode greater income security and predictability of hours and while no final decisions have been made, we’re consulting to get the detail right and ensure this works in the real world.”

News.title: What time is the Clacton by-election result? When to expect the winner announcement and full list of candidates
News.content:
CLACTON voters will soon discover who will be their next MP after a record-breaking by-election.

Polling stations open at 7am on Thursday, but the 34-candidate ballot means the count could run later than usual.



What time is the Clacton by-election result?

There is no guaranteed declaration time, but the result is expected before breakfast on Friday.

Reports say the winner should be known in the early hours, while the complicated count could push the announcement back to around 5am.



Once voting ends, ballot boxes from 51 polling stations must reach the count centre.

Officials verify that the number of papers matches the polling-station records before counting all votes.



That job may take longer than normal because Clacton’s ballot paper is almost a metre long.

Acting Returning Officer Ian Davidson said its record size created practical problems, including how staff would spread the sheets out while allowing candidates’ representatives to watch.

He explained: “Administratively, it’s about how we fit this ballot into the envelopes for postal voters, and – when the voters receive their postal votes – how they get it into an envelope and get it back to us because it is that long.

“We also have an issue for the counters, how we’re going to lay it out, how we’re going to ensure that those who are watching can see while at the same time managing these metre long ballot papers.



No exit poll is planned, so voters should not expect a 10pm projection.

When do polls close in Clacton?

Voting runs from 7am until 10pm on August 13.

The contest uses first past the post, so each elector chooses one candidate and the person with the most votes becomes MP – they don’t need to secure more than 50% of the vote.

The by-election was triggered when Nigel Farage resigned as Clacton’s MP on July 8, 2026.

Farage took 21,225 votes at the 2024 general election, finishing 8,405 ahead of Conservative runner-up Giles Watling.

News.title: How long is the Clacton by-election ballot paper? Why it’s broken records and full list of candidates

CLACTON voters face a record-breaking choice when they pick their next MP on Thursday.

The ballot paper for the August 13, 2026 by-election is around 3ft long after an unprecedented 34 candidates entered the race.



How long is the Clacton by-election ballot paper?

The Clacton by-election voting slip measures about 90cm from top to bottom — just short of a metre and longer than many people’s arms.

It includes Nigel Farage, Count Binface and three Official Monster Raving Loony Party hopefuls, as well as independents and smaller-party candidates.



Tendring District Council’s acting returning officer has said it is longer than any previous ballot paper used at a UK parliamentary election.

Its size has created practical problems before a single cross is cast.

News.title: Map reveals parts of UK with ZERO asylum seekers as Andy Burnham vows to send migrants to leafy middle-class suburbs
News.content:
MORE than a dozen local authorities house no taxpayer-backed asylum seekers, analysis shows – after Andy Burnham said more middle-class areas should take in migrants.

Our map reveals migrant hotspots across the country, with Glasgow, Hyndbyrn and Blackburn among the places supporting the most asylum seekers per capita.



Mr Burnham yesterday suggested that wealthier areas should take more people into dispersal accommodation.

He told GB News: “We cannot have a situation where it’s only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers.”



The PM added: “I do believe all parts of the country need to work, to play their part.”

Mr Burnham was responding to protests in Piddington, Oxfordshire, where the village of 350 people held a mock independence referendum over plans to house 1,000 asylum seekers at a MoD base.



Humans rights groups, the local council and MP Calum Miller have objected to the controversial plans for “Site A”.

The list of 17 areas, first compiled by the Daily Mail, shows posh areas like the Derbyshire Dales, the Isle of Wight and the Cotswolds house zero asylum seekers.

Migrants are more likely to be housed in areas with higher deprivation scores, a Government metric used to track poverty.

Areas with high numbers of asylum seekers and a high deprivation score include Burnley, where there are 455 migrants, or 46 for every 10,000 people.



Similar areas include Middlesborough (43 per 10,000), Blackpool (34) and South Tyneside (42).

The asylum seekers are split between emergency accommodation and dispersal accommodation including hotels and HMO properties, Home Office data shows.

The 17 areas with NO asylum seekers Ceredigion, population 72,599 Cotswold, population 91,661 Derbyshire Dales, population 71,757 East Hertfordshire, population 156,875 Hart, population 103,162 Highland, population 237,290 Isle of Wight, population 141,660 Isles of Scilly, population 2,366 Malvern Hills, population 83,227 Mid and East Antrim, population 139,913 Mid Devon, population 84,993 Mid Ulster, population 152,718 Na h-Eileanan Siar, population 26,020 New Forest, population 176,116 Orkney Islands, population 22,020 Shetland Islands, population 23,190 Tewkesbury, population 101,949

This morning, Anna Turley, the immigration minister, defended Mr Burnham’s remarks.

She said: “I think this is about fairness, and we won’t be asking anyone to take more than they can.

“It’s about their fair share, and we have to look across the country at what is appropriate for areas to take, what is the infrastructure, what is manageable with the local community.



“So this is about fairness.”

And pressed on the Piddington development, Ms Turley said: “The reality is, this is a military base that is outside the village. It’s self-contained.

“People there will be managed and processed properly with the services that they need there on site.

“So we are looking to reduce the impact on local communities.”

But Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: “Andy Burnham is planning to dish out another vindictive punishment beating to the UK’s middle classes.



“Labour has hammered hard-working families with punitive tax increases galore, increased regulation and soaring energy bills.

“Now, Burnham plans to deliberately flood more neighbourhoods with thousands of illegal immigrants who he has let into this country, and many of whom will commit serious crimes including rape and murder.”

Mr Burnham, who visited Dover for the first time as PM earlier this month, has already seen 3,000 people cross the Channel since July 20.

More than 15,000 have crossed from France this year, lower than in the same point of the last two years.

The tally includes 230 who arrived in a single “mega-dinghy” in the early hours of Monday morning.



Home Office sources insisted that migrant smugglers had only resorted to larger boats as interceptions were increasing.

A spokesman added: “We’re cracking down on these reckless and dangerous gangs – our work to disrupt their criminal supply chains has led to more than 1,100 small boats and engines seized since the election.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“There are also now more police on French beaches to intercept them before they set off.

“Small boat crossings are significantly down this year with the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.”

News.title: What time does Ucas Hub update on A-level results day 2026? When to check status of university offers
News.content:
STUDENTS will soon find out whether they have secured a place at their preferred university, with A-level results just around the corner.

Thursday, August 12, is results day for hundreds of thousands of teenagers – and for those seeking to remain in education, Ucas plays a big part of proceedings.

What is the difference between A-level results and a Ucas score?

A-level results are the traditional letter grades from A* to E that students receive from your exam boards.



Ucas score, also called tariff points, is a numerical value assigned to those letter grades, allowing universities to compare different types of qualifications equally.



Each letter grade you achieve in a full A-level translates into a specific number of UCAS points:

A*: 56 points

56 points A: 48 points

48 points B: 40 points

40 points C: 32 points

32 points D: 24 points

24 points E: 16 points

Your total Ucas score is calculated by adding the points of all your eligible qualifications together.

Your total Ucas score can also include points from other qualifications outside of your A-levels, such as Extended Project, AS-levels, T-levels, BTECs or music exams.

You can use the official Ucas calculator to total up your projected score.

What time does the Ucas Hub update on A-level results day 2026?

Students will be able to access their applications from 8am when the embargo is lifted.

Individual records typically process across the system between 8am and 8.15am.

However, with thousands of students logging in simultaneously, expect slow loading and be patient.



Avoid refreshing the page constantly, as this could worsen server traffic.

The Ucas customer experience centre phone lines open at 8.30am if you need direct troubleshooting assistance.

The Ucas Hub tells you where you stand with your firm and insurance university choices.

It will not show your actual grades – those only come from your school or college.

It could show one of the following outcomes:



Your place at your first choice is confirmed

You have been placed at your backup

You have been offered a changed course, which might mean a different course, a different start date or a different point of entry

Your application is still awaiting a decision

You are eligible for Clearing

You then need to check the details of the offer and do what the university asks, which may include proving your qualifications or meeting any outstanding conditions.

A changed-course offer requires a quick decision – you normally have five days to accept or decline, and letting it sit could cost you the place.

Awaiting a decision does not mean you have been rejected.

Universities sometimes take students who have narrowly missed an offer, so it is worth getting on the phone.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Students can only use Clearing once their status says they are eligible, or when they have formally declined or released themselves from a place they are holding.



Clearing choices will become available to students from 1pm on results day.

News.title: Three ways to watch the solar eclipse safely without glasses
News.content:
With most online orders not able to arrive in time and shops running out of stock, it may be too late to buy eclipse glasses for Wednesday evening.

But you can still safely watch the spectacle using some household items.

People in the UK will see a partial eclipse - rather than the total eclipse that will be seen in parts of Spain, Greenland and Iceland - but it is the country's most significant eclipse since 1999.

Experts say enthusiasts should not look directly at the Sun without specialist glasses.

And you shouldn't be tempted to try using sunglasses or dark goggles instead.

They often don't give enough UV protection when looking directly at the Sun and you could end up seriously damaging your eyesight, according to The Royal Astronomical Society.

Here are some viewing methods to try instead.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe's loved ones gather for her funeral
News.content:
Police officers and sniffer dogs were in the grounds of the abbey ahead of the service, which lasted about 90 minutes.

The private requiem mass included a homily from the Rt Rev David Charlesworth, Abbot of Buckfast.

He said: "In the midst of the shock, clamour and sometimes unwarranted comment surrounding her death, our response is to pray for the repose of her soul, to give thanks for her fortitude, and offer Holy Mass in this Abbey Church which Ann called her safe haven."

A statement from the Abbey Church earlier said Widdecombe would be "missed and fondly remembered" and "many in our worshipping community knew her as a kind and warm character".

"Ann was a woman of profound faith, a faith which found expression in the public forum of politics," it said.

It added: "Ann was unafraid to express her unwavering convictions, formed through her Roman Catholic faith. She had a sharp intellect and was a dedicated public servant."

The order of service also included tributes paid by the Rev Roger Widdecombe, Widdecombe's nephew, and Sir Christian Sweeting, a close friend.

A public memorial for Widdecombe is due to be held later this year.

News.title: Double killer and rapist given whole life sentence
News.content:
A serial sex attacker who had a "morbid fascination" with sex has been jailed for the rest of his life after he was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third.

Simon Levy, 40, killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025 and 39-year-old Sheryl Wilkins five months later. Earlier that year, he raped a third woman in the same Tottenham car park where Wilkins was later found dead.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, Judge Mark Lucraft KC sentenced Levy to a whole life order, meaning he will never be released.

The sentence comes after police and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) apologised over a series of disastrous decisions that left him free to roam the streets.

When Levy carried out the attacks, he was on bail and being monitored by the Met.

The police watchdog is currently examining how he was managed over a four-year period, from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

Following Wednesday's sentencing, Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said the handling of Levy's case was a "whole system failing".

News.title: Burnham urges shops not to sell disposable BBQs over wildfire risks
News.content:
Andy Burnham has urged shops to stop selling disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister said he was urging retailers "big and small" to adhere to voluntary guidance to suspend sales during extreme heat.

He added that in the "longer term" the government would look at potentially banning the single-use grills during summer months.

It comes after a potential ban was discussed at an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures.

A number of large retailers and supermarkets have voluntarily stopped selling the devices under a framework, external agreed in 2023 between fire chiefs and the British Retail Consortium (BRC).

This says that retailers should suspend sales once an extreme heat event has been declared as imminent, or in response to "reasonable, evidence based" requests from local councils.

Earlier, Burnham told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

"We do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires."

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

News.title: Jasper Carrott says family is 'so proud' of Lucy Davis after cancer diagnosis
News.content:
Actor and comedian Jasper Carrott has spoken about his pride and love for daughter Lucy Davis after she announced she has incurable breast cancer.

The actress, best known for playing receptionist Dawn Tinsley in BBC sitcom The Office, has received an outpouring of support since she revealed her diagnosis on Tuesday.

Carrott, who was one of the most familiar faces on British television over several decades, told BBC News: "This is a very difficult time for the whole family and we have been supporting her in every way possible since her diagnosis.

"We are so grateful for all the support we have had over this trying time and we are very hopeful for her future being what she wants it to be."

He added: "We are so proud of our daughter and love her so much. The way she has conducted herself through many traumatic health issues is a lesson to us all.

"We would request privacy for the coming months, but thanks once again for the love and concern shown by so many people."

Carrott, whose real name is Robert Davis, became a household name in the 1970s thanks to his stand-up comedy and novelty songs.

He has presented programmes such as Canned Carrott, Golden Balls and Carrott's Commercial Breakdown, and acted in comedy series such as The Detectives.

News.title: PM warned of Iran war impact on UK growth next year
News.content:
Andy Burnham has been warned that the UK economy could barely grow next year if disruption in the Strait of Hormuz continues until the end of 2026.

Treasury sources have confirmed that internal modelling presented to the new prime minister and chancellor suggests UK GDP growth could be as low as 0.3% in 2027, as first reported by Bloomberg.

Government officials say they routinely plan for all possible scenarios.

The UK economy saw a strong start to the year, but growth then faltered with the conflict in the Middle East affecting some businesses. The Iran war has pushed up oil and fuel prices, and also disrupted supply chains.

On Thursday, official figures will show how much the economy grew between April and June of this year.

Economists are expecting growth of 0.4% for the three months.

Burnham and Chancellor John Healey were presented with a reasonable worst-case scenario of the Strait of Hormuz remaining effectively closed for the next five months, and no permanent US-Iran peace deal until the new year.

The Treasury modelling for that scenario was that the UK economy would grow by 0.9% over 2026 - slightly under the 1.1% forecast by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March.

The prospect was much dimmer for next year, with just 0.3% growth projected - much lower than the OBR's 1.6% forecast for 2027.

Under the modelling, inflation would peak at 4.3% in the first three months of next year. It currently stands at 2.6%, just above the Bank of England's 2% target.

The prime minister and chancellor will face pressure to use the upcoming Budget on 28 October to ease the financial burden on households and businesses.

Since taking office three weeks ago, Burnham has announced policies including the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills and bringing forward an already planned end to "subscription traps".

But this week he told the BBC's Wake up to Money the announcements, aimed at tackling the cost of living, are not enough on their own, hinting at further support.

He has asked Healey to look at what more the government can do on the cost of living in the Budget, with the chancellor saying it will be his "main focus".

But Healey has said he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

Burnham has said his government will stick to the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase people's income tax, VAT or National Insurance contributions.

He also promised to follow the fiscal rules imposed by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

News.title: Eurovision Song Contest changes rules for countries at war
News.content:
Organisers of the Eurovision Song Contest have updated their rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year.

The amendment was approved by the contest's governing body, following feedback from participating broadcasters after Eurovision 2026 in Vienna.

It states that winning countries will also be disqualified from hosting if a "sensitive geopolitical situation" affects the "security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region".

The update will be interpreted as a reaction to Israel's continued presence at the contest, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East.

Last November, following a failed attempt to have Israel suspended, five broadcasters announced they were boycotting the competition - including Eurovision powerhouses Spain and Ireland.

Despite the protests, Israel's Noam Bettan ultimately took second place with his song Michelle.

It marked the second year in a row that Israel had taken the runners-up position - and some participating broadcasters have privately expressed safety concerns over the contest being staged in Jerusalem or Tel Aviv, should the country win in the future.

Although Israel will undoubtedly be seen as the target of the rule change, it will also affect Ukraine, which has been engaged in a protracted war since it was invaded by Russia in 2022.

Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra went on to win Eurovision that same year, in a symbolic show of public support.

Following their victory, Eurovision organisers undertook a "full assessment and feasibility study" to decide whether the 2023 contest could proceed in Kyiv.

They ultimately decided the security risks were too great, and the UK stepped in to host the competition in Liverpool.

News.title: Lucy Davis urges women to check their breasts for cancer - here's how
News.content:
Signs of breast cancer are not always a lump in the traditional sense, so what should you look for?

Actress Lucy Davis, who played Dawn Tinsley in the original UK version of the popular TV series The Office, has revealed she has incurable breast cancer.

On Instagram, external, the 53-year-old said it had spread to her bones and it was too late for chemo.

She added: "The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny."

Here's how to check yourself at home.

News.title: Ministers push ahead with housing asylum seekers on ex-military sites
News.content:
Home Office minister Anna Turley has said the government is sticking with plans to accommodate asylum-seekers on former military bases despite protests from local residents.

She told the BBC the government's priority was to ensure asylum-seekers were looked after in a "secure" and "appropriate" place.

That included disused Ministry of Defence properties because they had on-site facilities and were "more contained," she added.

But campaigners in areas earmarked for asylum centres have said small communities with limited infrastructure would not be able to cope with large numbers of people.

There have been protests in Piddington, Oxfordshire, over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers at a site near the village.

Mike Nixon, the vice-chairman of Piddington Parish Council, said there was a "huge amount of concern and worry" among residents and that an asylum centre would have a "dramatic effect" on the way they lived their lives.

The proposal has prompted Piddington to hold a symbolic independence referendum, asking its 400 or so residents if they want to remain part of the UK.

Nixon said: "We're still very frustrated. Andy Burnham did say that he's willing to listen, but we've had no formal contact. No consultation, nothing from the Home Office.

"We felt that the only way of making our views felt was to say 'well if we're not going to be listened to, what's the point of being a part of the country?'"

The government has promised to end the use of hotels for asylum seekers, announcing on Wednesday that a further 13 across England had been closed.

It plans to use former military sites instead with two already up and running - RAF Wethersfield in Essex, and Crowborough Training Camp in East Sussex.

In June, it announced proposals to open three more, including the site near Piddington.

The two other planned sites are a former RAF base in Barnham in Suffolk where there were protests last week and RAF Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire where the area's Labour mayor said it was "simply the wrong place".

Defending the proposals on BBC Breakfast, Turley said the public wanted the government to end the use of hotels, pointing to how an "iconic" hotel in Blackpool, the Metropole, was no longer being used to accommodate asylum-seekers.

She said it sent "an important message" that the government wanted the hotel to be part of Blackpool's future.

"The priority is to ensure we look after asylum seekers in a secure place that is more appropriate and we limit the impact on communities."

Asked what she meant by secure, she said: "Examples we are looking at is former military bases and we have two up and running and possibly another three.

"They have have facilities on site and are more contained and it limits the impact on on communities.

"We are looking at other sites such as former industrial sites, student accommodation - accommodation that is more more appropriate than hotels."

News.title: Victim of fatal Clapham shooting named
News.content:
A man who was shot dead in south-west London has been named by police as Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa.

Officers and paramedics were called to Willington Road, Clapham, just before 22:00 BST on Monday following reports of gunshots near The Landor pub.

The 25-year-old, who worked as a bus driver, was pronounced dead at the scene, the Metropolitan Police said.

A 22-year-old man was later arrested on suspicion of murder after attending hospital with a gunshot wound on Tuesday. He remains in hospital under police guard.

Det Ch Insp Claire Guiver said her thoughts were with the victim's family as they "come to terms with this tragic incident".

News.title: Man bled to death after being bitten by American XL Bully, court hears
News.content:
A man died from extreme blood loss after suffering "catastrophic injuries" when he was bitten on the leg by an American XL bully in his daughter-in-law's garden, a court has heard.

Keven Jones, 62, from Chester, who was in poor health, taking methadone and blood thinning medication, was staying at Chanel Fong's house at the time of the incident.

The incident took place before XL Bullies were added to the banned dog list in October 2023.

Fong, 33, denies being the owner of the dog, which the prosecution said was dangerously out of control at the time, and also denies an alternative charge of being the person in charge of a dog at the time of the attack.

Opening the case at Caernarfon Crown Court, prosecutor Mark Connor said it was a "sad and tragic case for everyone concerned" and told the jury they would be shown some "graphic images" of Jones' injuries during the trial.

He said it was not a case of whether the XL Bully, named Cookie, was a banned breed, but rather that the dog had been "dangerously out of control" and whether Fong was legally responsible for it, either as its owner or the person responsible for it at the time.

The court was told the dog was owned by Fong and her partner, Joshua Jones, the son of the victim, but that he was not present at the time of the attack.

Connor added that, in her police interview, Fong said on paper Cookie belonged to her partner.

He went on to describe how there were a number of dogs at the property on Holt Road in Wrexham, including Cookie and another XL Bully called Fire, who were in the back garden at the time.

Cookie's mother, an XL Bully called Rogue, was inside the property and was "in season" meaning she had been kept separate from the other dogs in the house.

News.title: Estonia rejects proposals to take prisoners from UK jails
News.content:
The Estonian government has rejected the idea of taking prisoners from the UK to help ease the overcrowding crisis in British jails.

Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta told the BBC Estonia would not rent jail cells to other countries while it was housing criminals from Sweden in its half-empty Tartu prison under a deal signed last week.

The Conservatives and Reform UK have both suggested renting cells in foreign prisons, including in Estonia, to free up space and prevent the early releases of some offenders in England and Wales.

The Labour government also explored the idea in 2024 but talks with Estonia came to nothing.

Pakosta said Estonia had received no proposals to rent its prison space from the UK, adding that if one was to be made "our answer would be unequivocal - in Margaret Thatcher's famous words: No. No. No."

She added: "Such a proposal would not merely be mistaken, misguided or unacceptable; it would deserve to be rejected outright."

Thatcher memorably repeated "no" three times in 1990 speech, as she fiercely rejected calls for deeper political and economic integration of the European Community, which later evolved into the European Union.

In 2024, the Labour government, when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister, held talks with Estonia to discuss the Baltic state's policy to house some prisoners from abroad.

Pakosta previously told the BBC she had met then-UK Justice Secretary Shabana Mahmood in Lithuania.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government is planning to release thousands of prisoners early this October, as it scrambles to free up space in jails almost at 100% capacity.

On Monday, Downing Street did not rule out renting space in foreign prisons, when asked by reporters if the government was considering doing so.

A No 10 spokesperson said the government was focused on "creating that extra capacity within the system domestically".

"In terms of renting prison places abroad, it's just not a quick fix," the spokesperson added.

"It will require primary legislation underpinned by a complex international agreement which would take several years to agree."

A government source told the BBC that renting foreign prison space would not help with the short-term crisis in jails.

Burnham has ordered the justice secretary to come up with a plan to create more space in jails by September.

He said the plan would be based on removing more foreign national offenders from prisons, releasing some offenders on indefinite sentences, and using space in women's jails for male inmates.

News.title: Windermere signs to warn of algae poisoning risk
News.content:
Dozens of signs warning people about the dangers of algae poisoning are to be placed around England's largest lake.

About 40 notice boards alerting visitors to blue-green algae blooms, which can produce toxins that make humans ill and be fatal to pets, will be installed at Windermere, in the Lake District.

Blooms occur naturally but are more frequent during warm, dry weather and are exacerbated by nutrients from phosphate in pollutants such as sewage.

Funded by the Environment Agency (EA), a further 40 signs will be placed at other locations across Cumbria.

The Love Windermere Partnership, which includes organisations such as the EA, Lake District National Park Authority and United Utilities, said it was installing the permanent signs in response to requests for "clearer and more consistent public information".

As well as explaining what blue-green algae looks like, the notices will provide guidance on where to find current information about blooms and how to report suspected sightings using the Bloomin' Algae app, external.

The microscopic organisms can look like blue-green paint, scum or greenish-brown discolouration.

News.title: I share concerns over Arday appointment, says Cambridge University head
News.content:
The vice-chancellor of the University of Cambridge has said she understands the concerns raised by the appointment of Jason Arday and shares them too.

In a letter to staff, Prof Deborah Prentice acknowledged the "anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case".

The university head also announced Cambridge's investigation would be independent and carried out by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge and will begin "as soon as possible".

Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week amid allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements.

The 41-year-old - who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - denies any plagiarism and said the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

In a letter to university staff, Prof Deborah Prentice said: "I fully understand the concerns being raised across the University and well beyond it, regarding Jason Arday's appointment and I share them...

"We will now investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education back in 2022 and his time here in Cambridge since his appointment nearly four years ago.

"That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge."

The findings of the investigation, previously announced on Friday, will inform a review into the process for the appointment of senior academic roles, the university has said.

Prentice added "our staff of colour are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements, and the contributions they make" and said the case "should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge".

Cambridge had previously said allegations of plagiarism regarding Arday's thesis and some journal publications had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University (LMJU) and the journals in question.

LJMU - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated the allegations that were made last year, and found he did not commit plagiarism.

In an interview with the Times, Arday defended himself by arguing that he had not received adequate supervision during his PhD given his autism and "learning disabilities".

The University of Cambridge said it had advised people to contact the relevant institution or pass on complaints.

But after Cambridge announced its own investigation, some academics pushed for the inquiry to be independent, questioning whether the university could adequately investigate its own processes.

It is not yet clear how the independent investigation will work or who will lead it. The university said it will look at the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education in 2022 and his time in Cambridge since his appointment.

Arday worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at LMJU and going on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.

Glasgow has also announced a review into Arday's previous academic post.

When he resigned from his post, Arday said he was not a "liar" and that his resignation "should not be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

News.title: Early release scheme risks more serious crimes, probation chief inspector warns
News.content:
The chief inspector of probation for England and Wales has told the BBC the early release of thousands of prisoners could lead to "a serious sexual or violent offence or even murder" because of the demands on probation staff to monitor offenders.

The government is set to release 5,000 offenders from October as part of new laws to create more space in overcrowded prisons.

Probation officers supervise offenders after prison sentences and check they follow the terms of their release, such as sticking to curfews and not taking drugs.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said "protecting the public is our top priority", adding it had invested in probation and hiring trainee officers.

But Martin Jones, His Majesty's Chief Inspector of probation for England and Wales, told the BBC that "ultimately I'm not fully confident that the probation system will be able to cope with this massive work and there's a risk that things will go wrong".

"Probation services are already under unprecedented pressure.

"I mean, they're managing a caseload of 258,000 cases, that's nearly three times the number that are in our prisons, and obviously the early release scheme will be increasing that pressure considerably."

On Tuesday, 50 police chiefs across the UK signed a letter to the prime minister urging him to pursue "every legal option" to prevent the early release of PC Andrew Harper's killers under the scheme.

They called for called for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their sentences altered, adding: "Families across the country are now facing the distress of learning that offenders may be released earlier than they understood when sentence was passed."

They also welcomed Burnham's intervention on Tuesday, when he said he was "confident" the early release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were jailed for 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, in January could be stopped.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp told BBC Breakfast the early release plans had "put public safety at risk as well as disrespecting victims and undermining confidence in the criminal justice system".

He urged Burnham to "pay attention and listen" to the senior police officers, adding he had "never seen every chief constable in the country write to the prime minister directly in this way".

Philip and Nick Timothy, the Conservative shadow justice secretary, wrote to Burnham on Tuesday urging him to introduce emergency primary legislation in September to amend the Sentencing Act 2026.

The letter said grooming gang perpetrators, including those convicted of indecent assault, and those convicted of the manslaughter of an emergency worker should be exempt from the early release scheme.

News.title: Semi-pro footballer filmed driving at 191mph
News.content:
A semi-professional footballer who was filmed driving at 191mph has been jailed.

Connor Charlton, 32, was also involved in a scam where other drivers took penalty points for speeding offences in return for cash, the Crown Prosecution Service said.

The centre forward, who plays for Nostell Miners Welfare FC in the Northern Counties East League, was seen in footage drifting his BMW at a roundabout, almost crashing into a van. A passenger also filmed him driving at 191mph on a motorway.

Charlton, from Hunslet, was sentenced on Wednesday at Leeds Crown Court to four years in jail and banned from driving for four years and seven months.

He had admitted 10 counts of dangerous driving and four offences of perverting the course of justice.

Organisers of the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham remain confident of delivering a "special atmosphere", but have urged fans to buy tickets following criticism over empty seats.

Turnout at the Alexander Stadium has grown daily since the championships began on Monday after the opening morning brought 12,844 fans, with 13,623 present that night as Amy Hunt won the women’s 100m.

On Tuesday, 12,921 attended the morning session, before 16,208 watched Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu secure a British one-two in the men’s 100m final, but this was still some way off a full capacity, as the Birmingham venue holds approximately 23,000 people.

However, European Athletics issued a defiant statement on Wednesday which read: "We are seeing a truly outstanding European Championships, with athletes from the host country Great Britain and across Europe producing performances worthy of this stage – and there is so much more still to come.

open image in gallery Amy Hunt claimed 100m gold on the opening night ( PA Wire )

"Naturally, we would love to see a full stadium for every session, because nothing compares with the energy of a packed Alexander Stadium and the support it gives to the athletes.

"We are very pleased that demand for tickets to the second half of the championships is strong, and we want to encourage people to come and experience this incredible event for themselves.

"Championships have a way of building momentum as the days go by and we are confident Birmingham will continue to deliver that special atmosphere."

On Tuesday, the Birmingham26 local organising committee said it was "delighted" by ticket sales, adding: "(Sales) far surpassed our targets. Friday, Saturday and Sunday evening sessions are approaching sell-out, with several other sessions close to capacity."

open image in gallery Keely Hodgkinson will go for gold later this week ( PA Wire )

Yet social media criticism persisted on Wednesday, with onlookers blaming admission costs for the sparse crowds. The cheapest morning tickets from Monday to Wednesday were £10 for adults and £5 for children aged 2-16, while evening sessions began at £26.

Prices rise towards the end of the week as high-profile competitors take to the track, including British Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson and Swedish pole vault world record-holder Mondo Duplantis. The most expensive "category A" tickets cost £150 for Monday night and Thursday through Sunday evening.

Donald Trump has spent several days criticizing his top federal prosecutor in Washington, D.C., Jeanine Pirro, after she dropped charges against a man accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in a stunning rebuke of the administration’s allegations against him.

Pirro’s job appeared to be on the line; the president has not confirmed whether he plans to fire her, and the White House has pressed her to deliver on cases that Trump wants to prosecute. He most recently urged her office to revive the case against David Hearn despite there being no evidence against him.

The former Fox News personality — who now answers to Trump’s former criminal defense attorney Todd Blanche after his confirmation as U.S. Attorney General this week — now appears to be leading a special grand jury that could be used to investigate the president’s political enemies, according to The Washington Post.

Pirro’s office has repeatedly failed to land criminal convictions in cases stemming from the Trump administration’s federal takeover of the nation’s capital and other politically charged cases. She is also now tasked with deciding whether to charge Dr. Anthony Fauci, another target among Trump’s allies, after House Republicans accused him of lying to Congress.

After repeatedly losing cases in D.C., the Trump administration could have a workaround in the form of Pirro’s office. With a rare and secretive special grand jury at the disposal of Trump’s Justice Department, Pirro’s office could be used to draft damaging reports about Trump’s critics, including current and former Democratic officials.

open image in gallery US Attorney for Washington DC Jeanine Pirro is reportedly convening a special grand jury, which typically investigate organized crime and wider conspiracy cases, including government corruption ( Getty )

The subject and scope of the special grand jury’s inquiry is unclear. The Independent has requested comment from Pirro’s office and the Justice Department.

“We don’t confirm or deny the existence of investigations,” a spokesperson for Pirro’s office told The Independent.

But special grand juries are typically convened to investigate wider conspiracies and organized crime, including corruption among government officials.

Unlike a typical grand jury, a special grand jury could release a damaging report after an investigation, even if prosecutors fail to develop evidence to bring a case to a trial, and giving Trump valuable political ammunition.

The 23-person body needs only to show a “preponderance of evidence” to draft a report, which would need to be approved by a judge.

In D.C., that request would need to go before Chief Judge James Boasberg, who has overseen several high-profile cases targeting the Trump administration. Trump has demanded his impeachment.

A final report, like those from a special counsel, could then be used to implicate high-profile figures that Pirro’s office could not otherwise charge.

Critics fear those allegations could then be weaponized by Trump and his allies before midterm elections and the 2028 presidential election.

open image in gallery News of the alleged investigation follows Donald Trump’s ongoing criticism of the top prosecutor after she dropped charges against a man the president has accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool ( AFP/Getty )

According to The Post, the grand jury will be overseen by Steven Vandervelden, who previously led controversial investigations into now-former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell and D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department.

Pirro’s office is in the middle of a streak of losses. Grand juries in D.C. have repeatedly declined to indict people at the center of politically loaded cases, and juries at trial have also rejected the government’s efforts to prosecute protesters caught up in the administration’s military occupation of the capital.

But her motion to dismiss the case against Hearn, weeks after she publicly accused him of “forcefully and violently” ripping out the Reflecting Pool’s Trump-requested blue liner, has outraged the president, who has spent days disputing the lack of evidence that Hearn vandalized the monument.

In a court filing asking for charges to be dropped, Pirro’s office admitted that the sealant started to peel “almost immediately” after the work was completed It was not until after the indictment was filed that the Department of Interior determined that the “damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism,” according to Pirro.

Last week, the judge overseeing the case agreed to dismiss charges against him and will hold a hearing next month on whether the dismissal should be granted “with prejudice,” which would prevent the Justice Department from charging him for the same alleged conduct.

News.title: Ebola outbreak ‘doubling every 20 days’, warns UN chief
News.content:
Congo’s runaway Ebola outbreak is doubling in size every 20 days, according to the United Nations humanitarian chief, putting it on track to soon be the largest ever seen.

Three months after the outbreak was officially declared, the case load is expanding exponentially and many believe the true toll is far higher than recorded.

If cases continue to double at the same rate, the flare-up in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) will surpass the record West African outbreak sometime around the end of September.

Modelling by one health analytics firm already predicts there is a more than 90 per cent chance that the DRC will become the largest on record.

The two-year West African outbreak grew to more than 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths across Sierra Leone, Liberia and Guinea from late 2013 to 2016.

This year’s outbreak centred on the DRC province of Ituri has already seen 4,449 cases and 2,061 deaths in only a few months.

News.title: Madagascar forced to divide and share mpox vaccine as epidemic takes off
News.content:
Authorities in Madagascar are being forced to split single vaccines into fifths to try to protect as many people as possible during an ongoing mpox outbreak.

The method, known as “fractional dosing”, is authorised by the World Health Organization (WHO) in emergencies when there are critical vaccine shortages, but is not routinely recommended and carries a level of risk.

Madagascar, the African island with a population of roughly 33 million people, is currently battling its largest-ever outbreak of the virus formerly known as monkeypox, with at least 4,000 cases recorded so far.

Another one million people are thought to be at risk of contracting clade 1b mpox, a fast-spreading strain of the virus that emerged from the Democratic Republic of the Congo in late 2023.

High risk groups include sex workers, young children, and people living with HIV/Aids. Medical workers are also at risk.

“Public health authorities in Madagascar have been given too few doses to protect the at-risk population; they were initially given 30,000 doses in May, and a subsequent 30,000 have just arrived at the end of July,” said Akhil Bansal, a doctor of internal medicine working on the mpox response in Madagascar and a policy fellow at the Centre for Global Development.

“However, we need to vaccinate more than one million people, so we have been “fractionally dosing”, or splitting vaccines, into fifths, to stretch the supply as far as we can.

“This is a somewhat established approach for vaccines, but even then, the number of doses we have is insufficient,” said Dr Bansal.

News.title: Sudan exodus threatens humanitarian catastrophe in Chad
News.content:
Trapped in a desert encampment in Chad, Abakar Adam, 70, dreams of returning to his small farm in neighbouring Sudan, nearby to the village where he was born.

But Mr Adam can’t go home.

Hidden from sight, he watched soldiers set fire to his farmhouse and slaughter his livestock three years ago. One month later, after resettling in the city of El Geneina in West Darfur he heard 40mm grenades rain down on hospitals while patients fought for their lives inside and witnessed civilians executed in the street.

Shortly after, a bullet from the rifle of a Rapid Support Force (RSF) soldier ripped through his gut, and he recalls how he struggled to pull his daughter from the blood-soaked sand after her eye was gouged out by a militiaman during their escape from Sudan.

Now, sitting outside his rotting, wooden shelter in eastern Chad, just 20 miles from the border with Sudan, he tells The Telegraph that he can’t forget the faces of the blind and disabled who he witnessed being thrown onto piles of hay and burnt alive.

Adam’s story is not unique and the refugee camp where he finds himself with tens of thousands of others is on the brink of collapse.

News.title: Telegraph Fantasy Football 2026/27: Everything you need to know and FAQs
News.content:
What’s new for 2026/27?





You’ll need to re-register

When signing up to Telegraph Fantasy Football this season you will notice your old logins do not work.

New for this season you will need to register, or login to an existing, telegraph.co.uk account to play.

NOTE: you do not need to subscribe in order to play Telegraph Fantasy Football - it is free to play.

Having trouble making a new account or logging in to an existing telegraph.co.uk account? Click here and look at our troubleshooting guide that can guide you through the process.



We’ve had a makeover and Leagues have moved

Over the summer we changed game provider meaning the site was built again from scratch. We hope you like the new look and feel.

We know nobody likes change, but take your time to get to know the new layout as some aspects of the site may have moved slightly.

The most notable change is that Leagues are now created and joined below your team selection.



Back to basics

With such a short space of time to get the TFF live for this season, the game has been stripped back to basics.

You’ll notice there are no Public Leagues and no prizes for Weekly and Monthly Leaderboard winners. Assistant Manager has also not been integrated for launch.



The Fixture Tracker

Whilst the game has been stripped back to basics, you’ll notice a new fixture tracker above your team selection. This is there to help you make transfer decisions and we hope you like it.

When you see a + in the tracker it indicates how many other games start at that time.



No rule changes.

Whilst some things may have changed, the rules remain unchanged.

Telegraph Fantasy Football is fantasy football at its purest. No gimmicks, no boosts, no captains. Simply pick the best XI players you can.



Assists

However, one exception is this season assists will no longer follow Opta’s “Fantasy Assist” definition and revert back to standard assists.



Did you miss it? League Cup fixtures and five more transfers

In case you missed it last year, this season will also feature League Cup fixtures meaning all competitive domestic football containing Premier League fixtures will count towards your Telegraph Fantasy Football points tally.

Why the change? Well for years the general advice early in the season is to hold onto your transfers and we thought that was getting a bit stale. With League Cup fixtures starting as early as Game Week 3 some seasons, you’d be a fool not to take advantage of some fixture gains against lower-league opposition.

To help with the additional fixtures we have also added five more transfers to your season total.



Paid leagues are no more

Unfortunately Plucky Paid Leagues are not integrated this season.



Three new teams

Ipswich are no strangers to Telegraph Fantasy Football as they both return from relegations in 2025. They bring with them a host of talent including two big names you might recognise, including Jaden Philogene (£2.9m) and Leif Davis (£2.6m).

It has been a fair few years since Hull City (2016/17) and Coventry City (2000/01) last featured in Telegraph Fantasy Football - memories may even flood back of posting in your transfers for the Sky Blues’ players. Both clubs are favourites to go down, but with some exciting signings like Tzolakis (£2.5m) and Thomas-Asante (£2.7m) they will certainly put up a fight.

Start creating your team >



FAQs





When does Telegraph Fantasy Football start?

The 2026/27 edition of Telegraph Fantasy Football will launch in the two weeks leading up to the start of the Premier League. The scoring will commence on Friday August 21, 2026 at 8pm when the Premier League champions Arsenal host Coventry.



How do I register for Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You will need to create a new, or use your existing telegraph.co.uk account in order to play Telegraph Fantasy Football. Simply click “SIGN UP”, then “Continue with Telegraph” and you will be temporarily taken to telegraph.co.uk to login with your existing Telegraph account or create a new account, before automatically returning back to the Telegraph Fantasy Football site.

Note: this account is not the same as your account from previous Telegraph Fantasy Football seasons.

Having trouble making a new account or logging in to an existing telegraph.co.uk account? Click here and look at our troubleshooting guide that can guide you through the process.



How much does it cost to play Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Telegraph Fantasy Football is completely free to play. All managers compete for the £5,000 prize pool as well the chance to challenge friends, family, colleagues and fellow managers in private mini-leagues.



How many players can I pick in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You only have to pick a squad of XI players in Telegraph Fantasy Football. With no bench to rely on, finding players who get minutes on the pitch is key and we help you out there by allowing transfers right up until every kick-off.



How many teams can I pick in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You can create up to five teams in Telegraph Fantasy Football with a budget of £50m for each, meaning you have a better chance of being in contention for the prizes come the end of the season if some of your selections prove to be unsuccessful.



How many transfers can I make in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Up until the first game on Friday August 21, 2025, there is a transfer amnesty, meaning you can make as many changes as you like. After the season has started you have 45 transfers for the whole campaign with a maximum of five per Game Week (00:00 Tuesday to 23:59 Monday).





How do I join a private league in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Leagues have now moved below your team selection.

This should make it easier for managers to see which league the team is in that they are making changes to.

To join a league click “Join a league” and then add the 6 digit code that the League Chairman will have access to.

To create a league click “Create a league”, name the league and then copy the league code generated to share with your fellow managers.

League Chairmen will have the ability to lock and unlock a league to new joiners.



Do ALL Cup games count in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Yes. All League Cup fixtures plus all FA Cup games involving Premier League sides count towards your TFF points tally. This adds a great dimension to the game as you will want to load your teams with players who make the latter stages for an advantage over your competitors. However, one thing to note is that penalty shoot-outs do not count towards your score.



How many players are in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You can expect to compete against more than 100,000 other teams in Telegraph Fantasy Football – a vast but tight-knit community of players where you have every chance of winning one of our many prizes on offer throughout the year.

We aim to include every player in a squad who has a chance of getting some game time. From time to time we may miss a youngster on debut, but rest assured they will soon be added to the player list and feel free to let us know on Facebook or Twitter if you feel someone is missing.

Having technical issues with TFF? Check our Troubleshooting page for help.



What else do I need to know?



Get your strategy right. Getting the balance of your team right can be a tricky business, especially with limited funds, but there are a few tried and trusted methods that will stand you in good stead:



Pick regular starters

Okay, so this isn’t always straightforward in the world of squad rotation where world-class players routinely find themselves sitting on the bench. That said, there are certain players who, if fit, are almost always the first name on the team sheet. Think Bruno Fernandes at Manchester United, Jordan Pickford for Everton and Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk.



Find a couple of budget ‘gems’

Igor Thiago, Nico O’Reilly and James Garner were among a crop of players who began last term in the ‘unfancied’ category and were must-have ‘enablers’ by the time the season was over. If you’re able to identify one or two of this type of player early in the season, you could be on to a winner.



Be transfer savvy

We’ve all been there – you spend hours selecting your team for the big kick-off then half of them don’t start, the other half have stinkers and your star striker gets a season-ending injury. If you do get off to a slow start, don’t panic. Lurching from one strategy to another could do more harm than good, wasting precious transfers in the process. Trust your instincts, tweak where necessary and the points will come.



Read our weekly Selection Guide

The best advice comes from experts at the Fantasy Football Hub who make our weekly selection guide a prolific source of Telegraph Fantasy Football tips and Telegraph Fantasy Football match facts.

If you subscribe to the weekly newsletter this will hit your inbox on Friday around lunchtime; alternatively it can be found on our social channels or Telegraph Fantasy Football content hub.



Telegraph Fantasy Football Player List

We aim to keep our player list up to date with all comings and goings in the transfer window and the first place to look is our trusted Stats Centre. However, if you fancy yourself as a bit of a Telegraph Fantasy Football expert like the team at Fantasy Football Hub, you can find a player list below in a spreadsheet format so you can do your own analysis.

On the document simply click “file”, then “make a copy” and you will have your own version of the player list at that time to edit as you please.



Download the Telegraph Fantasy Football App

Never miss a chance to make a transfer and download the Telegraph Fantasy Football App which is available on iOS and Android.

News.title: Telegraph Fantasy Football: transfers explained and top transfer tips
News.content:
As the new Telegraph Fantasy Football season approaches, the fantasy football experts at Fantasy Football Hub will continue to bring you the very best in fantasy football knowledge, tips and tools to help you rise up the ranks and win your mini-leagues.

To join the Hub and get access to all their great resources and expert tips you can take advantage of its 50% pre-season discount here.



Transfers explained



A good place to start is by explaining the Telegraph Fantasy Football rules on transfers. First thing to note is the pre-season transfer amnesty, so you can make unlimited changes to your teams right up until the first scheduled kick-off on Friday 21 August, 20:00.

45 is the magic number of transfers you receive during the season, five more than last season to help negotiate the new League Cup fixtures. This equates to a little more than one a week. You can use a maximum of five transfers in any Game Week which run from 00:00 on Tuesdays to 23:59 on Mondays.

Four seasons ago we scrapped the two-hour rule, meaning you can make transfers right up until a game kicks off. However, we don’t suggest you leave it that late as if a transfer is not completed in time you will not gain any points for the game from the player transferred in. Starting XIs are released an hour before kick-off so you have an ample window to implement any changes.

Scrapping the two-hour rule also means that this year you can be more flexible with your transfers each week. Once a player’s game has started you will amass their points for the entire game and are free to transfer them out for another player who may be kicking off while the previous game is being played, thus benefiting from two players’ points.



Top transfer strategy tips



1) Utilise fixture gains



Telegraph Fantasy Football is unique amongst other fantasy games in that you can transfer a player out as soon as they’ve played for a player yet to play that day or match week. So if Haaland (£8.3m) played in the 12.30pm Saturday kick-off, managers can transfer him out for Saka (£6.0m) who plays in the 3pm kick-off, and score points for both. Picking up extra fixtures each time a transfer is made is key to TFF success.



2) Find enablers early and stick



To fit in a combination of Erling Haaland (£8.3m), Bruno Fernandes (£6.5m) and Cole Palmer (£6.2m) or similar, requires TFF managers to find cheaper players to balance teams. Finding those players early into the season, and sticking with them to utilise transfers on the other strategy tips, can ensure avoiding wasting transfers on constant restructuring of squads.



3) FA Cup and League Cup (new for 2025/26)

Players in TFF gain points for the League Cup and FA Cup as well as the Premier League, so often players topping points charts at the season end have progressed far in the competition. When seeing lineups for early League Cup and FA Cup Rounds, if big hitting players who are regulars in the league start against lowly opposition, it’s a prime opportunity to stock up on those assets.

New for this season League Cup fixtures have been included which will make the early stages of the season even more exciting when Premier League teams who are not competing in Europe will gain a fixture against the rest.



4) Favourable fixture runs

Picking players who are playing against weaker opposition often score more points, therefore keeping an eye on the fixtures for teams is important.



5) Balance transfers out over the season

There are ~37 gameweeks in the season, so averaging around one transfer a week is a rule of thumb that keeps managers from running out early. The start of the season is the only time your team is reset, so it’s important to set a structure that works for you so that you don’t need to use too many moves at the start to identify those players who are likely to shine. It’s a marathon, not a sprint, so keeping pace early isn’t a necessity, and often keeping a few extra back until the end run sees TFF managers get a late boost.
