World.title: Burnham chairs crisis meeting as UK swelters in extreme heat
World.content:
A Downing Street spokesperson said: “We know how challenging this summer is proving, particularly for firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units.

“We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies, support farming communities and safeguard the environment.”

Britons are this week bracing for their fifth heatwave of 2026, with some temperatures forecast to exceed 36C. The Met Office, Britain's national weather service, has warned that this summer is set to be the U.K.'s hottest since records began.

More than two-thirds of England is now in drought after the driest July since records began in 1836. The whole of Wales is also in drought, and more than 27 million people across the U.K. are facing water restrictions including hosepipe bans.

The U.K. is grappling with wildfires including at the New Forest national park in south England. The National Fire Chiefs Council responded to 458 wildfires last month, its busiest month on record.

'Snail's pace'

The rival Green Party first demanded a COBR meeting weeks ago after a wildfire engulfed parts of Suffolk in eastern England. Green Leader Zack Polanski said Wednesday's meeting is “only a first step. This is a climate emergency which is leading to hundreds of deaths and stretching our firefighters, health staff and farmers to the limit. What we urgently need is concrete action.”

World.title: Who will miss the 12 August eclipse: geography, clouds or work
World.content:
Spain is already looking to the sky. Or at least, getting ready to. But not everyone in the country will see the same thing. The total solar eclipse on 12 August is, meteorologists and astronomers agree, a phenomenon that will literally split the country in two: those who will see the Sun disappear completely and those who will be left at the threshold.

 

Outside the path: Madrid, Barcelona and much of the south

The path of totality, the narrow corridor where the Moon covers the Sun 100%, crosses the peninsula from west to east and takes in capitals such as La Coruña, Oviedo, León, Bilbao, Zaragoza, Valencia and Palma. Outside that track, the rest of the country will see a partial eclipse, deeper or shallower depending on the distance from the central line.

Madrid and Barcelona are the two big absentees. The band passes right between the two cities, so residents will experience an afternoon with the Sun almost completely covered, up to 99% in some places, but without those few seconds of total darkness that turn the event into something unlike anything else.

Huesca and Zamora lie right on the edge of totality, meaning that the uneven lunar profile could make the key moment imperceptible to the naked eye. And the entire southern half of the peninsula will, quite simply, have to settle for a partial eclipse.

The enemy nobody can control: the clouds

Being in the right strip is no guarantee of anything if the sky does not cooperate. The Cantabrian coast, Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, has a meteorological track record that is not very favourable at this time of year, with clear-sky probabilities that in some analyses do not exceed 50%.

A solar eclipse in 2024 seen from Arlington, Texas (USA) AP Photo

The latest forecasts point to better chances in the west and interior of Galicia, Castile and León and the Balearic Islands, although the models can still shift up to the last minute. For anyone who has travelled hundreds of kilometres chasing totality, a poorly placed cloud on the western horizon can ruin in seconds what geography had granted them.

Those who will keep working as the sky goes dark

There is no special permit in Spain to leave your workplace during the eclipse, and labour legislation does not treat it as a force majeure event. So drivers, hospitality staff or construction workers on shift this afternoon will, in principle, continue their working day while everything around them stops to look up.

At most, the moment of totality, barely a minute or so in the best locations, can be fitted into the 15-minute break laid down in the Workers' Statute for working days of more than six hours, but that requires prior agreement with the employer.

The DGT, in fact, has set up a special operation in anticipation of traffic jams in the busiest areas, so a large part of road personnel will have a much busier afternoon than usual.

For safety, it is better not to look at it directly

Some people could watch it and choose not to, or should not. Ophthalmologists have been insisting for weeks that looking at the Sun without ISO 12312-2 certified glasses, not even for a few seconds, and not with normal sunglasses, X-ray films or homemade filters, can cause solar retinopathy: a burn on the retina that does not hurt, is not noticeable at the time and can take between 4 and 48 hours to appear as a dark spot in the centre of your vision.

The ONCE Social Group has distributed nearly two million certified glasses across the country precisely to avoid accidents, and ophthalmology societies recommend that young children in particular should not watch the event without an adult directly supervising them. Anyone without certified protection to hand really has two safe options: either not to look, or to watch it via a 'streaming'.

Watching the eclipse through binoculars is another option AP Photo

ESA will provide two live feeds. The first will be the official broadcast, produced from the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory in Teruel. It will include live interviews, explanations, images and information about eclipses, as well as live coverage of totality at 20:31. It will be in English and can be followed via ESA Web TV and YouTube.

ESA's second live feed will show images captured by telescopes, without commentary or explanations: just the eclipse live, also available on YouTube.

For its part, NASA will also offer its own streaming, starting at 19:15. The broadcast will show different views of the eclipse as it moves along its path and will include interviews with experts. It can be followed both on NASA's website and on YouTube, with links to different locations where totality can be observed, such as Iceland at 19:45 or Spain at 20:28.

A phenomenon you can listen to as well

For blind and partially sighted people, an eclipse has traditionally been a spectacle from which they were, by definition, excluded. That changes this year with the Inclusive Eclipse project, led by the CSIC research council, which is distributing LightSound devices at different viewing points around the country.

The device converts the intensity of sunlight into sound in real time: a tone that gradually fades and lowers in pitch as the Moon covers the solar disc, almost disappearing during totality. It is not the same as seeing it, but it is a way to follow the same moment that millions of people will be spending this afternoon looking up at the sky to share.

Those who do not want to watch it

Not everyone missing out on the eclipse this afternoon does so because they cannot watch it: some people simply prefer not to go out and look. In recent weeks, several hoaxes have circulated on social media mixing the event with conspiracy theories, from warnings about supposed neurological problems caused by observing it to the claim, without any scientific basis, that the Earth would lose gravity for seven seconds, attributed to a non-existent leaked NASA document.

Be especially careful with young children and with them taking off their glasses in the middle of the eclipse AP Photo

Fact-checkers have spent days dismantling these messages, but they keep being repeated, and some literally warn people "not to go out" during the eclipse. For part of the population, that constant murmur is enough to make them stay at home with the blinds down.

Then there are those who do not fear the event itself, but what surrounds it. Villages lying in the path of totality have seen an increase of more than 800% in tourism searches compared with a normal year, and many locals in those areas are already saying they will spend the afternoon away from the crowds, leaving the best spots to watch the Sun to the thousands of visitors who have ended up clogging roads and accommodation. For them, the eclipse is less an astronomical spectacle than an annual invasion they prefer to avoid.

World.title: Trump hails 'wall of steel' blockade, says US will keep control of Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that the United States is in control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz and will "keep it."

 

"The U.S.A. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!" Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform.

"Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, 'A WALL OF STEEL,' and there is nothing Iran can do about it."

Trump has repeatedly claimed the United States controls the strait, which is vital for the flow of energy and other commodity shipping through the Middle East.

However, Iran says it effectively controls much of the waterway and intends to impose a toll system in response to the US war launched by Trump on 28 February.

Late on Tuesday, Trump told reporters: "We have total control over the Hormuz Strait right now. They don't have control. We have total control. We own it."

A screenshot of a post on US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account, 12 August, 2026 @realDonaldTrump

US and Israeli forces have heavily bombed Iran's military and killed a swathe of the country's leadership so far in the nearly six month war, launched initially with goals including forcing Tehran to abandon its nuclear power programme and regime change.

Iran has resisted with missile attacks on US bases in the region, Israel and targets in US-allied Gulf countries.

Its most effective response has been to strike shipping in Hormuz, effectively snarling the trade route, rattling the world economy.

With his political popularity sinking at home ahead of the November midterm congressional elections, Trump has backed off threats to escalate the war in search of a decisive victory.

Residents swim as cargo and commercial vessels are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, 6 August, 2026 AP Photo

That leaves the war in a standoff.

However, the Republican says that the United States is prepared to focus on blockading Iranian ports in a strategy that he told Axios was "low-keying."

"We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," Trump told Axios on Sunday.

World.title: Grand Voyager | Exploring Switzerland and its wonders
World.content:
Set in the heart of Europe, Switzerland welcomes millions of international visitors each year. The Alps cover 60% of the country, which is also home to more than 1,500 lakes.

 

Lilly starts her journey in Zurich, Switzerland’s largest city, known for its charming Old Town and beautiful lake.

Her first stop is the Polybahn, a historic funicular that has been carrying passengers up the hillside for over a century. At the top, she takes in panoramic views of the city.

The viewpoint sits next to ETH Zurich, one of Switzerland’s most prestigious universities. A centre for science and technology, it once taught Albert Einstein.

Zurich is home to more than 1,200 fountains and numerous public gardens. One of them is Lindenhof Tree Court, an ancient hilltop public square considered to be the birthplace of the city.

Zurich is also closely linked to one of Switzerland's famous exports, Swiss chocolate. Inside Switzerland’s Chocolate Museum, Lilly visits the world's largest chocolate fountain and learns how to make her own chocolate creation.

After exploring the city, Lilly takes a boat across Lake Lucerne and checks into the historic Bürgenstock Resort. The Qatari-owned resort sits 500 meters above the lake and can be reached by a 150-year-old funicular.

Lake Lucerne covers more than 100 square kilometres and is surrounded by mountains. Here, Lilly follows one of the popular hiking trails famous for its dramatic views.

Switzerland is a country of rich heritage and stunning natural beauty. With Zurich’s historic Old Town and its nearby lakes and mountains, the country offers the perfect mix of culture and Alpine luxury.

World.title: Libyan Marshal Haftar's intelligence chief killed in Benghazi car bombing
World.content:
The head of military intelligence for the Libyan National Army (LNA) led by Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar has been killed in a car bombing in Benghazi, authorities confirmed on Tuesday.

 

Fawzi al-Mansouri was assassinated on Monday when an explosive stuck to his car detonated as he was leaving a local mosque at night, the statement said.

Al-Mansouri was a senior figure within the LNA's intelligence apparatus and had close ties to the Haftar family.

He played a key role in the LNA's campaign against jihadist groups, including the so-called Islamic State group (IS), between 2014 and 2017 in eastern Libya.

Al-Mansouri, whom the LNA described as a "heroic martyr," was also a leading figure during Haftar's 2019 offensive to seize the capital Tripoli in an operation backed by Russia and Egypt.

Haftar's offensive was eventually beaten back by forces loyal to the Tripoli government, which was in turn supported by Turkey.

Khaled Haftar, the son of Khalifa and LNA's chief of the general staff, said in a statement that an investigation was opened, adding that "indicators point to a despicable terrorist tactic".

"Terrorism is a project targeting the entire region, not just Libya," the statement added.

The bombing was a setback to efforts by the Haftars to paint a picture of stability in the areas they control.

"An attack of this sophistication in an LNA stronghold is also a major blow to the group's security credentials," analyst with UK-based Verisk Maplecroft Hamish Kinnear said.

"The intelligence required to target such a high-profile figure successfully is indicative of significant capabilities on the part of the responsible actor," Kinnear added.

Authorities have yet to identify the perpetrators.

Tripoli government condemns 'terrorist attack'

Libya has been split between rival administrations since NATO's intervention helped topple Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

Two governments are currently vying for power: the UN-recognised administration in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, and a rival administration in Benghazi backed by the elder Haftar, who is considered the de facto ruler.

Dbeibah has governed since 2021 following a UN-brokered political agreement but without a fresh electoral mandate, as a planned December 2021 election was cancelled amid disputes over candidate eligibility and the legal basis for the vote.

His government has faced sustained domestic opposition, including protests in Tripoli earlier this year over electricity cuts.

A former Gaddafi general and close ally who defected and lived in the US for nearly two decades before returning to Libya after 2011, Haftar built the LNA into the main force in the east and south.

FILE: Libyan army forces and vehicles are stationed in a street in the capital Tripoli, 22 July 222 AP Photo

The Tripoli-based government issued a statement denouncing a "terrorist attack" against al-Mansouri, saying it condemned the killing "regardless of one party's positions or alliances".

Khaled's office later said in a statement that authorities arrested a "terrorist cell in Benghazi that was preparing to carry out acts of sabotage" but did not say whether it was linked with al-Mansouri's killing.

Authorities in Benghazi held al-Mansouri's funeral on Tuesday afternoon, publishing photos that showed armed men in military fatigues with the attendance of senior LNA officials at the ceremony, including Khaled and Saddam Haftar.

In a statement, the LNA said it would "not cease fighting terrorism and will continue our struggle for the stability and security of Libya, as well as for the unification of its institutions".

US wants Saddam to take over Libya?

Libya holds Africa's largest proven oil reserves, which have fuelled both sides of the political divide.

Yet efforts remain under way to unify the country's executive powers under a Washington-mediated plan that the LNA has publicly backed.

Under the leaked terms of the plan, Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah would remain in charge of the Tripoli-based government while Lieutenant General Saddam Haftar — also Khalifa's son — would be elevated to a senior national executive role, possibly heading a unified presidential structure.

Saddam Haftar was appointed deputy commander-in-chief of the LNA in August 2025 as part of a restructuring that effectively distributed operational command among Khalifa's main heirs.

FILE: Deputy Commander of the LNA, Lt Gen Saddam Haftar looks on during his meeting with the Greek foreign minister in Athens, on Monday, 15 June 2026 AP Photo

"None of this bodes well for a US plan to re-unify Libya," Kinnear said, adding that under the roadmap, neither side "is likely to be satisfied with their respective positions for long".

"A new, destabilising power struggle could soon emerge."

Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui said the killing would "disrupt, or at the very least delay" the US-brokered deal.

"The agreement rests on two premises: that security reigns supreme in Benghazi, and that for senior officers, loyalty to Saddam (Haftar's son and heir apparent) guarantees protection in the Benghazi stronghold," Harchaoui explained.

But "a bomb that kills the head of military intelligence as he leaves a mosque undermines these premises," he said.

Meanwhile, reunification would "require some gestures of openness toward reform and change within the army", Harchaoui concluded.

World.title: Extreme heat: Half of Europe's population exposed to temperatures exceeding 30C
World.content:
Yet another heatwave has struck Europe, with more than half of the continent's population forecast to see temperatures of above 30 degrees Celcius on Wednesday, while areas home to at least 92 million will see temperatures over 35 degrees Celcius.

 

The most intense heat is expected across Western and Southern Europe, with France, Italy and Spain among the hardest-hit countries.

Much of Spain is under alert on Wednesday, with temperatures expected to climb above 35 degrees Celsius across the northwest to the southeast of the country.

Also in France, temperatures are expected to reach similar levels in some regions, while cooler conditions are forecast in the northeast and mountainous areas.

France recorded a 20% shortfall in its nuclear power generation capacity on Wednesday, with the record outage attributed to drought, extreme heat and a jellyfish invasion that clogged pumps used to cool the reactors, French newspaper Le Monde reported.

Boats lie on the dried riverbed at a tourist dock along the Po river during a drought in Torricella, Italy, Monday, Aug. 10, 2026. AP PhotoAP Photo/Antonio Calanni

According to experts, overfishing, plastic pollution and warmer waters linked to climate change have created conditions favourable to reproduction of jellyfish.

The heatwave also extends into the Balkans, particularly Greece and the Adriatic coast. Persistent high temperatures across the region have contributed to severe drought, placing strain on national energy systems, damaging crops and fuelling wildfires.

Wildfire warnings also continue to be in place for large parts of Scotland, several British media outlets report, as the UK government prepares to hold an emergency Cobra committee in response to the extreme heat.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham will chair the committee, which will mark the nation's second meeting of its sort this year after another one took place in June.

"Temperatures will rise quickly tomorrow, with many areas reaching 35°C+ and highs of 36-37°C possible, especially across the Midlands, east and southeast," the Met Office wrote on X, adding that an Amber Extreme Heat Warning has been activated.

The United Kingdom is on course to record its "warmest summer on record," according to the country's national weather service.

Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent and the first two months of summer have been marked by successive heatwaves, scorching temperatures and bone-dry conditions.

France and Spain have battled their worst infernos in living memory this summer, while other nations in Europe and as well as the US northwest and Canada have also experienced serious blazes.

Scientists warn the frequency of extreme fire-prone weather in Europe is increasing with climate change.

World.title: ‘The Office’ star British actor Lucy Davis reveals incurable cancer diagnosis
World.content:
Lucy Davis, best known for roles in British television series The Office, and films including 'Shaun of the Dead', 'Wonder Woman' and 'Chilling Adventures of Sabrina', shared the news in a lengthy Instagram post.

 

The 53-year-old actor said the cancer had spread to her bones, including her spine, right hip and ribs, and that it was too late for chemotherapy.

She said the first sign was not an obvious lump, but a very small hard spot that she almost decided not to have checked.

Davis also said she is not afraid of what comes next and feels at peace with her situation but acknowledged that the prospect of her death is harder for her family than it is for her, saying that any grieving is “for my family”.

The actor said she still hopes to continue working, describing acting as one of the biggest joys in her life.

World.title: Due to the Iran war, Iraq is running out of money
World.content:
Because of the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, Iraq cannot export enough oil to fund the country's huge public sector. Protests have already started. Will the Iran war destabilize Iraq again?

They may be thousands of kilometers away but the Strait of Hormuz — or more specifically, its blockade — is making life increasingly difficult for many ordinary Iraqis.

For the last three months or so, Mahmoud Waleed's salary has been arriving later and later. The 38-year-old teacher is paid by the Iraqi Ministry of Education, but because Iraq cannot export enough oil through the Strait of Hormuz, the government is running out of cash.

As a result, thousands of Iraqis like Waleed are not being paid on time.

"The delay affects you a lot," the Mosul local told DW. "Like most people, we have financial obligations as well as basic living expenses. We're just more and more convinced that we need to reduce expenses and keep some money aside for emergencies — just until things return to normal. It makes you really anxious and fearful."

"The future looks more uncertain," adds Ahmed, a doctor from the same city who didn't want to give DW his full name for personal reasons. "This month, our salaries were delayed by more than 10 days. The Minister of Health explained the state doesn't have sufficient cash flow and that's why there was a delay. But we just don't know how long the next delay will be."

In early August, there were a number of small demonstrations about the delayed salaries. Staff from universities around the country protested as did employees at the Ministry of Electricity.

Before the war, Iraq was the fourth largest oil producer in the world, sitting behind sector heavyweights like Saudi Arabia and the US Image: Nabil Al-Jurani/AP Photo/picture alliance

Why doesn't Iraq have cash for salaries?

Almost all of Iraq's national budget, somewhere between 85% and 90%, comes from the export of its oil.

At the same time, Iraq has a huge and growing public sector, with about two-thirds of the around 30 million working-age Iraqis relying on the state for their livelihoods. That's why the majority of the state budget now goes towards salaries, pensions and social welfare; every month the Iraqi government needs somewhere between $6.5 billion and $8.2 billion for those payments.

But recently that money has become much harder to find.

Since Israel and the US bombed Iran in late February, Iran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz. Almost all of Iraq's oil — between 80% to 90% — was shipped out through there because unlike other countries in the region, Iraq doesn't have significant alternative routes.

As a result of the blockade, Iraqi oil exports decreased by around 83% in March, compared to the same period last year. By May, Iraq's seaborne crude exports were down 97%.

This means Iraq's national income has also been severely reduced. Government sources told various local media that Iraq's monthly income in May and June was somewhere between $2 billion and $2.3 billion, far less than is needed.

Iraq has also had to deal with much higher costs for shipping and insurance Image: Hussein Faleh/AFP

It's that kind of news that recently led to panicked rumors that state salaries would only be paid every 45 days, instead of each month.

Over the past few days, the Iraqi government put out several statements , firstly denying the 45-day rumor and then saying it still had $83 billion in reserves, plus gold holdings and non-oil income. This means salaries can be paid for the next 10 to 11 months, it said on Tuesday.

However that might not be enough. A report by UK advisory firm Oxford Economics this week noted that maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is unlikely to return to normal anytime soon.

"Until at least 2028, traffic levels are expected to fluctuate as tensions ebb and flow, while on average remaining well below pre-conflict norms," Ben May, director of global macro research said in a statement.

This is a serious crisis, one which "transcends the oil sector," Iraqi economist Ali Al-Rawi argued in an August report for Baghdad-based think tank the Al Bayan Center. "The entirety of the Iraqi economy is now hostage to… oil revenues."

In the first half of the year, new vehicle sales fell 28.6% in Iraq, reflecting the impact the cash crisis is having on the whole economy Image: Khalil Dawood/Xinhua/picture alliance

Iraq destabilized?

None of the state employees DW spoke to were planning to attend protests if their salaries were delayed again.

And right now, this situation is unlikely to destabilize Iraq, Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow at the British think tank Chatham House told DW.

"If salary delays continue, I would expect more protests, but initially they are likely to remain sectoral rather than develop into another nationwide movement like Tishreen," al-Shakeri said, referring to huge youth-led, anti-government protests between 2019 and 2021. "The government has learned from 2019 and now has a range of political, administrative and security mechanisms to contain protests before they broaden."

Things could get more dangerous later though if a combination of different problems arise, some of which have sparked larger protests in the past.

"If salary delays are combined with electricity shortages, inflation and deteriorating services over a sustained period, these separate protests could begin to connect," al-Shakeri predicts. "At that point, Iraq's recent stability would face a much more serious test."

What can Iraq do?

Iraq has tried to work around its Strait of Hormuz problem. A small proportion of Iraqi oil is exported via a Turkish pipeline. Oil has also been trucked out of Iraq, then loaded onto ships at Syrian ports. Last week, the Iraqi government announced it was reviving a long-shuttered Iraq-Lebanon pipeline.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi also said that when he visited Iran in late July, he asked Iranian officials for special dispensation allowing Iraqi oil to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The two countries have a good relationship.

Far more important, experts say, is that the new Iraqi government finally implement realistic reforms, measures that reduce corruption and encourage the private sector, moving the country away from oil dependency and offering locals jobs outside of the civil service.

But reforms also require funding — and the latest statistics indicate that this is not what is happening, researchers at economic consultancy Iraqi Horizons wrote this month.

In May, total government expenditure fell by around a quarter compared to last year. Of that, money for salaries, pensions and social security accounted for 99% of all operational spending. Which means there's very little cash left for anything else, the consultants pointed out.

"Fiscal crises have pushed Iraqi governments towards reform before," al-Shakeri from Chatham House suggested. "When oil revenues fall, governments become more willing to discuss combatting corruption, increasing non-oil revenues and supporting the private sector. But once oil money begins flowing again, the political incentives for reform weaken."

The current crisis could create an opening for reform in Iraq, al-Shakeri concluded. "But whether those openings survive once the immediate pressure eases is the real question."

World.title: Mozart tribute ends on sour note after mass figurine theft
World.content:
A playful tribute to Mozart has turned into a whodunit after 210 gold-colored figures disappeared from one of Austria's busiest tourist spots. The mass theft forced organizers to end the outdoor display early.

More than 200 gold-colored Mozart figures have vanished from a public art installation in Salzburg, forcing organizers to end part of the exhibition early.

The theft has disrupted a major public art project marking the 270th anniversary of composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's birth in his home city.

What do we know about the theft of the mini-Mozarts?

The Mozarteum Foundation said 210 of the 320 figures installed in the city's Mirabell Garden had disappeared. The theft forced organizers to end the garden display early.

Organizers had kept some replacements in reserve, but not enough to offset the scale of the theft.

The manufacturer is also on summer holiday, leaving no quick way to replace them.

Several dozen figures remain on display at the Mozarteum and Mozart's birthplace until the end of August.

The figures had been placed in the Mirabell Garden and at several Mozart-related sites around Austria's fourth-largest city.

German artist Ottmar Hörl said he thought the theft was cheeky, and organized Image: Matthias Schrader/AP Photo/picture alliance

The polymer figures show Mozart with his dog Pimperl, a nod to the composer's everyday life in Salzburg.

German conceptual artist Ottmar Hörl, who is behind the display, said he wanted to show Mozart not as a monument but "as a normal human being despite his genius."

Who might have taken the mini-Mozarts?

Hörl is known for installations made up of large numbers of identical figures depicting famous personalities.

"The worst thing for an artist is when his work dissolves," Hörl said.

Hörl said he did not believe tourists had simply walked off with the 50-centimeter (20-inch) figures.

"This is organized theft," he said, suggesting they were probably taken at night after the garden had closed. "I find it a bit cheeky."

Hörl had planned to sell the figures after the exhibition for around €90 each, putting the loss at roughly €20,000.

A previous Hörl display in Bayreuth suffered a similar fate when 100 figures of composer Richard Wagner disappeared.

"That's just the nature of public space," Hörl said. "When you work as an artist in a public space, you mustn't complain about what is happening there. It ranges from destruction to theft. That’s just how it is."

World.title: Germany: More power for the intelligence agencies
World.content:
German intelligence agencies have been calling for more powers in the fight against cyberattacks, terrorism and extremism. Now the government has given the go. Critics warn that red lines are being crossed.

The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (Bundesverfassungsschutz, BfV) and the Federal Intelligence Service (Bundesnachrichtendienst, BND) are secret services. Both operate covertly — the former domestically, the latter abroad. They have long complained that they have fewer powers than their counterparts in other countries.

To better defend Germany against internal and external threats, the cabinet approved a draft bill on Wednesday. Parliamentary approval is still pending; the MPs' summer recess ends in early September. However, it is considered a mere formality that the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, with the government majority of conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) and center-left Social Democrats (SPD), will give it the green light.

Germany's largest intelligence reform since World War II

A new era for the German intelligence services is then expected to begin in early 2027. Their scope of operations would extend far beyond their current powers. It would then be possible, for example, to counter a cyberattack by neutralizing enemy IT systems.

What is cyber warfare? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Should a state of tension or military defense arise, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) could carry out acts of sabotage abroad. In addition, the BND, like the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, would be given the ability to manipulate or delete data. Proponents and opponents alike agree that this reform would be the largest in German history since the end of World War II in 1945.

Intelligence services and police: Will they remain separate?

After World War II, as a lesson learned from the atrocities committed by the Secret State Police (Gestapo) during the Nazi era, separate areas of responsibility were established in West Germany. Since then, intelligence services have been primarily responsible for gathering information, while the police handle threat prevention and law enforcement. This so-called principle of separation is now in jeopardy.

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) speaks of "real intelligence agencies" and hopes that the planned reform will result in a more stable security architecture.

"Sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks and covert operations by foreign powers require new responses," Dobrindt said.

The agencies would be granted operational capabilities and active powers to effectively combat modern state terrorism and extremist violence.

AI and drones: Possibilities and Risks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Is the draft bill unconstitutional?

The BND and the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution are also set to be granted new powers in their traditional core mission of collecting and analyzing information. These include the analysis of large volumes of data using artificial intelligence (AI) and the cross-referencing of biometric data with the internet. Data retention periods are also set to be extended.

The Society for Civil Rights (GFF) considers large parts of the federal government's draft bill — which spans more than 700 pages — to be unconstitutional. With regard to the domestic intelligence service, the far-reaching access to private and public video surveillance in real time is seen as particularly problematic, GFF expert Kai Dittmann replied in response to a written inquiry from DW.

The donation-funded nonprofit GFF believes the same applies to biometric matching against publicly available images on the internet and the training of AI using data collected by intelligence agencies.

"There are no sufficient and clearly defined limits for such far-reaching intrusions, which above all affect countless innocent people," Dittmann criticizes.

The GFF argues the planned additional powers for the BND would violate constitutional rights: The foreign intelligence service would no longer be limited to gathering intelligence, but would also be tasked with warding off threats, operating domestically and carrying out active cyber operations.

"This blurs the constitutional boundaries between intelligence services, the police and the military," Dittmann says.

Germany's spy chief believes US cooperation will continue To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Will there still be parliamentary control?

The GFF also has serious concerns regarding the proposed reform of intelligence agency oversight, which is to be consolidated under the Independent Oversight Council. At the same time, there are plans to largely strip the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) of its authority to oversee intelligence activities. Dittmann's conclusion: "The agencies are gaining significantly more power, while oversight is likely to be weakened."

Clara Bünger, the domestic policy expert for the opposition socialist Left Party in the Bundestag, echoes this sentiment: "Because the intelligence agencies will no longer be required to inform those affected in many cases, effective legal protection is no longer guaranteed."

Bünger announced that the Left Party will oppose what they see as authoritarian restructuring of the state. "There must never again be a secret police in Germany," she said.

The Association of the Internet Industry (eco) has also expressed concerns: In light of the changing security landscape, intelligence agencies need modern technical capabilities, emphasizes board member Klaus Landefeld.

"But the line is crossed when the state develops an interest in keeping security gaps open so it can continue to have access. Vulnerabilities must be closed and must not become a tool for intelligence agency access," Landefeld added.

Meanwhile, Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the Parliamentary Oversight Committee for the Intelligence Services, has no such concerns.

"I believe it's time to trust our own government, including our own security agencies," the Christian Democrat said in a Table Media podcast.

Germany has the best-regulated intelligence services in the world, he said, and that should remain the case.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Eritrea: An emerging key player in the geopolitical gamble at the Horn
World.content:
Amid growing tensions and security risks at the Horn of Africa, Eritrea, with its strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea and a perceived lack of conflict, is emerging as important player in the region.

Across the Horn of Africa, geopolitical interests of various countries continue to cause tensions and conflict as part of the growing competition for political influence over the region.

In its own right, the small country of Eritrea appears to be gaining in importance within this context: The autocratic state run by long-standing ruler Isaias Afewerki controls strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea, especially with its ports of Assab and Massawa.

In July, a series of diplomatic consultations in Cairo involving regional powers like Egypt, Somalia, Eritrea, and a high-ranking US envoy highlighted Eritrea's growing role in helping to coordinate approaches to resolving serious security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea, and to facilitate trade.

Eritrea's unique location along this maritime route is notably becoming more and more strategic in light of international trade conflicts. The small nation's coastline near the Bab-al-Mandab Strait stretches for more than 1,000 kilometers (621.4 miles), bordering Sudan to the northwest and Djibouti to its southeast.

But Eritrea's main strategic importance relies on who is on the other side of the strait, which at its narrowest point measures fess than 30 kilometers.

A small country at a strategically important location

"Yemen lies on the other side of the Red Sea, which makes Eritrea's location particularly interesting, as Yemen is in a state of crisis and maritime security in the region is at risk," Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration (CRI) in London, told DW.

"The only safe route in this area runs through Eritrea, where there are currently no security concerns."

Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki has been ruling the country since its independence in 1993 as a strict one-party authoritarian regime Image: Khalil Senosi/AP Photo/picture alliance

The Houthi terrorist militia, propped up by Iran, have been attacking merchant ships in the Red Sea from the Yemeni coastline.

For the past ten years, Yemen has also been witnessing one of the world's worst humanitarian crises in its midst: Ongoing violence, economic collapse, droughts and floods have exacerbated the suffering in the country, according to a report published by the UN Refugee Agency last month.

Sayed meanwhile emphasizes that in Eritrea, the strong dictatorship entrenched for decades does not tolerate any type of dissent. In many international freedom indexes, the African nation often only comes second to North Korea.

Since the country was officially founded 32 years ago, there have been no elections in the one-party state under long-time ruler Afewerki.

A unique sense of stability — for now

But this is also exactly why there are no violent conflicts in the country. Compared to other players in the broader region like Ethiopia, Sudan, and Yemen, Eritrea appears to be an island of peace where it is easy to do business.

"For this reason, all countries — including regional powers such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt, which controls the Suez Canal — want to maintain stable relations with Eritrea," Sayed highlights.

At the same time, this could eventually prove to be the country's Achilles' heel: "The country is ruled by a single man, and there are no constitutional institutions. That makes the state very vulnerable should this strongman be removed from power," says Sayed.

There is no strong figure in the 80-year-old autocrat's inner circle seen as a clear successor. This has raised some concern that the security situation could collapse once the president might no longer be in power, according to Sayed.

This sailor from Yemen's internationally recognized government is in charge of controlling activity on the Red Sea Image: Khaled Ziad/AFP

Alternative to the Strait of Hormuz

Still, Eritrea continues to exert its influence as the Red Sea has now emerged as one of the the most important sea route in the world, especially for the Gulf states — Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, according to Sayed.

The war with Iran has further reinforced the nation's position, as this crisis has once again showed the central geopolitical importance of maritime chokepoints such as Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb.

One viable alternative, should the Strait of Hormuz remain repeatedly blocked, would be for these Gulf nations and their partners to find routes via Saudi ports located further up on the Red Sea.

While the Saudis have pipelines running from some of the interior regions of the country from where oil is extracted and produced to the port of Yanbu-Al-Bahr on the Red Sea, this alternative route could easily be compromised when it comes to security, potentially driving up oil prices even higher than what they currently are.

"For this reason, Eritrea today is of great strategic importance. This has been the case for centuries and will continue to be the case," Sayed emphasizes.

Why Ethiopia seeks control over Assab port To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ethiopia demands direct Red Sea access

Meanwhile, Eritrea's neighbors, particularly landlocked Ethiopia, are fighting hard to maintain access to the Red Sea as a trade route, Sayed adds, in particular for oil exports from the Horn of Africa to the rest of the world, especially to Europe and the Americas.

For decades, Djibouti has dominated regional trade logistics as Ethiopia's most important seaport partner, while Eritrea has been sidelined economically.

But Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has for years been demanding sovereign access to the sea — more than three decades after the country's split with Eritrea: when Eritrea gained its independence in 1993, Ethiopia lost its direct access, and has since been relying on its neighbors for all its sea trade.

However, maintaining a sense of neutrality and balance is proving to be a walk on a tightrope: Earlier 2026, the fragile relations with between Ethiopia and Eritrea's Asmara region had already threatened to escalate amid a dispute over Ethiopia's access to the maritime trade route.

Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The key context for Eritrea's recent strategic maneuvers in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea is the escalating tensions with Ethiopia," says Michael Woldemariam, a researcher at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland and the Atlantic Council.

"Asmara is seeking to forge partnerships that can serve as a counterweight to Addis Ababa. Its recent diplomatic outreach to Egypt, Somalia, the United Arab Emirates' armed forces, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopian opposition groups, and even the US should be viewed against this backdrop," he tells DW.

Meanwhile, a new trade corridor on the Red Sea is also taking shape: In May 2026, Eritrea and Egypt signed an agreement to establish direct freight connections between Egyptian and Eritrean ports on the Red Sea in order to expand independent trade and supply chains in the region.

A grave record of human rights violations

Still, there are no longterm guarantees with Eritrea, since the country's short history is almost entirely marked by violence, resulting in many people seeking a better life elsewhere.

"The first people fled Eritrea for Sudan in 1967 to escape [former Ethiopian ruler] Haile Selassie's imperial army. In the 1980s, people fled in large numbers from the Ethiopian military dictatorship. Since 2001, people have once again been fleeing in large numbers from human rights violations, military service, war, and a lack of prospects," says Magnus Treiber, a migration researcher specializing in the Horn of Africa at the Institute of Ethnology at the University of Munich.

"The causes of flight have hardly changed. However, since the European Union now offers virtually no opportunities to seek asylum, Eritreans are now fleeing all over the world."

Displacement is rife around the Horn of Africa, where various conflicts repeatedly force entire populations to seek safety elsewhere Image: GIULIA PARAVICINI/REUTERS

At least 700,000 people have left the country since its founding, which is about a fifth of its total population. The country's population growth meanwhile is under 2% — a low number compared to many countries in the region.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Italy: Etna eruption in Sicily halts Catania flights
World.content:
Sicily's Catania airport has suspended flights again as Mount Etna continues to spew lava and volcanic ash. The eruption has disrupted travel during the peak summer holiday season.

Sicily's Catania airport on Wednesday suspended flights until at least 4 p.m. local time (1400 GMT/UTC) on Thursday, responding to fresh ash emissions from Mount Etna.

The volcanic ash can pose a danger to aircraft and so has forced regulators to restrict access to the airspace around eastern Sicily, disrupting the peak summer holiday season.

Where were flights affected?

"Passengers are advised to check the status of their flights with their airlines," airport operator SAC said. "Further updates will follow in the coming hours."

Catania airport flights have faced disruptions since late last week, becoming more intense as the eruption continues Image: Darrin Zammit Lupi/REUTERS

Travel disruptions have impacted eastern Sicily in particular since last Friday, when renewed rumblings from Europe's most active volcano and shifting winds started carrying ash over the region. The airspace was fully closed only in recent days as the eruption continued.

The prolonged restrictions at Catania — on Sicily's eastern coast just south of Mount Etna — have placed extra strain on Sicily's other airports during one of the busiest seasons for vacationers.

Palermo Mayor Roberto Lagalla said that his city's airport had taken in around 190 flights originally scheduled to land on the eastern side of the island in recent days.

For milennia, the port of Catania has sat in the foothills of Mount Etna, sometimes facing severe disruption or even damage from its eruptions Image: Giuseppe Di Stefano/Etna Walk/REUTERS

Italy's ANSA news agency also reported on Wednesday that flights were resuming at Comiso airport, a smaller hub south of Catania, after it had suspended traffic late on Tuesday.

Some of the volcanic ash was also drifting south across the Mediterranean towards Malta, which had reported significant delays and some cancellations. On Wednesday, Malta International Airport continued to warn passengers of possible disruptions but said that conditions were improving.

What is Mount Etna?

Mount Etna is a roughly 3,400 meter (roughly 11,100 feet) stratovolcano on Sicily's eastern coast. Its precise height is ever changing, particularly amid periods of high activity when it can shed a few meters.

The city of Catania is located in its foothills.

Volcanic activity can lead to particularly fertile soils and other benefits that explain why cities like Catania were built so close to mountains like Etna Image: Etna Walk/AFP

It is one of the tallest active volcanoes in Europe and Italy's highest peak south of the Alps.

It's in an almost constant state of low-level activity and erupts in a more pronounced manner fairly frequently. It has caused disruptions at Catania airport several times in recent years.

A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the first volcanic activity took place at Etna about half a million years ago.

Both Roman and Greek mythology asserted that the god of blacksmithing — either Vulcan or Hephaestus — had his forge beneath Mount Etna.

Roman poet Virgil wrote about an eruption at Etna in his epic poem the Aeneid, in what's thought to be a first-hand account Image: Etna Walk/AFP

Edited by: Louis Oelofse
