World.title: Poland unveils first warship under major naval modernisation programme
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic Sea port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed. The development marks a major milestone in a 15 billion zloty (€3.5 billion) programme to modernise the ageing Polish navy and strengthen NATO’s maritime defences. “Poland is becoming a maritime power in the Baltic Sea,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a ceremony to name the new ship, which he attended alongside opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki in a rare show of unity. Na terenie PGZ Stoczni Wojennej w Gdyni prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki, @PremierRP @donaldtusk oraz wiceministrowie @MON_GOV_PL @magdasobkowiak i @pawelbejda uczestniczą w uroczystości chrztu pierwszej jednostki programu „Miecznik”, fregaty wielozadaniowej – przyszłego ORP Wicher. pic.twitter.com/X2ftjoKTLZ — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026 The ORP Wicher, a medium-sized warship designed for escort, air defence and other fleet protection duties, is the first of three multi-role frigates based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design being built under Poland’s Miecznik programme, the largest modernisation project in the history of the Polish Navy. It is due to be launched on Thursday in a complex manoeuvre involving its transfer and controlled launch from a semi-submersible barge. Shipyard officials have described the operation as one of the most demanding engineering projects undertaken by Poland’s shipbuilding industry. The three frigates are intended to form the core of Poland’s surface fleet and will replace Poland’s two current Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigates, which were constructed in the 1970s and transferred from the US Navy in the years 2000 and 2002. Ahead of Wicher’s launch, leading Polish officials attended the naming ceremony in Gdynia, including Tusk and Nawrocki, who are normally bitter rivals but have sought to present a more united front when it comes to national defence. “There can be no arguments or disputes when it comes to our country’s security,” said Tusk, who declared that Poland was seeking to play a role in “determining not only its own future, but also the entire region and Europe”. Nawrocki, meanwhile, said that the modernisation of the Polish navy “sends a clear message that we will develop our armed forces in every theatre – on water, on land, and in the air”. Both leaders also hailed the fact that the new frigates are being built in Poland itself, helping bolster the Polish shipbuilding industry. Prezydent RP @NawrockiKn w #Gdynia: Życzę, abyście zawsze szczęśliwie wracali do portu, któremu na imię Polska. pic.twitter.com/hHia2sCZfn — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) August 12, 2026 The contract for the three frigates was signed in 2021 between Poland’s state Armament Agency (AU) and a consortium led by state-owned defence group PGZ, with British defence firm Babcock and other foreign partners also involved. The project was initially valued at about 8 billion zloty but had risen to around 15 billion zloty by the end of 2023 following amendments. Construction of the second frigate in Gdynia’s military shipyard began in May 2025, while work on the third began in April this year. The programme is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2031. Swedish defence giant Saab has signed a strategic collaboration agreement with Polish state defence group PGZ. The firms will cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology, including establishing an underwater technology centre in Poland https://t.co/dykKjMIAzX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 The ships are more than 140 metres long and are based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design, developed by Babcock and adapted to Polish military requirements. The frigates will be equipped with British CAMM and CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles, naval guns and anti-ship missiles capable of striking targets at ranges of more than 200 km. Their missions will include protecting shipping lanes and critical energy infrastructure and taking part in NATO naval groups. NATO has launched a new military operation in the Baltic Sea, an idea promoted by Poland last year in response to sabotage targeting undersea cables.@donaldtusk said at today's summit that "all signs point to Russia" being responsible for the damage https://t.co/cBPdL1fKkK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 14, 2025 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on a major defence procurement spree. It now has the highest relative defence budget in NATO and is also the alliance’s largest arms importer. In recent years, Poland has also increasingly oriented itself towards the Baltic region, forming closer economic, energy and military ties with allies around the sea. Last year, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership on defence and economic ties. They subsequently held their first ever bilateral military exercises in the Baltic. As part of its naval modernisation programme, Poland has selected Sweden’s Saab as the supplier for three advanced A26 stealth submarines. Poland has signed a €4.5 billion deal to buy three A26 submarines from Sweden. The agreement was announced amid intergovernmental consultations today between the two countries, further cementing an increasingly important alliance in the Baltic region https://t.co/VsiOTVRzPI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Negative views of Poland’s justice system have grown under Tusk government, finds state pollster
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess their country’s justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law and ensure that courts function more effectively and independently. New polling by state research agency CBOS found that, in June this year, 61% of Poles had a negative view of the functioning of the justice system, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017, when the former Law and Justice (PiS) government was in power. Only 26% now positively assess the system, down from 28% in 2022 and 36% in 2017. The last time positive views were lower was in 2005 (22%). The findings come two and a half years after the current government, a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power in December 2023, replacing the national-conservative PiS administration. One of Tusk’s main promises was to restore the rule of law after eight years in which PiS had implemented a series of contested judicial reforms that experts, European courts and many Polish judges had condemned as undermining the independence and functioning of the judiciary. However, Tusk’s government has struggled to implement its promised changes. In many cases, its efforts have been blocked by PiS-aligned Presidents Andrzej Duda and Karol Nawrocki or other officials appointed under the former government. But in other cases, such as with a pledge to separate the functions of justice minister and prosecutor general, which were fused by PiS in 2016, the current ruling coalition has simply not followed through on its promises. In its latest polling, CBOS found that supporters of the current opposition are most dissatisfied with the functioning of the justice system: 72% of PiS voters have a negative view, as do 71% of those who support the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, even among voters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, a majority, 53%, have a negative opinion, with only 38% holding a positive one. Interestingly, public attitudes towards judges themselves have hardly changed. Currently, 19% of Poles have a positive view towards them and 23% a negative one. That is similar to findings in 2017 (22% positive, 24% negative) and 2012 (19% positive, 23% negative). More Poles (35%) think that the rule of law has got worse under Tusk's government than believe it has improved (24%). A further 28% think there has been no change, finds a new poll https://t.co/KkiuY2vDSW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2025 When asked to identify the greatest problems with the justice system, Poles instead often point to structural issues – that is, those that are under the control of politicians. The most commonly identified problem (chosen by 38% of respondents, who could select up to three main problems) was “prolonged proceedings” in court cases. The second biggest issue was “politicisation of courts” (18%). Only 4% said that “judges’ neglect of duty, incompetence and impunity” were among the biggest problems. However, 23% of respondents were unable to name a single major issue that the justice system faces. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 CBOS’s findings echo a number of other polls. After the first year of Tusk’s government, a survey by SW Research for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 35% of Poles thought the rule-of-law situation had got worse, compared to only 24% who thought it had improved. Another poll by the same agency for Onet, a news website, in January this year similarly found that 40% of Poles believe the justice system has not improved under the current government, while only 33% think it has got better. In response to the latter poll, justice minister Waldemar Żurek admitted to Onet that there had been problems in addressing the rule of law. But he blamed the “hurdles [put] in our path” by Presidents Duda and Nawrocki. Opposition-aligned President @NawrockiKn has vetoed a government bill intended to reform a judicial body at the heart of Poland’s rule-of-law crisis. He argued that the measures would simply create even greater “legal chaos” https://t.co/I7FHRKIoP1 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 19, 2026 In 2024, Duda refused to sign government bills overhauling the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which still contains judges illegitimately appointed under the former PiS administration. As a result, Tusk’s government refuses to recognise rulings issued by the TK. In February this year, Duda’s successor, Nawrocki, vetoed a government bill intended to restore the legitimacy of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), the body responsible for nominating judges to positions on courts. In 2017, the KRS was overhauled under PiS in a manner that rendered it illegitimate, according to multiple Polish and European court rulings. That in turn has led to doubts over the legal status of around 3,000 judges appointed by the KRS since 2017 and all the rulings issued by them. Nawrocki has also refused to swear in four new TK judges nominated by parliament this year, despite an order by the European Court of Human Rights that they be allowed to take up their positions. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Indians and Colombians now third and fourth largest groups of foreign workers in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians. The figures also show that the overall number of registered foreign workers has risen more than 8% over the last year, a faster rate of growth than in recent years. However, the government official responsible for migration strategy says this is because stricter government measures have pushed some employers to register previously uninsured workers. The ZUS data, reported by Dziennik Gazeta Prawna (DGP), a leading daily, show that there were 1.34 million foreign workers registered in ZUS at the end of June, up from 1.24 million at the same point last year. That 8.2% increase is larger than the growth rate of around 6% seen in each of the previous two years, notes the newspaper. Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister responsible for migration, commented that the rise actually reflects the government’s tougher migration strategy, which he said “forces employers to report for insurance those who arrived earlier” but were working unregistered The official pointed to recent data showing that, in fact, in the first half of this year, Poland issued 50% fewer work permits to foreigners than in the same period of 2025. Dane ZUS pokazują dokładnie to co zakładaliśmy w Strategi Migracyjnej. Radykalny spadek liczby wydawanych, nowych zezwoleń na pracę (ponad 50% rok do roku) wymusza na pracodawcach zgłaszanie do ubezpieczenia, tych którzy przyjechali wcześniej. Tylko w pełni legalne zatrudnienie! — Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) August 11, 2026 Ukrainians remain by far the largest group of registered foreign workers, with 901,000 now in the system, a 10.1% rise from a year earlier. Belarusians (144,000, up 4.9%) remain in second. But two non-European migrant groups whose numbers have been growing rapidly in recent years now occupy third and fourth place: Indians (25,500, up 4.9%) and Colombians (23,000, up 31%, which was the fastest growth of any national group). Georgians, who had previously been the third-largest group, saw their number fall by 17% to 22,000, meaning they are now in fifth, ahead of Filipinos (15,400, down 2%), Moldovans (14,200, down 1%), Nepalis (13,400, up 8.3%), Vietnamese (12,200, up 6.1%), and Russians (11,800, down 2.5%). Latin American migration to Poland is booming, with 45,000 work permits issued last year, five times more than in 2022@Gosia_Tomczak looks at what is driving this trend and what challenges and opportunities it has created for both the migrants and Poland https://t.co/tl1wUTCaC0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2025 ZUS’s data also show that foreign workers are increasingly establishing their own businesses in Poland, which Dziennik Gazeta Prawna notes is a sign that they are establishing longer-term ties with the country but also a result of an easier online system for registering businesses. In 2021, only 22,700 foreigners had a registered business in Poland, a figure that now is now almost five times higher, at 102,000. The rise has been driven in particular by Ukrainians, many of whom are legally entitled to establish companies in Poland under the same terms as Polish citizens. As a result, 7.6% of foreign workers now run their own business, up from 6.7% a year ago and from 2.7% before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which led to a wave of Ukrainian refugees settling in Poland. Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.7% last year while not raising unemployment or lowering wages, finds a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte "Whoever thinks refugees are a burden on the economy should think again," says @UNHCRPoland https://t.co/rOvtOvBNwG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2025 Over the last decade, even before the war in Ukraine, Poland has experienced a wave of migration unprecedented in its history and among the largest anywhere in Europe. For six years running, between 2017 and 2022, it issued more first residence permits to immigrants from outside the European Union than did any other member state. Much of the surge in immigration came during the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government from 2015 to 2023, despite its strong anti-migrant rhetoric. The current government, a more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power pledging to reduce immigration, which it said had got out of control under PiS. Under Tusk’s government, in 2024, Poland issued the lowest number of residence permits to non-EU immigrants in a decade. In 2025, the government introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students. It has also stepped up deportations of foreigners who have broken the law. However, Duszczyk notes that the current government still sees “selective and responsible migration” as a way to “maintain the competitiveness of the economy without limiting wage growth”. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Mother bear and cubs spotted on busy hiking trail in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A female brown bear and her three cubs have been spotted in Poland’s Tatra mountains crossing a popular trail filled with hikers, with the animals coming unusually close to people. According to an official from Tatra National Park, where the incident took place, the behaviour could be a survival strategy by the mother to protect her young from male bears, which can kill cubs but tend to avoid humans. In a video posted on Sunday, the mother and three cubs were seen crossing the Chochołowska Valley trail in broad daylight, as crowds of people looked on Videos of the bear family have appeared increasingly often on social media, prompting questions about whether the animals are becoming less wary of people. But park officials say the female’s behaviour may have a biological explanation. “As we know, male brown bears are infanticidal. They kill not only other bears’ cubs, but their own as well. So the females, to avoid contact with the males, tend to stay closer to people,” Tomasz Zwijacz-Kozica, a park official, told local newspaper Gazeta Krakowska. “Females sense this instinctively and generally use the presence of people as a sort of shield to defend themselves against these males,” he added. The park staff hope to gather more detailed data on the female bear’s movements and behaviour in the future by possibly fitting her with a telemetry collar. They note that similar behaviour has been seen before. Around 20 years ago, a female bear drew attention when hundreds of tourists photographed her. They advise visitors to remain calm if they encounter a bear and to follow several basic rules, including staying calm and not running or making sudden movements, which may trigger a pursuit; not approaching the animals; and not attempting to take close-up photographs or use a flash. If a bear is encountered, visitors should slowly retreat in the direction from which they came while maintaining eye contact with the animal. Particular caution is required when cubs are present. Visitors should also avoid feeding bears or leaving rubbish behind. The smell of food can attract animals to trails and encourage behaviour that brings them into dangerous contact with people. A woman has died after being attacked by a bear in a forest in southeastern Poland. Such incidents are extremely rare, with the last fatal bear attack in the country reported in 2014 https://t.co/sAC2MPAvfh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 23, 2026 Estimates of Poland’s brown bear population vary between 120 and 400, with most found in the southeastern Bieszczady mountains as well as the Tatras and Beskids further west. The population is thought to be growing, with a rise in reports of encounters with humans. In April this year, a woman was killed in a bear attack, Poland’s first such fatality since 2014. Another bear attack earlier in the year in the same region left a man with head and limb injuries. In March, the government launched a new 16 million zloty (€3.7 million) scheme aimed at both protecting bears and ensuring the safety of their human neighbours. It includes the creation of a special force to monitor and respond to bear sightings, including fitting the animals with tracking collars. In 2022, the town of Zakopane, located at the foot of the Tatra mountains, installed bear-proof rubbish bins to prevent animals from foraging in them – and thereby coming closer to areas of human population Poland has launched a new programme to protect brown bears and ensure the safety of their human neighbours, amid growing reports of encounters. World.title: Kaczyński appeals to President Nawrocki to unify Poland’s right-wing opposition ahead of elections
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called on opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. His appeal comes as PiS, which for the last two decades has dominated the Polish right, is in crisis, amid falling polling numbers, a split by a breakaway faction, and a growing challenge from far-right parties that have long been critical of PiS. That has created a fragmented opposition, with parties competing against one another as much as or more than with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition. Some on the right hope that Nawrocki, who enjoys good relations with various parts of the opposition, could act as a unifying figurehead bridging those divides. 🔴 Jarosław Kaczyński ujawnił, o co osobiście poprosił Karola Nawrockiego. Podczas miesięcznicy smoleńskiej prezes PiS odniósł się do podziałów na prawicy i przyznał, że widzi dla prezydenta wyjątkowo ważną rolę: ma pomóc scalić zwaśnione środowiska. „Ja prezydenta swego czasu… pic.twitter.com/qwXhmccun2 — Super Express (@se_pl) August 10, 2026 Speaking on Sunday at a monthly commemoration of the 2010 Smolensk air disaster that killed his identical twin brother, then-President Lech Kaczyński, Jarosław was reported by a variety of Polish media outlets as saying that he had asked Nawrocki to act as a “patron” for a unified right. “I asked the president some time ago, and I hope he will do it,” said Kaczyński, quoted by newspaper Fakt. “It would be very good if the president took up this matter energetically.” “We could continue to develop – as we did during our years of government – not only in terms of achieving GDP growth, but also by undertaking major investments, by undertaking everything that would truly change Poland.” Kaczyński was referring to the period between 2015 and 2023 when a PiS-dominated coalition, known as the United Right (Zjednoczona Prawica), ruled Poland. In the latter year, it was ousted from power by a more liberal coalition led by Tusk, Kaczyński’s great rival. Since then, the landscape on the Polish right has changed dramatically. One of PiS’s partners in the United Right, the hard-right Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), merged with PiS in 2024. The other, the centre-right Agreement (Porozumienie), is now defunct. Meanwhile, support for PiS itself has collapsed. Having won 35% of the vote at the 2023 elections, it now averages only around 20% in polls – the party’s lowest figures for almost 20 years. To make matters worse, last month, around a fifth of the party’s MPs formed a breakaway group in parliament led by PiS deputy leader and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. They plan to soon form their own, separate party, Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), with a more moderate, centre-right agenda than PiS. At the same time, PiS has found itself challenged by a growing far right. Confederation (Konfederacja), which won 7% of the vote in 2023, is now polling around 12-13%. The even more radical Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which broke away from Confederation last year, is at 9%. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 That has resulted in a much more fragmented right, with four separate entities not only opposed to Tusk’s government but also competing with one another for overlapping electorates. With parliamentary elections scheduled for autumn 2027, there have been questions over whether and to what extent the opposition should seek to cooperate with one another. One option would be an agreement not to stand candidates against one another for seats in the upper-house Senate, which are contested on a single-member-district system rather than through the proportional representation that decides the share of seats in the more powerful lower-house Sejm. Parties in Tusk’s current ruling coalition themselves formed such a “Senate pact” at the 2019 elections, helping them win control of the upper house, then repeated that in 2023, when they retained control. Although the Senate has a limited legislative role, it would be a significant prize for Nawrocki and the opposition, especially if Tusk’s coalition wins the Sejm, because the Senate has the power to approve or reject national referendums proposed by the president. An even more ambitious plan that has been rumoured is for some elements of the right-wing opposition to run joint electoral lists for the Sejm. That would require a far greater degree of programmatic consensus and longer negotiations over how to distribute places on lists. The government's majority in the Senate has, for the second time, rejected a proposal by opposition-aligned President Nawrocki to hold a referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the EU's climate policies, which he argues are too costly https://t.co/Idm6dnzQEH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Nawrocki is seen as key to any such plan coming to fruition. He was elected last year to the presidency as an independent, but with the formal backing of PiS. Ahead of the second-round run-off vote, he also received endorsements from defeated first-round rivals Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of Confederation, and Grzegorz Braun, the leader of KKP. Since taking office, Nawrocki has continued to cultivate good relations with PiS and Confederation, as well as with Morawiecki’s new breakaway faction. However, he has kept his distance from Braun, whose anti-Americanism, antisemitism and sympathy towards Russia makes him something of a pariah. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 Media reports have suggested that Nawrocki is planning to play a role in creating a “broad patriotic camp” among the opposition ahead of next year’s elections. Last week, during an event celebrating the first anniversary of his swearing in, the president also hinted at this role. He noted he will, in the coming months, be presenting “a presidential development strategy”, which “I believe will become a point of reference in the upcoming parliamentary elections for all those who aspire to govern Poland, a real plan for the future of the republic”. The strategy would be aimed in particular at “patriotic forces” who are “ready for dialogue between the offices of the president and future prime minister”. Given that Nawrocki and Tusk’s government are bitterly opposed to one another, that was a clear reference to opposition parties. A report on Sunday by Newsweek Polska, based on unnamed inside sources, claimed that Kaczyński is hoping to form a single electoral list for the Sejm elections compromising PiS, Development Plus and all or parts of Confederation, under the patronage of Nawrocki. 💥 Nowa obsesja Jarosława Kaczyńskiego, w jaki sposób odzyskać władzę. Prezes PiS naciska na Karola Nawrockiego, by prezydent stworzył "listę Nawrockiego" prawicy do Sejmu. To najbardziej ryzykowna, ale też o ogromnej stawce, decyzja prezydenta.https://t.co/sqRPFUuiZ7 — Jacek Gądek (@JacekGadek) August 9, 2026 Other leaders on the right have expressed varying degrees of willingness to work with one another. Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Saturday, Krzystof Bosak, another of Confederation’s leaders, expressed support for the idea of a Senate pact. On Friday, Morawiecki said that he can “fully imagine working with Sławomir Mentzen”, who “I believe is absolutely part of the patriotic camp”. However, Mentzen himself quickly ruled out the idea, tweeting that he’d rather “quit politics than join this gang leading Poland to disaster”, adding that Tusk, Kaczyński and Morawiecki are “one and the same”. Whereas Bosak represents a nationalist faction of Confederation seen as more compatible with PiS, Mentzen represent’s a libertarian wing that is bitterly opposed to the former PiS’ government’s high social spending, support for Ukraine, and the restrictions it introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic. Prędzej mi ręka uschnie, niż poprę kolejne programy socjalne. Prędzej zrezygnuję z polityki, niż dołączę się do tej bandy prowadzącej Polskę do katastrofy. Tusk, Kaczyński, Morawiecki, Czarzasty, jeden pies. Dla nich wszystkich słupki sondażowe są ważniejsze od przyszłości… — Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) August 7, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Protests against anti-Ukrainian violence held in 25 Polish cities
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Demonstrations took place in around 25 Polish cities on Sunday against a “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. The protests came after police data showed a significant increase in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland so far this year, including a number of high-profile incidents of verbal and physical aggression. Sunday’s demonstrations, which took place under the slogan “Do Not Be Indifferent”, were organised by the Committee for the Defence of Democracy (KOD), an NGO, with support from other groups, including Amnesty International. “[This is] a nationwide campaign aimed at expressing opposition to the growing wave of hate, xenophobia, nationalism and violence directed against Ukrainians and members of other minorities,” wrote KOD ahead of the events. On Sunday, hundreds gathered on Warsaw’s Castle Square carrying Ukrainian and Polish flags and many waving signs saying “With U”, with the letter “U” coloured in Ukrainian national colours. #Siódemka Plac Zamkowy w Warszawie, protest w ramach: 🛑 NIE BĄDŹMY OBOJĘTNI! WSPÓLNIE PRZECIWKO NIENAWIŚCI! W wielu miastach Polski wyszliśmy na ulice, żeby jasno powiedzieć: nie ma zgody na hejt, przemoc i agresję wobec Ukraińców. W ostatnim czasie coraz częściej słyszymy… pic.twitter.com/kOfq4zBuGT — Piotr #FBPE Fijałkowski (@piotr4913) August 9, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, local media reported that around 150 people attended a demonstration, carrying placards saying “Let’s defend our neighbours from the aggression and stupidity of others” and “Putin is the enemy, Ukraine is our neighbour”. In Gdańsk, on Poland’s northern coast, around 300 people gathered, according to local media. However, they were also met with a small counter-demonstration of around a dozen people, led by the New Hope party that is part of Poland’s far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) opposition group. The counter-protesters held a banner declaring “Solidarity with victims of mass immigration” and “Down with Bandera”, a reference to historical Ukrainian nationalist leader Stepan Bandera, who in Poland is associated with the massacres of around 100,000 Poles by Ukrainians during World War Two. Separately, on Friday, a group of NGOs organised a demonstration against anti-Ukrainian violence outside the prime minister’s chancellery, during which they delivered a petition, signed by over 11,000 people, calling for the government to take “decisive action against xenophobic attacks”. Police data published last month showed that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025. Among those incidents have been a number of high-profile cases, including two 11-year-old Ukrainian girls being verbally abused by a man on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała and a violent attack on young Ukrainians by a group of Polish teenagers in Warsaw. Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. Tenions have been stoked further by a diplomatic crisis that began in May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after a group responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two. That prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Last week, PiS announced that, if it returns to power, one of its first actions would be to deport Ukrainian conscription-age men who are not in legal employment. At one of Sunday’s protests, in Kraków, a demonstrator responded with a placard declaring “Deport xenophobia”. Poland’s more liberal ruling coalition has condemned anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from the right-wing opposition. Last month, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for a “war against this violence”, saying that “thugs and hooligans have gained courage, audacity and political patronage” from the opposition. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative PiS, has called for Ukrainian men of conscription age who are not legally working to be deported to Ukraine. World.title: Brazilian Summer Vibes Coming to Střelecký ostrov This Weekend
World.content:
Prague’s Střelecký ostrov will turn into a Brazilian-inspired summer spot this Friday and Saturday, with live music, DJs, food, drinks and a riverside atmosphere.

The two-day event will take place from 12 p.m. to 10 p.m. on both days, bringing Brazilian music and summer energy to one of the city’s most picturesque islands.

Visitors can expect live Brazilian music and DJ sets, alongside a selection of food and drinks. The menu will include wine, cheese, Czech dishes, cocktails, frozen margaritas and frozen daiquiris.

The event offers a relaxed way to spend the weekend in central Prague, with music, drinks and food overlooking the Vltava.

World.title: Czech Rivers Reach Record Lows as Drought Deepens
World.content:
Rivers and streams across the Czech Republic are experiencing exceptionally low flows as a prolonged drought continues to worsen, with several waterways approaching or reaching their lowest levels since records began.

According to the latest data from the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute, the vast majority of monitored rivers and streams are flowing well below their long-term averages.

Some of the country’s smallest watercourses have dried up completely, while critical conditions are emerging on several major rivers.



The Elbe is among the most affected. Its flow has fallen to one of the lowest levels ever recorded and is approaching the historic minimum for the entire period of regular observations.

The Vltava is in a somewhat better position in some sections because the reservoir system is being regulated to help stabilize water levels. But even the Vltava has reached an unprecedented low in České Budějovice, where the river is recording its lowest measured flow.

The effects of the drought are particularly visible at the Orlík Reservoir. As water levels have fallen sharply, the remains of a former hydroelectric power plant at Dubrava have emerged from beneath the reservoir.

The plant was built in 1929 but was demolished and flooded in the 1960s when the Orlík Reservoir was created. Its remains have now resurfaced as the reservoir continues to shrink.

The worsening conditions are not limited to rivers and reservoirs. Groundwater levels are also declining, affecting wells and raising concerns about the availability of water supplies in some areas.

Hydrologists are not expecting a significant improvement in the coming days. According to the medium-range weather forecast, there are currently no clear conditions that would bring a substantial recovery in river flows or groundwater levels.

World.title: How to Find a GP in Prague When Practices Aren’t Accepting New Patients
World.content:
Finding a general practitioner in Prague can look simple until the first calls begin.

One practice does not answer. Another says it is full. A third can offer an appointment, but not in English. Your insurer’s list may not show who is accepting new patients today or what kind of visit is available.

If registration is blocked, first clarify whether you need long-term GP care, a one-time consultation, a specialist, an urgent route, or a private self-paid visit.



Decide whether this is really a GP problem

A GP is often the right first contact for common health concerns, preventive care, prescription questions, basic tests, and referrals. In Czech, this doctor is called a praktický lékař.

Not every situation should wait for GP registration. For a sudden and serious health problem or a possible threat to life, call 155 for the medical emergency service or 112 for the European emergency number.

If the issue clearly belongs to a dentist, gynaecologist, or specialist, ask that provider whether direct booking is possible or a referral is required. Patients in Czechia can generally approach a specialist without a GP referral, but an individual provider, insurer, or procedure may have its own requirements.

Tell the provider if you already have results, imaging, a hospital discharge report, or a specialist recommendation, because those documents may affect the next step.

Ask your insurer for help finding a provider

If you have Czech public health insurance and cannot find a GP, contact your insurer directly. Czech health insurers are responsible for helping their members access contracted care under the applicable rules on geographical and time availability.

Ask for practical information:

• Which contracted GPs in my area should be available to new patients?

• Which providers can communicate in English?

• Does the provider have a contract for my care?

• Do I need a referral, approval, or particular documents?

Availability can change, so confirm the details with the practice before travelling there.

If you have commercial insurance, check the provider network and approval process in your policy or contact the insurer. Do not assume that a clinic visit is covered simply because the clinic appears in a search result.

Understand why a practice may say no

A practice may lawfully refuse to accept a patient into care for reasons such as capacity, operational limits, distance that prevents home visits, or the absence of a contract with the patient’s public insurer.

If a provider refuses to accept you as a patient, ask for written confirmation with the reason. This gives you something concrete to show your insurer when requesting another available provider.

Clarify whether the refusal covers long-term registration, all appointments, only publicly insured care, the requested language, or a service the practice does not provide. A limited “no” does not necessarily close every route.

Separate registration from a one-time appointment

Registration and a medical appointment are related, but they are not identical.

Registration creates a long-term relationship with a primary-care doctor. It matters for continuity and for services whose public-insurance reimbursement is linked to the registered GP.

A provider may also offer care without registering you, particularly through a one-time, self-pay appointment. The scope and payment conditions vary, so never assume that a single consultation also means registration or that public insurance will cover it.

Before booking, ask whether the offer is long-term registration, a one-time consultation, a preventive check-up, an urgent appointment, specialist care, or a self-paid visit. Do not leave a clinic assuming that one consultation means you are registered there.

Prepare the information the provider needs

Share only enough information for the provider to understand the request, and use its approved secure channel for medical documents.

Prepare:

• the main reason for the appointment;

• how long the issue has been present;

• whether the request is routine, worsening, urgent, or preventive;

• your insurer or intention to self-pay;

• your preferred language;

• current medicines and allergies;

• relevant reports, results, imaging, or referrals.

A concise request helps the provider determine whether it can help and which appointment type is appropriate.

Make sure the visit has a clear ending

Getting an appointment is only the first part of the process.

A doctor may order tests, issue a referral, prescribe medication, or recommend another consultation. It should be clear who will explain the results and arrange the next step.

Before leaving, ask:

• What happens next?

• When should I expect the results?

• Who will explain them?

• Do I need another appointment?

• Should I send anything to another doctor?

A useful appointment should leave you knowing what comes afterwards.

When coordination support can help

OpenMedical helps patients find suitable English-speaking GPs and other medical specialists in Prague, confirm current availability and appointment conditions, and coordinate the booking process. The service also helps prepare documents, communicate with selected providers, and keep follow-up steps clear.

Quick checklist when GP registration is blocked

• Decide whether the situation is an emergency or can wait for a planned appointment.

• Ask your public insurer to help identify an available contracted provider.

• Ask the practice whether its refusal applies to registration or to all appointments.

• Request written confirmation if a provider refuses to take you into care.

• Confirm language, payment route, referral requirements, and whether a one-time appointment is available.

• Keep copies of medical reports and results.

• Before leaving an appointment, confirm who will explain the results and arrange the next step.

Finding a GP in Prague can take patience. A blocked registration does not mean there is no possible way forward. It means the next route needs to be identified more precisely.

Questions to ask before confirming a GP appointment

• Are you accepting new registered patients?

• Is this a registration visit or a one-time consultation?

• Can the appointment be handled in English?

• Do you have a contract with my public health insurer?

• What is the price if the appointment is self-paid?

• Do I need a referral or prior approval?

• Which documents should I provide, and how should I send them securely?

• How will results and further steps be handled?

World.title: Prague Plans 1.9 Billion Crown Reconstruction of Kasárna Karlín
World.content:
Prague plans to invest around CZK 1.93 billion, including VAT, to transform Kasárna Karlín into a mixed-use complex with shops, offices, student housing and space for cultural and artistic activities.

The city acquired the former military complex in 2023 and has since been working on plans for its long-term redevelopment.

Prague City Council has now approved the next step, allowing the city-owned Trade Centre Prague (TCP), which manages the site, to launch a tender for the preparation of the reconstruction project.



Construction is scheduled to follow between 2027 and 2032, with the investment financed from Prague’s municipal budget.

The first stage will focus on the complex’s main building. A separate building in the courtyard, currently used by the Karlín Barracks Cultural Center, will be addressed in later phases.

Deputy Mayor for Territorial and Strategic Development Petr Hlaváček said the reconstruction should open the site to the surrounding neighborhood while preserving its historic character and protected architectural elements.

One of the main changes will be to improve access to the courtyard, which currently has just one entrance and is largely hidden from the surrounding streets.

Adam Zábranský, Prague’s councilor for property, transparency and legislation, said new passages from the street would lead into the complex, with shops and services occupying the ground floor. The arcade running alongside these commercial spaces would form part of the new circulation system through the site.

The upper levels could eventually accommodate student housing, studios and offices. Zábranský also mentioned the possibility of using some of the space for businesses such as a technology park.

The exact future use of many of the rooms has not yet been decided. According to Zábranský, the project should therefore prioritize flexible layouts that can be adapted for different purposes over time.

The initial investment will focus in particular on replacing and upgrading essential infrastructure, including water, electricity and waste systems, as well as preparing the commercial areas on the ground floor. Work on the upper floors is expected to come later.

World.title: Czechia Sees Lyme Disease Surge With 90 New Cases a Day
World.content:
Lyme disease cases are rising sharply across the Czech Republic, with more than 8,000 infections recorded since the beginning of the year.

Health officials warn that the summer peak may not have arrived yet.

A total of 8,108 cases were reported through the end of July, according to data from the Czech State Institute of Health (SZÚ). July alone accounted for 2,792 infections, meaning that roughly one in three cases recorded so far this year occurred during the month.



Doctors registered an average of about 90 new cases each day in July.

The figures are significantly higher than those seen in previous years. Between January and July, the Czech Republic typically recorded between 1,500 and 2,000 Lyme disease cases.

Part of the increase may be linked to a change in the way infectious diseases are reported.

The number of tick-borne infections depends on several factors, including tick populations and seasonal weather conditions. Climate change is also playing an increasingly important role.

The highest numbers of Lyme disease infections have so far been reported in the Central Bohemian and South Moravian regions.

The risk is not limited to forests and countryside. Prague’s parks and wooded areas can also provide suitable conditions for ticks.

“Prague’s parks and forest parks create a specific microclimate where ticks thrive, so the risk of infection is real for residents even during an ordinary walk,” said Martina Marešová, head of the anti-epidemic department at the Prague Hygiene Station.

Early treatment can prevent complications

One of the most recognizable signs of Lyme disease is an expanding red rash that develops around the site of a tick bite and may have a paler area in the center.

Anyone who develops such a rash should seek medical attention rather than waiting for it to disappear.

The most common form initially affects the skin. If left untreated, the infection can progress and cause further skin problems. More serious complications can involve the nervous system, heart or eyes.

World.title: Shella Radio Visualizes Struggling Culture Scene At National Gallery
World.content:
A radio tower installation at Prague’s National Gallery is showcasing local efforts to preserve alternative culture as the Czech government seeks to cut funding to the arts and other public sectors.

Created by members of Prague-based Shella Radio, the tower is adorned with fabrics and relics of previous parties hosted in Ankali & Planeta Za, a nightclub that has faced closure due to financial problems.

“We believe in the idea of this radio as an amplification of voices that are often neglected in other spaces,” Shania Rodriguez, a Prague-based DJ and Shella radio host, said in an interview. “Here, they can be vocal about the issues and problems within our system and also share ideas of change.”



Many artists and curators say the environment for cultural organizations has grown more challenging due to financial cuts by the new right wing government led by Andrej Babiš.

The planned budget for this year shrank by 3.9 billion crowns – an almost 20 percent decrease from the previous year, according to the Czech Ministry of Culture. The cuts sparked widespread backlash across the country in April, and many took to the streets.

Shella, an Egyptian Arabic slang word meaning “a group of friends who do things together,” hosts political talk shows, electronic music club nights, and summer markets featuring local artists.

“The idea behind our installation was to be able to transmit parts of our identity that have been fundamental in Shella Radio’s trajectory,” Rodriguez said. “This DIY approach gives us the freedom to customize and handcraft our installation and studio space using materials from our temporary home: Ankali.”

The installation is part of the Necessary Wishes exhibition at the National Gallery which brings together more than 50 collectives and artists.

The event is free of charge and ends on September 13.

By: Lili Anna Lempek, Adam Pohořilský, Milena Gevorgyan, Isabella Fattore

World.title: Where to See the Partial Solar Eclipse in Prague and Across Czechia
World.content:
Skywatchers in the Czech Republic will have two reasons to look up on the night of August 12.

A partial solar eclipse will be visible in the evening, followed by favorable conditions for watching the annual Perseid meteor shower.

The eclipse will be visible across Czechia shortly before sunset, with the Sun low over the western and northwestern horizon. In Prague, the partial eclipse is expected to begin at about 7:19 p.m., reach its maximum at 8:12 p.m. and end around 8:27 p.m.



At the height of the eclipse, the Moon will cover about 86 percent of the Sun’s disk in Prague, making the event particularly noticeable if skies are clear.

The eclipse will look different depending on where observers are located. The farther east they are, the later the eclipse will begin and the less of it will be visible. In eastern Czechia and much of Slovakia, the maximum phase will take place after sunset, when the Sun is already below the horizon.

The event will be a partial eclipse in Central Europe, while a total solar eclipse will be visible in parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain. Astronomers and eclipse enthusiasts are expected to travel to those areas to experience totality.

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, blocking part or all of the Sun from view. In Czechia, the eclipse will be especially low on the horizon, so observers will need an unobstructed view toward the west and northwest.

Several Czech observatories are preparing public observing events. A list of locations and other information about the eclipse is available through the Czech astronomical website astro.cz.

Perseid meteor shower will follow

The same night will also offer good conditions for watching the Perseids, one of the most prominent annual meteor showers.

The shower will reach its peak during the early hours of August 13, when the Moon will be only a few hours past its new-moon phase. With virtually no moonlight in the sky, faint meteors should be easier to spot.

The Perseids are active from July 17 through August 24, but the best opportunity this year will come during the night of August 12-13.

Under dark skies and favorable weather, observers away from cities could see between 50 and 80 meteors per hour.

Light pollution will be the main obstacle for anyone hoping to see large numbers of meteors. The best locations are well away from major cities, ideally several dozen kilometers from strong sources of artificial light.

World.title: Non-Alcoholic Beer Sales Rise by More Than 25% in Czechia
World.content:
Beer remains a staple of the Czech shopping basket, but new sales data from online supermarket Rohlík shows that drinking habits are gradually changing.

Traditional lagers still dominate, while non-alcoholic beer is recording the fastest growth among the main beer categories.

The category has grown by more than a quarter over the past year, with Birell among the brands driving the increase. Birell sales alone are up by almost 20%.



Together with flavoured beers and radlers, non-alcoholic beer now accounts for close to one-third of all beer sales on Rohlík.

Beer from small and regional breweries is also gaining ground, with sales increasing by more than 11%.

The biggest decline is being recorded among craft beers grouped by style, including IPA and APA. This is currently the only major beer segment experiencing a year-on-year drop.

Czech brands continue to dominate the market. More than nine out of every 10 beers sold through Rohlík are from domestic brands.

Imported beers, however, are growing at a faster rate. Their sales have increased by 18% year-on-year.

Beer sales peak at the weekend

Friday is the busiest day for beer sales, with roughly twice as much beer sold as on Monday. Friday and Saturday together account for almost two-fifths of the category’s weekly sales.

Orders containing beer also tend to include significantly more items than orders without beer, suggesting that customers often buy it as part of a larger meal or weekend shop rather than as a standalone purchase.

Seasonal patterns have also shifted. Beer sales during this year’s summer months have reached levels comparable with the December Christmas peak.

World.title: Budapest’s long-awaited metro extension is finally moving: dozens of homes stand in its way
World.content:
Budapest’s long-discussed plan to extend Metro Line 3 could finally be moving towards construction, with the city now reviewing existing plans for a new section reaching Rákospalota-Újpest. But before work can begin, around 24 properties – most of them residential – must be acquired, while the project faces a tight timetable and an unusual challenge: the extension would initially have to be served by the line’s existing Russian-built trains.

M3 extension plans are back on the table

The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) has begun reviewing the existing plans for extending Metro Line 3 from Újpest-Központ towards Rákospalota-Újpest. The review will assess how the roughly 1.9-kilometre extension could be built, how the project could be divided into phases, how long construction might take and what risks could stand in its way.

Metro Line 3 reached Újpest-Központ from the city centre in 1990. Despite earlier plans to continue the line towards Káposztásmegyer, the extension never materialised.

The project has now returned to the agenda as part of the government’s Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan. The first phase would extend the line as far as Rákospalota-Újpest railway station.

If you missed it: Hungary set to launch EUR 5.5 billion railway upgrade as development plan gets green light

Two new stations could transform northern Budapest connections

According to the existing plans, the new section would begin near Árpád út 119, at the end of the existing underground structure, and run for approximately 1.9 kilometres. Two new stations would be built: one near Rózsa Street and another at Rákospalota-Újpest railway station.

The latter could be particularly significant for commuters, as it would create connections with the Budapest–Vác–Szob and Budapest–Veresegyház–Vác railway lines. Passengers arriving from the northern suburbs could therefore transfer to the M3 at Újpest rather than travelling all the way to Nyugati railway station.

The extension is planned using a cut-and-cover construction method rather than conventional deep tunnelling. BKK has also extended all the relevant railway authority permits, which will remain valid until December 2028. The organisation is now preparing to order the tender documentation needed for the construction procurement process.

24 properties need to be acquired first

There is, however, a major obstacle before construction can get properly underway.

Around 24 properties along the planned route would have to be acquired. Most are residential buildings located on land that was designated for the future metro project decades ago.

The Budapest municipal asset management company will therefore have to begin purchasing the properties or launching compulsory acquisition procedures as soon as possible. A 2021 estimate put the cost of acquiring the properties at around HUF 2.8 billion, although the current figure could be considerably higher following changes in property prices.

The project will also require close cooperation between the capital, its companies and the municipalities of Budapest’s Districts IV and XV.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The clock is already ticking

BKK has warned that the project could only be delivered under an extremely tight schedule. The amount of time available is limited compared with the scale and complexity of the investment, making cooperation between national and local authorities particularly important.

The permits expiring at the end of 2028 add another deadline to the equation. If sufficient progress is not made by then, further extensions or additional permitting work could be required. The construction itself could also be a substantial investment. An earlier analysis by MBH Bank estimated that, at current prices, the two-station extension could cost HUF 120–160 billion.

The project would not necessarily pay for itself through ticket revenue. Its wider benefits, however, could include shorter journeys, lower commuting costs, better access to employment, fewer road accidents and reduced environmental damage.

The analysis estimated that the extension would need to generate around HUF 8 billion in annual indirect social benefits to be considered economically worthwhile over a 30-year assessment period.

The new metro connection could also push up property values around the future stations. According to the analysis, homes within roughly 500–800 metres of Rákospalota-Újpest station could eventually be worth up to 10% more than they would be without the investment.

The Russian-built trains are here to stay

One of the project’s more unusual challenges concerns the trains themselves. BKK says the M3’s existing Metrowagonmash rolling stock will have to be treated as a given for at least the next 20 years. That means the planned extension to Rákospalota-Újpest would initially have to be operated using the existing fleet.

This would put greater pressure on BKV’s fleet management, although BKK believes the current trains could still be sufficient to operate the two-stop extension.

The situation is partly a consequence of the fact that an option for seven additional trains under BKV’s contract with the Russian manufacturer has expired. Metrowagonmash is also subject to sanctions because of Russia’s war against Ukraine, making the straightforward purchase of additional trains impossible at present. New rolling stock would become more important if the full extension to Káposztásmegyer eventually goes ahead.

Could Budapest finally get the extension it has been waiting for?

The M3 extension is not necessarily the most urgent rail transport investment Budapest could undertake. However, it has one major advantage over many other proposed projects: much of the groundwork has already been done.

The current review will determine whether the existing plans, permits, property arrangements and available trains provide a realistic basis for finally moving the project from paper to construction. After more than three decades of waiting since the M3 reached Újpest-Központ, the long-promised northern extension may finally be getting another chance.

World.title: Prisoner beaten so badly by guards in Hungary that his spleen had to be removed
World.content:
A Hungarian court has ordered a prison to pay HUF 8 million in compensation to a former inmate who was beaten by guards so severely that he required life-saving surgery to remove his spleen. The man was also left with permanent health damage and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

The Budapest Court of Appeal has issued a final ruling awarding HUF 8 million in non-pecuniary damages to a former prisoner who was violently assaulted by guards at Tököl Prison in 2018.

The man, represented by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, was left with permanent health problems after the assault, as well as PTSD requiring psychiatric and psychotherapy treatment. The prison must also send him a personal letter of apology for the abuse.

The beating left him with a life-threatening injury

The man had been working at the prison’s paper factory when he decided to rest in a quieter area of the workplace because he had struggled to sleep in his crowded cell. He fell asleep for longer than planned, and two prison guards eventually found him lying underneath a printing machine.

According to the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, the guards began punching him, including repeatedly hitting him in the abdomen and stomach area. The prisoner immediately complained of pain following the assault. Although he did not go to work the following day, he subsequently worked two more shifts.

On 10 September 2018, however, he collapsed during an inspection. Medical examinations revealed that his spleen had been critically damaged by the beating.

Doctors had to remove the organ in life-saving surgery two days later.

Both the man and the hospital subsequently filed complaints over the incident.

Prison initially claimed it could not find the CCTV footage

According to the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, the prison initially claimed that the crucial footage could not be found. The recordings were eventually recovered following pressure from a military prosecutor, allowing criminal proceedings to be brought against the two guards.

In 2020, both men were found guilty of causing life-threatening bodily harm and assault committed in an official capacity. They received suspended prison sentences.

The former inmate subsequently sought compensation for the physical and psychological damage he had suffered. Attempts to settle the matter out of court were unsuccessful, however, leaving him to pursue the case through the courts.

His health and ability to work were permanently affected

Medical experts determined that the man had suffered 13.5% permanent health impairment as a result of the assault. His injuries have significantly restricted the types of work he can undertake. Among other things, he can no longer work with a drill or on scaffolding.

The psychological consequences have also been severe. He developed post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) following the beating and requires psychiatric and psychotherapeutic treatment.

The court ultimately recognised both the physical and psychological harm caused by the assault when determining the compensation.

Court orders prison to apologise

The Budapest Court of Appeal has now issued a final ruling awarding the former prisoner HUF 8 million (EUR 22,000) in non-pecuniary damages. The court also ordered Tököl Prison to apologise to him in a personal letter. The man will have the right to make the apology public.

The Hungarian Helsinki Committee described the compensation as unusually high by Hungarian standards and welcomed the ruling.

The court stressed that prison staff should have been capable of dealing with the inmate’s conduct within the framework of the law, and that correctional institutions have a particular responsibility to ensure lawful treatment in order to maintain public trust.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

‘The money has a place’

The man, who now lives with his partner and their four children in Salgótarján, said the ruling finally gave him a sense of relief. After the assault, he had worried about how he would support his family if he could no longer take on physically demanding work.

He now hopes the compensation will help the family become financially more secure and eventually buy a home.

“I would like to buy a flat, because until now we have spent what I earned on rent.”

The Hungarian Helsinki Committee said it hoped the ruling would encourage the prison authorities to provide appropriate compensation for clear violations without forcing victims to endure years of litigation.

World.title: PM Magyar announces moves to raise the Danube near Paks nuclear power plant
World.content:
The Hungarian government has ordered the immediate construction of a submerged riverbed weir on the Danube near Paks and is preparing an extraordinary temporary measure: two 80-metre barges could be deliberately sunk to raise the river level if necessary.

The government has taken urgent measures to protect the cooling-water supply of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant as exceptionally low Danube water levels continue to pose a challenge.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Wednesday that construction of a riverbed weir will begin immediately between the nuclear power plant and the settlement of Dunaszentbenedek. The project is intended to ensure that the water level at the plant’s cooling channel does not fall below -90 centimetres, allowing the country’s most important power plant to continue operating at full capacity.

A 150,000-cubic-metre construction project

Following an on-site government meeting at Paks, Magyar said work would begin as early as Thursday. Around 150,000 cubic metres of rock will ultimately be used to construct the submerged barrier in the Danube.

The project is being treated as a priority investment, with the authorities ordering round-the-clock construction work. One hundred soldiers have also been deployed to support the project, while General Pál Kádár has been appointed to coordinate the construction.

The technical planning will involve Budapest University of Technology and Economics, while the necessary permitting procedures will run alongside the construction work. According to Magyar, the permanent structure could secure the necessary water level within a matter of weeks.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Two barges could be sunk if the water drops again

The government is also preparing a rather unusual emergency measure. Two 80-metre-long barges will be placed on standby near Paks. If the Danube level falls rapidly again before the permanent weir is completed, the government could deliberately sink the vessels at a controlled location.

According to Magyar, this could temporarily raise the river level by up to 20 centimetres, helping prevent a complete shutdown of the nuclear power plant.

The measure is being considered because water levels have already fallen to exceptionally low levels this summer. Although the Danube rose temporarily in recent days, forecasts indicate that it could soon fall below -140 centimetres again.

Paks shutdown could cost billions

The government says the extraordinary intervention is justified by the potential economic consequences of losing the plant’s full output. Magyar said a complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant would impose a cost of at least HUF 50 billion per month on the state budget. By comparison, the measures currently ordered by the government are expected to cost around HUF 6 billion.

The low water levels have already affected the plant’s operation. One of the units was previously operating at reduced capacity, although the third turbine of Unit 2 was switched back on earlier this week after the Danube rose 19 centimetres above its recent low. The latest trend, however, suggests that the river could soon return to extremely low levels.

Read more about Hungary’s water and energy crisis on Daily News Hungary.

Paks has warned about the problem before

The long-term implications of increasingly low Danube water levels have also raised concerns among experts. Paks deputy mayor István Barnabás recently called on the government to examine all possible solutions for guaranteeing the nuclear plant’s long-term cooling-water supply in changing climatic conditions.

Meanwhile, Attila Aszódi, former government commissioner responsible for the Paks expansion, recently told 24.hu that he had warned the government as early as 2018 that future Danube water levels and temperatures could create problems for the reliable operation of the plant once the new reactors come online.

World.title: Hungary’s relentless heat may finally break – here’s when widespread rain could arrive
World.content:
After weeks of scorching temperatures and desperately dry conditions, Hungary may finally be heading for a major weather change. Forecasts currently suggest that a slow-moving weather front could bring widespread rain across the country next week – although another burst of extreme heat is expected before then.

Relief may finally be on the way

A persistent area of high pressure over Western Europe has continued to draw hot, dry air from Africa towards Hungary, keeping temperatures exceptionally high and rainfall scarce. According to meteorologist László Molnár, however, the current weather pattern could finally change next week.

“According to the current situation, a wavy frontal system will reach Hungary at this time, which could finally bring more significant, nationwide rainfall,” he told 24.hu.

Current forecasts suggest that the frontal system could arrive around 17–18 August, with the most significant rainfall expected on 18–19 August.

Across the country, 10–30 millimetres of rain could fall on average, potentially providing some much-needed relief after weeks of severe dryness.

But the heat is not over yet

There is still plenty of hot weather to come before the rain arrives. Temperatures could reach 31–37°C on Monday, while some parts of Hungary could see highs of 39°C on Tuesday. A weak front is expected to arrive overnight on Tuesday, bringing temporary relief on Wednesday and Thursday, when temperatures are forecast to fall to around 27–34°C.

The respite will be short-lived, however. From Friday, temperatures are expected to climb again, with highs of 35–40°C possible over the weekend. The chance of meaningful rainfall will remain very low.

Photo: Anadolu/Németi Róbert

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The rain could bring some relief from the drought

The anticipated rainfall would be particularly welcome after Hungary’s prolonged dry spell. The country’s upper soil layers have been suffering from severe moisture shortages, while recent weather fronts have generally produced only isolated and sometimes intense thunderstorms rather than the widespread, soaking rainfall needed by agriculture and nature.

The extreme heat has made the situation even more difficult. Hungary has experienced repeated periods of temperatures around or above 35°C, with authorities previously issuing the country’s highest-level heat warning.

The forecast rainfall next week could therefore bring a significant, if temporary, improvement.

Another dry spell could follow

Unfortunately, the change may not last for long. From 20 August, an area of high pressure is expected to return, bringing another period of warm and dry weather. Current forecasts suggest that these conditions could persist until around 25 August, when another rain-bearing front may arrive.

For now, however, there is at least some hope on the horizon: after weeks of heat and drought, Hungary could finally see widespread rain in the middle of next week. Forecasts can still change several days ahead, particularly regarding the exact location and amount of rainfall.

World.title: Bad news for beer drinkers, good news for the sweet-toothed? 20 August celebrations prices and Hungary’s cake revealed
World.content:
Hungary’s 20 August national holiday celebrations will be significantly cheaper this year, with the government planning to spend around HUF 4 billion on the three-day programme instead of the HUF 18 billion originally budgeted by the previous government.

The celebrations will also feature a much shorter fireworks display, a major audiovisual show projected onto Parliament, concerts and family programmes across Budapest. However, visitors looking forward to the heavily discounted beer available at previous celebrations may be disappointed.

Government spokesperson Éva Magyar announced the details at a press conference on Wednesday, while representatives of the organising Centrum Production, Mátyás Kálmán and Dániel Besnyő, presented the programme. Read more details here: Major changes are coming to Hungary’s 20 August celebrations this year: here’s what’s in store

A cheaper 20 August celebration with a different concept

The celebrations will begin on 19 August and are designed around the theme of telling Hungary’s thousand-year history while offering something for different generations. The organisers said they did not expect everyone to be interested in the same type of programme, but wanted visitors to be able to find something they could connect with.

Kossuth Square, for example, will once again become an entertainment venue after the traditional daytime ceremonies, while Margaret Island will offer family-friendly activities during the day and a light exhibition in the evening.

The celebrations will take place at ten major locations across Budapest, including Kossuth Square, Parliament, Margaret Island, City Park, Buda Castle and the area around St Stephen’s Basilica.

Beer will be more expensive than last year

While the overall event will cost considerably less, there is less positive news for visitors hoping for the exceptionally cheap beer prices offered in previous years. Last year, beer was available for as little as HUF 380 (EUR 1) at the celebrations. This year, the organisers said they would cap the price of beer, but will not use state funding to subsidise it.

According to Mátyás Kálmán, a half-litre beer will cost less than HUF 1,000 (EUR 2.75), while half a litre of mineral water will cost less than HUF 500 (EUR 1.4). The organisers stressed that the price cap will be maintained despite the absence of state support.

Hungary’s 2026 national cake has also been announced

The press conference also revealed the winners of this year’s national cake competitions. The Bíborfehér (“Purple-White”) created by master confectioners László Balogh, Zoltán Balogh and Roland Kis of Kézműves Cukrászda in Gyula has been named Hungary’s Cake 2026.

The cake combines forest berries, roasted almonds, a smooth sour-cream mousse and curd cheese, with sweet blackcurrant wine adding a distinctive flavour. Chocolate, vanilla and lemon are also part of the creation, while freeze-dried raspberries are used as a finishing touch.

The same confectionery won the title last year, making this its second consecutive victory.

The Sugar-Free Cake of the Year 2026 was won by the team from Promenád Café in Balatongyörök with its Szilvafácska (“Little Plum Tree”) cake. The dessert centres on plum, combined with walnut and milk chocolate, while cinnamon mousse and green tea provide additional flavours.

Both winning cakes will be available to taste from 20 August at the Hungarian Flavours Street at Várkert Bazaar and at nearly 500 confectioneries across Hungary.

To protect the quality and authenticity of the winning cakes, their recipes will not be made publicly available until early 2027. Until then, only members of the Hungarian Confectionery Industry Association will be officially permitted to produce them under the prescribed conditions.
