World.title: ‘There was no precedent’: The moment that had Alone producers terrified
World.content:
CultureTV & radioReality TV ‘There was no precedent’: The moment that had Alone producers terrified Karl Quinn August 12, 2026 — 8:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For producers and contestants alike, making Alone is all about anticipating risks and being prepared to meet them. But as viewers of the latest season of the Australian iteration will know, this year the survival competition broke the sort of new ground nobody wanted: a contestant went missing. “It was a world first, which is why the panic levels were so high,” says executive producer Riima Daher. “There was no precedent, nothing to fall back on in this scenario.” Former refugee Arash ascribes his behaviour to going into “survival mode”. SBS When Afghanistan-born wrecking-yard worker and taekwondo champion Arash went AWOL after 26 days, Daher says, “honestly, the first thought was ‘Is he dead?’ I was absolutely terrified. You worry that something really bad has happened, the sorts of things you don’t want to think about, but the sorts of things that can happen in the woods sometimes. And you start to check the water to make sure he hasn’t fallen in there.” The Sapmi region of northern Finland, where this season was filmed, is home to bears, wolves and reindeer, all of which posed potential threats to the 10 contestants from the other end of the Earth. But Arash’s disappearance – leaving behind the GPS tracker and emergency phone he was supposed to carry at all times, as well as his camera equipment – was not down to any of those things. It was, rather, the result of some sort of brain snap.



Though he declined to answer questions from this masthead, Arash does offer some insight into what happened in the episode that aired on Wednesday night. In a voiceover as he is being extracted by boat, Arash attempts to explain what was going through his mind when he ditched everything and wandered away from his camp. “I grew up in a war zone. I crossed seven countries with no documents. I’ve been lost in the sea, slept in the jungle, and I think this experience activated a survival mode that I know the best,” he said. “And when I get in that mode, the rules do not matter. I only rely on myself. All I was thinking was just to survive.”



He labelled his behaviour a “blunder” that had cost him a “very beautiful great opportunity” to change his life by winning the $250,000 prize for whichever contestant stays the longest. “I made a mistake, and I take full responsibility for it,” he said. “That will stay with me for the rest of my life.” It will stay with Daher and her team, too. Riima Daher and team search frantically for Arash. SBS At the height of the panic, there were “about 15 or 20 people” on the ground searching for Arash. “We called on people who weren’t even part of our rescue team to help,” Daher says. The six or seven hours it took to find him was, she says, “the most scared I’ve ever been personally or professionally. You question your career choices. I’m like, ‘Why am I not just working on Love Island? Everyone’s in the villa. What am I thinking?’ And you do start to fear the worst. You start to spiral, you start to see headlines.”



Did you see yourself in the dock in a courtroom? Related Article Reality TV Alone Australia’s new season is ‘the polar opposite’ of what we’ve seen before “One hundred per cent I did, I can’t lie. And then you retrace your steps. You go, ‘Did I do everything I’m supposed to do? Where are the holes in my responsibility?’” And when you finally did locate him? “We could have killed him.” Despite the anxiety he had caused, the producers didn’t immediately want to pull Arash from the contest. “You always want to give the participants as much rope as possible,” Daher says.



The problem was, he couldn’t articulate why he had done what he had, and that cast serious questions over his mental state. “It was a serious breach,” Daher says. “I mean, it placed him in real danger, it placed all of us in danger to have to go and look for him. Had he been able to explain it in a way that made sense, perhaps we could have left him in there, but he couldn’t. “From a duty-of-care point of view – as well as a rule-break point of view – we just couldn’t put him back in.” Alone Australia is on SBS, Wednesdays from 7.30pm

World.title: The dairy farmer behind latest grocery price comparison app
World.content:
A dairy farmer has launched a free app that lets shoppers check their online grocery list to see which local supermarket is the cheapest on the day.

CheckMyTrolley is the latest grocery comparison tool to hit the market as the cost of living continues to bite into household budgets.

Will Duff said people are surprised to learn he's behind a new food price-checking app when he tells them what he does for a day job.

"People get thrown back quite a bit when I say I'm a dairy farmer and I'm not an IT person but I am the person behind the idea."

He works at a dairy farm on the Taiere plain near Dunedin.

After returning from a decade working in Australia, he found grocery prices had become a pinch-point for most and tested his theory in a social media post that received more than 100,000 views.

People agreed supermarket shopping had become a part-time job if they wanted to check for the best prices.

"To me, that was pretty simple to go, right, this is a problem in New Zealand and I think building this app is going to actually make a huge difference for New Zealanders to save money."

Duff took his idea to a developer and CheckMyTrolley launched a few months ago on Apple devices with android coming soon. It allows shoppers to create an online list and check which supermarket is the cheapest.

"If I can help New Zealanders, I guess that's my drive, that's what I'm hoping to get is to be like, look, someone's created this app that helps New Zealanders, saves money, well, hopefully saves a little bit of money for you. And I guess that's a success for me."

He saved $148 using the app in one month.

"It's easier to compare over those prices and be like, right, I'm definitely not shopping there because that's too expensive. I guess everyone feels it in New Zealand."

CheckMyTrolley is the latest grocery comparison app to launch, joining Grocer and Grosave, each with different features.

Both have roughly 70,000 users.

Consumer NZ researchers recently analysed the online prices of a basket of 16 everyday grocery items, across eight weeks and four cities, to find New Zealand's cheapest supermarket. Pak n Save came out top.

Consumer's head of research and advocacy Gemma Rasmussen said people prefer to shop online to stick to their budgets.

"It means that they can really stick to a list and purchase just that, whereas sometimes when you go into the store you might deviate a little bit," she said.

"Being able to compare your whole shop online can lead to some pretty significant savings."

A recent Consumer NZ survey shows the cost of groceries is a top financial concern for households, a change from five years ago when it ranked below rent and power.

"We are seeing a massive swing towards buying the private label brands with shoppers they're just trying to make any way they can to purchase their food as cheaply as possible."

Grocer is still a hobby project, according to its developer Roc Wong, a software engineer.

Grocer developer Roc Wong SUPPLIED

He started the price comparison app five years ago.

"I started this as a side hockey project to collect the price data points from the supermarkets, website apps, and help myself do a bit of comparison."

And so far the data has been interesting, some pricing patterns have emerged.

"I have this observation also backed by the data I've collected so far, a lot of products' prices have a high-low pattern," he said with one week being high and the next low.

"This is very common for processed goods like ice cream, chocolate, whereas the fresh produce is more bound to the season."

Wong said the supermarkets have not expressed any concern about the app or data scraped for it.

Dunedin student Lara Bishell uses the CheckMyTrolley app to compare prices and said over the last month she has saved $100.

"I'm on the app just to save some money because I don't eat meat and plant based foods can be expensive," she said.

"It was interesting because I thought Pak'nSave was the cheapest but when I was looking it was telling me Woolworths or New World."

Bishell said a brand of tofu she buys is $3 cheaper at one supermarket.

"It feels good because I try to be frugal and save. It makes me feel less stressed about money and supermarket shopping."

Christchurch based software developer Tim Hong co-founded the grocery price-comparison app Grosave in April last year, with Murray Wong and Jayon Thomas.

Christchurch based software developer Tim Hong co-founded Grosave in April last year. SUPPLIED

"There's this huge transparency issue for pricing that's why we did this first but as we expand this we want to make sure people have a healthy and affordable diet, that's our vision."

Hong said they plan to soon add a function to enable users to buy online, from the app, clicking through to the supermarket's cart.

As for scraping supermarket's data, he said Foodstuffs and Woolworths are yet to get in contact.

"We don't want to cause any trouble to their service. The data is publicly available so I think it's fine we haven't heard anything from the big players."

World.title: Māori and Pacific people have lower stigma towards mental illness  - study
World.content:
Māori and Pacific people have a lower stigma towards people with mental illness than Europeans and Asians, according to a University of Otago study.

It found integrating Māori and Pacific attitudes towards mental illness into health campaigns may result in a less judgemental New Zealand.

Using data from the long running New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS), the study examined more than 58,000 participants' 'ratings of warmth' towards those with mental illness.

Lead author Issac Jamieson told RNZ the study analysed the relationship between ethnicity and mental health stigma in Aotearoa.

"Stigma has many different components to it, and we focused just on one stigmatising attitude, which was how participants rated their feelings of warmth towards those with mental illness. Now, the findings challenged previous narratives held by past research and the general public to some extent that certain ethnicities or indigenous populations are synonymous with greater mental health stigma."

Jamieson said a holistic or a collective worldview that Māori and Pacific people hold might be the reason for the lower stigma findings in the study.

He also pointed to Māori health models such as Te Whare Tapa Whā, in which mental wellbeing is one of four pillars of overall health and wellbeing.

Other Māori health and wellbeing models recognise that individuals are live in wider environment systems that impact them, he said.

"One of the other things we discuss as well is how Māori have developed a language around mental health that may actually be less stigmatising than what we traditionally use today. So we talk about the example of ADHD, which stands for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, and Māori have developed the word, aroreretini, which means the mind goes to many things.

"Culture is really central to us understanding and reducing mental health stigma. And I guess to better understand the stigma associated with mental health challenges, we must better understand how different cultures define and perceive these challenges.

"For every culture has these strengths or maybe different ways of viewing mental health challenges, which may actually help us to have less stigmatising language or methods."

It was important that mental health campaigns and research not only acknowledged, but also integrated different cultural perspectives when it came to tackling mental health stigma, he said.

"So what we really want is some culturally responsive interventions that take into account these different world views."

Jamieson said despite positive shifts over the past couple of decades, the stigma of mental illness continues to be prominent in society.

"The research is still saying that there's still work to be done. And the more research we have around trying to understand what might be associated with more or less stigma or how different cultures perceive these challenges, we're gonna be better placed to try and actually reduce it, reduce the stigma of mental health and improve the livelihood of those struggling at the moment."

The study was published in Kotuitui: New Zealand Journal of Social Sciences Online, authored by Issac Jamieson, Taylor Winter, Ririwai Fox, Aaron Hapuku, Edmond Fehoko, Andre Mason, Chris Sibley and Damian Scarf.

World.title: 'Huge demand on services': North Shore ambulance patients diverted to Whāngarei
World.content:
Some Auckland ambulance patients are being taken to Whāngarei Hospital because North Shore Hospital is too full to take them.

That is despite the much smaller Whāngarei Hospital already struggling with extremely high patient numbers this winter.

RNZ understands diversions were taking place on Tuesday night which was also very busy at Whāngarei's emergency department.

Diversions were happening also last week.

Tim Malloy is a GP for Coast to Coast healthcare group which has a clinic in Auckland's most northern town Wellsford, just shy of the Northland border.

He was sent a letter by St John Ambulance last week telling him any patients from the northern part of the Rodney district who needed to go to an ED would be taken to Whāngarei. They were normally serviced by North Shore.

That was "due to the huge demand on the services at North Shore Hospital", he said.

RNZ understands Whāngarei was already under serious pressure itself. It is about half the size of North Shore.

Health NZ director of operations Brad Healy said it was a "very small number" of ambulances who were actually diverted to Whangarei.

"This practice is not unusual and used at times to manage demand and ensure patients can receive care as quickly as possible. In some instances, depending on the location of the patient, Whangārei Hospital is closer in travel time than North Shore Hospital," he said.

Malloy said the letter was the first his practice had ever received about the ambulance diversions.

Busy winter in northern Auckland

This winter was the busiest Malloy had seen in 37 years as a GP.

Patients in Coast to Coast's urgent care clinic were sometimes waiting five hours and staff have had to be brought in on their days off to help, he said

"When you have 15 people waiting for you and you have a serious illness you are trying to manage in a patient while you wait for an ambulance to arrive, and all these patients are just having to wait, it's incredibly stressful. For all of us," he said.

Most of the patients coming into urgent care had respiratory infections. The cases seemed to last longer - and there were a growing number of secondary infections, he said.

There were very high numbers of people with influenza.

Malloy wanted to see a campaign to encourage people to get vaccinated against flu - and for those vaccinations to be free.

It would help people stay healthy, in particular to avoid serious complications.

That would help the whole health system, he said.

World.title: Auckland Hospital's flea-infested carpet might not be replaced for decades
World.content:
Health NZ can not put a timeframe on the replacement of Auckland Hospital's flea-infested carpet, with one former project manager warning it could take decades.

Staff at Auckland Hospital have made hundreds of reports about fleas and other insects in the past year.

HNZ's group director of operations for Auckland Dr Michael Shepherd previously told RNZ that work to replace carpeted areas with vinyl flooring was underway across its facilities, but this had to be carefully planned to minimise disruption, as it often required clinical services to be temporarily relocated.

"This work is scheduled for periods when suitable decant space is available, allowing services to be temporarily relocated while minimising disruption to patient care," he told RNZ on Wednesday.

But a previous senior project manager for Auckland Hospital - who RNZ has agreed not to name - said about 40 wards and departments had carpeted hallways, with the carpet installed in 2003 when the building opened.

They said at the pace work was going, it would take more than four decades to complete.

On install, the lifespan of the carpet was five to 10 years, they said - meaning it was well overdue to be replaced - and fleas had emerged as a major issue in 2014.

Health NZ could not put a date on the programme's completion, and did not respond to these specific claims.

"While we do have decant space available at times when hospital occupancy is lower, particularly outside peak winter periods, capacity requirements vary throughout the year," Shepherd said.

"As a result, the programme remains flexible and is planned around the operational needs of the hospital.

World.title: 'Most challenging of recent times': SIS warns of intensified threats to NZ's security
World.content:
The NZSIS is warning that geopolitical upheaval has intensified threats to New Zealand's safety and security.

In its latest assessment, the agency's director-general of security Andrew Hampton described the threat environment as being the most challenging of recent times.

"The kinds of malign behaviours and activities we have seen over the past 12 months are proving even more threatening for a country like New Zealand given its size and location in the South Pacific," he said.

Hampton said this country's public and private sectors were being targeted by foreign states and their proxies to gain access to critical assets including intellectual property, innovative technology and other non-public information.

"States' pursuit of strategic advantage is affecting New Zealand's interests. Non-public information is increasingly sought, including policy insights, intellectual property or data sets. States are unsentimental in their pursuit of this information," he warned.

"They may seek to dupe a government insider with a lucrative job offer or try to bust through a cyber backdoor. Homegrown technological innovation, particularly that which has potential military uses like our rapidly expanding space sector, is also under threat from state-sponsored espionage."

The SIS said diaspora community groups in New Zealand were being unfairly targeted by foreign states and their proxies seeking to limit their democratic rights and freedoms.

"Authoritarian states seek to keep diaspora populations abroad under tight control so they can maintain their official narrative and lower the risk of perceived dissent. State proxies use deception and at times corruption to build long-term influence with decision makers," Hampton said.

However, he warned that New Zealand also faced homegrown threats.

"Extremist voices from within our shores are contributing to a polarised information environment, and we see some of these voices advocating for the use of violence," he said.

"Young and vulnerable people in New Zealand are particularly susceptible to violent extremist narratives, which are more readily accessible online and now exacerbated by artificial intelligence."

Hampton said that both antisemitism and Islamophobia were among the concerning themes seen running through the violent extremist environment in New Zealand, alongside "other hateful narratives".

"Such harmful rhetoric should be called out early to stop it from festering and crossing the threshold to violence."

The SIS said there were also New Zealanders, some deliberately and others unwittingly, acting in the interests of foreign states.

"This could be by handing over non-public information or influential New Zealanders self censoring to stay onside with a foreign state. Such behaviour harms our democracy and our economy," it said.

The SIS said the national terrorism threat level remained at possible, with lone actor attacks being the most likely scenario.

The agency's issued new resources, including new protective security advice for Māori businesses and entities - Tiaki Pakihi Māori, which it said was discussed with leaders at a recent meeting of the National Iwi Chairs Forum.

"As I've said previously, we're not trying be alarmist or cause fear," Hampton said.

World.title: Christopher Luxon's leadership victory: You come at the King, you best not miss
World.content:
Analysis: National MPs who tried and failed to take down Christopher Luxon on Wednesday should be embarrassed and ashamed.

After plotting, leaking, and destabilising the party enough to pressure the National Party leader into calling an emergency in-person caucus meeting, the agitators could not get the job done.

In the process they've left Luxon wounded and limping his way to the election with a caucus, which as far as the public is concerned, is more interested in itself and its own ambitions than the cost-of-living crisis much of the country is enduring.

Luxon has identified one of the detractors and made him the fall guy. After fleeing Parliament for Auckland, the prime minister sent out a statement saying Defence Minister Chris Penk was to blame for the destabilisation after launching a leadership challenge this week, resulting in the confidence vote.

"This makes his role untenable and as such I have removed his portfolios," Luxon said.

By 8pm Penk had given up any pretense he could stay on in the party and announced he wouldn't seek re-election in November in his safe seat of Kaipara ki Mahurangi - a seat once held by Sir John Key.

National MP Chris Penk arrives at Parliament ahead of urgent Caucus meeting on 12 August. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

It's a bold call to punish his opponents, and a bit of a farce when he's only gone after one of what is clearly a group of disgruntled MPs.

But he could hardly demote senior MPs like Erica Stanford and Chris Bishop - two of his best operators - who were clearly being lined up as the true leadership contenders.

So for now Luxon has to leave it at one and hope that that has sent a strong enough message to the rest of the anti-Luxon brigade to keep their grievances to themselves until the election has run its course.

The instigators of a second round of confidence vote chaos have now had their chance and must accept the mess the party is now left with until the election.

Luxon looked like he had been through 12 rounds in the ring when he fronted the media after a three hour caucus meeting.

He spoke for a total of 75 seconds where he confirmed he had won a confidence vote, and had the full confidence of a caucus that was "united and determined to win this election".

In a complete repeat of his April confidence vote, he made his remarks following the meeting in the Banquet Hall - the least prime ministerial room in Parliament - and took no questions from the waiting reporters.

Unlike in April he didn't label the whole saga a "media soap opera" or blame reporters for the speculation and rumour. Instead he trotted out National's tired promise to "fix the basics and build the future".

Yet National has failed in the basics of what is a functioning caucus - being unified behind its leader. Likewise it hasn't looked like a party with any idea who might be its leader tomorrow, let alone in the future.

Within hours of the short and sombre press conference ending, the party was trying to return to some sense of normality with a media advisory from Bishop about an announcement on Thursday morning and an education press release from Stanford.

Meanwhile, Luxon was straight back to Auckland to prepare for the arrival of the Vietnamese president, who up until 1pm on Wednesday would have been wondering who he would be meeting the next day.

RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

Exactly what Luxon said in the caucus room to persuade enough MPs to back him will never truly be known. Any leaks to the media would have to be taken with a grain of salt.

More surprising than Luxon successfully rallying his MPs to swing in behind him was the failure by his detractors to make a more convincing argument for change.

While Luxon's stared down his challengers, he's now crawling his way to election night with a target on his back.

Chances of him surviving after the election are slim and the uphill battle to get the party's polling up in the next 86 days has been made all the more difficult.

The pressure on Luxon intensified after he won the first confidence vote - it just ramped up again after coming through a second round.

Every blunder, gaffe, miscommunication or misjudgement will be analysed, scrutinised and tucked away as ammunition for a later date.

If Luxon can blow things out of the water in the next three months and get the party in a position to form a strong National-led government, not controlled by its coalition partners, he will have proven his opponents wrong.

World.title: Can National put the leadership questions behind them?
World.content:
National MPs are keen to put the leadership question behind them, and a former MP has told them to pull themselves together if the party has any hope of winning the election.

Following an emergency in-person caucus meeting on Wednesday, Christopher Luxon remains National leader and prime minister, having secured the confidence of his caucus.

As MPs left the capital and returned to their electorates it seemed, for a few hours at least, that that was that, until a further statement from the prime minister's office on Wednesday afternoon announced Luxon had sacked Chris Penk from all of his ministerial portfolios, and from Cabinet.

Penk, who had held the defence, veterans, space, GCSB, NZSIS, and building and construction portfolios, then announced he would stand down from politics altogether, and not seek re-election in November.

His statement did not address the allegations he was behind a leadership challenge, but it did say he backed National and Luxon to win the election.

Chris Penk. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

Luxon's office has confirmed to RNZ its position was that Penk was acting on his own behalf, a position backed up by rumoured challenger Chris Bishop, who said people did not launch leadership challenges on behalf of someone else.

However, former defence minister Wayne Mapp believed Penk had been made a sacrificial lamb.

Former defence minister Wayne Mapp. Pool / Fairfax Visuals

"You have to have at least someone be the fall guy, and you can't punish everyone who might have a different view. He's at the second level of the cabinet and doesn't have huge name recognition, and so he was chosen."

Mapp said there were four leadership challenges while he was an MP, but in every case there was a clear alternative.

He said it was notable that Luxon appeared at his brief press conference with his front-bench behind him, which showed the party was pulling together as a team and putting its best foot forward.

"I think they've got to do a bit of a reset in how they present themselves to the public. That press conference was very brief, no questions, not a lot of smiling faces there. So they're clearly going to have to do a bit of a reset. It's a little bit like a rugby team, the All Blacks who have lost a big game and they have to pull themselves together for the next game."

He, along with former National press secretary Janet Wilson, had earlier identified Stanford as the potential next leader.

Janet Wilson. RNZ

After the dust had settled, Wilson said while there had been numbers gathering force on Tuesday night, by Wednesday morning MPs were prevaricating.

"The fact that she was raised in dispatches, so to speak, in a media sense, and didn't speak to journalists as she arrived at Wellington Airport, signalled to me that she was absolutely going to be a contender, but that didn't occur. The whole thing's just laughable. It's a farce," she said.

Wilson believed Luxon and National's campaign had been "gazumped" by their own actions, and did not believe the matter had been settled.

"They are now facing endless questions of loyalty within the caucus, who backed who and why. His assertion that he had the numbers and the full support, and also his assertion that 'our caucus is united,' will be seriously questioned in coming weeks."

National MPs keen to move on

Leaving Parliament on Wednesday afternoon, National MPs were keen to put the leadership matter behind them.

Maungakiekie MP Greg Fleming, who on Tuesday evening was unable to say whether Luxon had his backing, now said he did.

Maungakiekie MP Greg Fleming. VNP/Phil Smith

Fleming said it had been "fantastic to re-assert the confidence" the caucus had in the prime minister, and did not think it would hurt National's chances at the election.

"I think it will actually strengthen, because it takes this subject out of play and gets the focus on all that I'm hearing on the doorstep, which is that people want us to carry on doing the job that we're doing of fixing the basics and building the future."

He was looking forward to returning to his electorate, and carrying on with the door-knocking he had originally had planned.

Commerce and consumer affairs minister Cameron Brewer said it had been a "great day" for the National caucus.

"We are re-emerged, re-launched, and re-energised, and we're going to win the election."

List MP Nancy Lu said the caucus did not want to be "distracted", while East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick said the caucus was "not disunited" and there would be no further leadership votes.

List MP Nancy Lu. VNP / Phil Smith

"We will not be back here in a couple of months. We are going to win the election."

ACT leader and Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour said it was a National Party political matter, but the government as a "common enterprise" was functioning well.

"It's been an awful lot of energy expended to end up exactly where they started. We need to be pointing the finger not at each other, but what we have achieved for New Zealand. And I actually think the government has a good story to tell."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said it was "irrelevant" whether or not Luxon stayed on as leader.

World.title: Pacific news in brief for 13 August
World.content:
Fiji

A Fijian military commander is calling for stronger military ties with Australia after attending Exercise Pitch Black 26.

Major General Jone Kalouniwai said closer cooperation would strengthen Fiji's command-and-control capabilities, intelligence support, and participation in regional exercises.

The call follows July's Vuvale Union and Ocean of Peace Alliance agreements between Fiji and Australia.

These treaties are commitments of integration in security, economies, and people between the two.

Tuvalu

Tuvalu's Police Force has sent four officers to be part of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in South Sudan.

In a statement, the government said three officers departed Tuvalu last week.

Prime Minister Feleti Teo acknowledged government concern for the wellbeing of the officers, but expressed confidence in the UN systems for the safety of personnel on peacekeeping missions.

According to the UN, more than 150 peacekeepers from the Pacific, predominantly from Fiji, were deployed somewhere in the world as peacekeepers, as of March this year.

Vanuatu

Vanuatu Prime Minister Jotham Napat has reportedly asked the country's President, Nikenike Vurobaravu, to revoke a pardon he granted to a convicted rapist.

The Vanuatu Daily Post reported that four men convicted on rape charges received presidential pardons at the end of July.

Napat said he intended to move for Parliament to review the president's pardoning powers, noting he has previously raised a similar concern with the president in May 2025.

Australia

Australia has tabled its Veitacini Mutual Defence Treaty with Fiji in the Senate.

The agreement establishes the Ocean of Peace alliance, committing each country to support the other if they are attacked.

Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong said it marked an important milestone in the way that the Pacific sees itself strategically.

The Vuvale Union Treaty was also tabled, which provides for more than a billion dollars in Australian grants and loans to Fiji.

Fiji

Fiji's Cabinet is expected to lay out its plans for constitutional reform next month.

Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga said a constitutional reform bill will be tabled in parliament before it goes to a referendum.

Cabinet is awaiting a report from the Constitutional Reform Commission, and Tuaraga said cabinet cannot agree to a makeup of the bill until then.

World.title: Ex-Wallabies, league star Brian Smith dies of cancer
World.content:
Wallabies prop Angus Bell is leading the tributes for dual rugby union international and former NRL star Brian Smith, who has died aged 59.

Smith, who played six Tests for Australia in 1987 and nine for Ireland after switching allegiance, had battled cancer.

Once described by former Wallabies coach Alan Jones as one of the world's most gifted players, Smith was most recently the Head of Sport at Scots College in Sydney, where Bell and many other Wallabies graduated from.

"He was coaching at the Scots school and coached a lot of us coming through the grades and I just wanted to say it's a really sad time," Bell said from Wallabies camp in Townsville on Wednesday.

"We're wishing the best for his wife and kids. He's an avid rugby person and helped a lot of individuals in the squad and in the Wallabies today, so just sending my condolences from both the Wallabies and myself."

Australia's 999th Wallaby's Test debut Isaac Henry will run the prospect of fresh ink past his wife but is otherwise assured he can make a permanent Wallabies mark after a hard-earned debut in Osaka.

Smith, who also played 43 games for Balmain and Eastern Suburbs from 1991 to 1994, coached Bell at GPS and NSW schoolboys' level when the emerging front-rower was only 16.

"Fair to say that I wouldn't have played as good or anywhere near as good without him," Bell said.

"Me, Jeremy Williams and Will Harris from the (Western) Force were really close with him and he was a great bloke, a great father and a great coach.

"So, yeah, very sad."

After playing schoolboys' rugby for Australia, Smith made his Wallabies debut under Jones in 1987, partnering Nick Farr-Jones in the halves and bagging 18 points from a try, five conversions and a penalty in a 65-18 win over South Korea.

Australian forward Angus Bell - in Wallabies camp in Townsville - paid tribute to his former high school coach and mentor Brian Smith. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

After his playing career, Smith coached in Japan and England, where he was the national team's attack coach, and served as Australia's sevens coach.

"Brian had been very unwell in recent months and was battling an aggressive cancer," Scots College principal Dr Ian PM Lambert wrote to school colleagues.

"This is very sad news for our College community and I know it will come as a shock to many of you who knew and worked closely with him.

"Our immediate thoughts are with Brian's wife Lisa, his daughters Ruby and Santana, and his son Chilli."

AAP

World.title: Former Hurricanes cricketer jailed for abusing 15yo girl
World.content:
A former Hobart Hurricanes cricket player will serve 10 months in prison for sexually abusing a child.

WARNING: This story contains details of child sexual abuse.

Aaron William Summers, 30, pleaded guilty to two counts of penetrative sexual abuse of a young person and one count of grooming in June in the Supreme Court of Tasmania, after having previously pleaded not guilty.

In court on Wednesday, he was sentenced to two-and-a-half years in jail, suspended after 10 months, meaning he will leave prison in April next year.

Justice Helen Wood told the court that Summers met the victim at a Hobart Hurricanes cricket match in 2017.

The following month, the 15-year-old girl attended another game and spoke to Summers, who was 21 at the time.

Aaron Summers was playing for the Hobart Hurricanes when he met the 15-year-old girl. (Getty Images: Robert Prezioso)

The pair began messaging on social media, and Summers arranged to pick her up from her home later that night.

The court heard he drove her to a local primary school, laid down a blanket, and sexually abused her twice.

Justice Wood told the court that Summers knew she was under the age of 17 and at high school, but did not ask how old she was.

"She thought they were meeting to talk; in reality, she represented a sexual opportunity to him," Justice Wood said.

"She was vulnerable because of her age and innocence; he had said nothing to warn her of his real motives."

The grooming charge related to social media conversations between Summers and the girl, in which Summers sent explicit photos of himself and requested photos from her.

"As a community, we look up to sportspeople; young people are likely to admire them, see them in a positive light," Justice Woods said.

"His role as a sportsperson gave him contact with young people, and enabled the commission of his crimes; this is an aggravating factor."

In November 2021, Summers pleaded guilty to charges in the Northern Territory, including possessing and transmitting child abuse material and transmitting communication with someone under 16 with the intention of procuring the recipient to engage in, or make, sexual activity.

Summers served three years and 11 months in prison in the NT. He was arrested on the day of his release and extradited to Tasmania to face these charges.

Cricket career 'at an end'

Justice Wood said Summers had experienced social isolation, loneliness and depressive symptoms while playing cricket in Tasmania and was spending excessive time on social media.

She said once he moved to the Northern Territory, he had established a successful career playing cricket in Australia and overseas and had a high profile.

"Due to the crimes, his future as a professional cricketer is at an end," she said.

Twenty months of the sentence was suspended, meaning Aaron Summers (left) is set for release in April next year. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Justice Wood said that Summers has accepted responsibility for his crimes and understood the impact his offending has had on his victims.

In the NT, he completed an intensive sex offender treatment program, which involved over 100 sessions, in which Justice Wood told the court he engaged appropriately and gained insight into his offending.

Justice Wood said when deciding on his sentence, she considered the lengthy jail time he had already served in the NT after the Tasmanian crimes were committed, and the significant progress he has taken towards his rehabilitation.

"[The] understanding he has about the harm he has caused and he is motivated to regain his life," she said.

Justice Wood imposed a sentence of two-and-a-half years, backdated to June 28 of this year, due to the time he has spent in remand.

She suspended the last 20 months of the sentence, with strict conditions, such as obliging him to comply with his probation officers and submit to psychological treatment.

The court heard that Summers would likely return to Western Australia, where he is from and his family live, to serve out his suspended sentence once he is able to leave prison in April next year.

World.title: 'Can't compete': Super coaches weigh into PNG Chiefs debate
World.content:
Trent Robinson won't be raging about the inequality of the tax breaks afforded to the PNG Chiefs, even if he believes the NRL's open market is no longer a "level playing field".

After Penrith winger Brian To'o became the sixth player wooed by the start-up franchise's tax-free wages, Panthers coach Ivan Cleary declared clubs "can't compete" with the bounty the Chiefs can provide from 2028.

Cleary revealed he was in tears when To'o informed him he would leave Penrith to join the Chiefs, who critics — led by South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett — have said now have an unfair advantage in attracting talent.

The salary cap has been an equaliser of talent but Bennett has claimed the NRL has eroded the competition's fairness by giving the Chiefs such an upper hand.

The Chiefs' advantages are in contrast to the few concessions afforded to the Perth Bears, who will enter the NRL next season.

Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

"It's not a level playing field and I think you can see that," said Sydney Roosters coach Robinson.

"We've got (it on) one (hand) where we feel like it's not a level playing field and the other where we feel like they need more assistance.

"We're going to debate … but do we want our game to grow?

"We're not going to stop at 19 (teams) … we should own the Pacific.

"If we want more money in the game, want to expand, we need more teams, so I think it's a positive thing — players are going to go."

Penrith were the latest club to feel that pinch when they gave To'o, who enters the last 12 months of his deal in November, a seven-day window to explore his options for 2028.

Premiership-winning Panthers Jarome Luai and Brian To'o will reunite in 2028 at the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The winger signed with the Chiefs without visiting PNG, joining Jarome Luai, Connor Watson, Alex Johnston and Zac Lomax in agreeing to deals with the NRL's 19th side.

Loading Instagram content

"I had a little moment the other day, just very sad that Bizza's going to be going," the usually stoic Cleary said.

"There would've been a few (tears) … It's just hard to imagine 'Biz' playing in any other jersey. But there's a few guys out there that I thought the same."

Since their rise to premiership dominance in 2020, the Panthers have become accustomed to salary cap pressure squeezing out key players.

But they are especially vulnerable after 2027, with the cashed-up Chiefs emerging just as they battle to hold on to co-captains Isaah Yeo and Nathan Cleary, as well as premiership players Paul Alamoti, Liam Martin and Moses Leota.

"I think everyone knows with the Chiefs, it's hard to match that stuff," Cleary said.

"It's not your average club, but if players want to go there, you can't compete."

Asked whether the Chiefs had unfairly skewed the player market, Cleary recalled some wisdom from Marty Gurr, who was on the coaching staff during his early playing days at Manly.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I remember when I first played 35 years ago, my first coach said to me 'rugby league isn't fair'," Cleary said.

"I think he was right. I've worked that out along the way. Whether it's fair or not, that's what the game's gone with. I can understand it."

Since overcoming the initial emotional blow of To'o's impending exit, Cleary has turned his attention to Penrith's task of retaining their stable of stars before September.

"We're very hopeful of having a few of them done (soon), you definitely don't want to be going into the finals doing this sort of stuff," he said.

World.title: Legendary boot-studder hangs up his own after 58 years with Port Adelaide
World.content:
He's outlasted big names and seen many more games without the limelight but after nearly six decades looking after boots for Port Adelaide Football Club, Alfie Trebilcock is hanging up his own.

A young butcher from Broken Hill who came to the club during 1968, the boot-studder enjoyed 11 SANFL premierships, one AFL premiership, and watched footwear evolve from ankle-high boots with wooden knock-in sprigs, to light-weight multi-coloured fashion statements.

"I came down here [to Adelaide] in 1961. My grandparents followed Port Adelaide so I started following them and used to go to their games and all that type of thing," Trebilcock told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"I got friendly with the runner, Harry Vincent, got talking one day and said I'd like to get into the club and he said, 'I'll keep an eye out for you'."

A position opened up in the boot department and Trebilcock was told to have a "talk to the sprigger" who was also a bootmaker.

"He said, 'Are you prepared to learn?', and I said, 'Oh yeah', so I did a seven-year apprenticeship with him," Trebilcock said.

"After those seven years he got leukaemia and said, 'You're going to have to take over', and I said, 'Gee whiz, I'm a butcher'.

" But I was pretty lucky because moulded soles were coming in then and so I took it on and I've been there ever since and enjoyed every single minute of it. "

But from the day Trebilcock started looking after the players' footwear in 1968 and up to 1976, the Port Adelaide Magpies played without winning a SANFL premiership.

"I was beginning to think I was jinx," Trebilcock said.

But the club won a flag in 1977 and another 10 during Trebilcock's time, as well as a 2004 AFL premiership with its AFL side, The Power.

"The 2004 AFL premiership was mighty.

"I always pictured standing on the MCG on Grand Final day, celebrating a flag. That dream came true in 2004. I'll never, ever forget that day."

Bobby to say farewell as well

Also retiring is fellow volunteer Bob "Bobby" O'Malley after 18 years at the club mixing water barrels and player rehydration bottles, and helping set up for training sessions.

Former Port Adelaide Power player and captain Travis Boak with Bob O'Malley during a game against Carlton. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

"I just loved being involved in this football club," he said.

"Port Adelaide was always a family club, and all my family barracked for Port Adelaide."

He will have his final home game with Port Adelaide against Melbourne on Saturday night.

Trebilcock will be saying goodbye after 58 years with the club.

He said he became "real friends" during this time with the late and great Russel Ebert OAM, who started with the Magpies the same year as him.

An Australian Football Hall of Fame member since 1996, Ebert played 392 games for the Magpies and remains the only SANFL player to win four Magarey Medals.

"He was a people's person," Trebilcock said.

"He was a player that never played a game of football in moulded sole boots. To the day he retired he still had knock-in sprigs.

"Every now and then you'd have to re-sprig his boots.

"As he got older his sprigging would change … then he got his Achilles problems and we made a [raised] heel for him."

The late Russell Ebert shares a laugh with Alfie Trebilcock at Port Adelaide Football Club. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

Ebert once said of Trebilcock that he loved the players and the club, and the players loved him.

"He can talk to any player at any time and would have the complete respect of the entire playing and coaching group … we couldn't have had the success we had without him," Ebert said.

The AFL awarded Trebilcock the Jack Titus Award for conspicuous service to the game in 2013.

He was awarded Life Membership at PAFC in 2013 and was inducted into its Hall of Fame in 2025.

PAFC chairman David Koch said the club was what it was today because of people like O'Malley and Trebilcock.

"Nearly 60 years of turning up, asking for nothing and giving everything to the club he loves," he said.

"On behalf of every player, coach and supporter we say thank you, Alfie, and thank you, Bobby. We are the club we are today because of people like you."

World.title: 'Nowhere to hide' for Australia's under-fire batters against Bangladesh
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan says some of Australia's batters are under pressure to make significant scores as the summer of cricket begins against Bangladesh in the Top End this week.

"If you're in the Australian Test team, and not performing regularly, there is just nowhere to hide," Cowan said on the ABC Cricket Podcast.

"And unfortunately, sometimes you get these weaker teams, and the expectation actually goes up. Cricket is hard enough, let alone with the weight of the world on your shoulders."

The Australian team is about to enter a 12-month period with potentially 21 Tests scheduled, including key away fixtures in India, South Africa and England.

Between June 2025 and the start of this cycle tomorrow, they played eight Tests, five of which were in Australia.

Australia played five of their eight Tests over the last 12 months at home, including the Ashes against England. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

"That's two careers, 21 Test matches. You could have two careers in that time. That's a lot of Test cricket," Cowan said.

That cycle begins in Darwin when they take on Bangladesh, a nation ranked ninth in the ICC Test rankings.

At the conclusion of the recent successful Ashes series against England, the average age of the Australian team was just under 34. This is a team that has played together and had great success for a long time.

The Test between Australia and Bangladesh starts on Thursday August 13 in Darwin, and you can hear every ball live on ABC Listen.

Cowan does not believe that playing lower-ranked opposition necessarily provides younger players with a chance to gain experience.

"I think you are trying to pick your best available team and there's always an opportunity to work through your portfolio of players, and they've done this in recent years, usually away from home and it's less opposition dependent and more condition dependent," he said.

The bowling attack has been well established for some time with the likes of Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon proving a recipe for success.

Where the questions creep in is around the batting line-up.

Jake Weatherald was given an opportunity to open the batting in the recent Ashes series but is yet to score an international century, with a top score of 72.

Jake Weatherald will be looking to impress in front of his home crowd in Darwin against Bangladesh (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Cowan expects the Northern Territory product to open in the first game, but says he remains under pressure.

"If Jake Weatherald doesn't get 100 in the next five Test matches, more than likely we'll find someone who will get an opportunity to open the batting. And so there's going to be some natural attrition over the coming months," he said.

He is not the only player who will be searching for form in this two-match series against Bangladesh. Marnus Labuschagne has averaged 26.61 with the bat in his last 20 tests and has taken time away from playing to focus on a training block in Queensland.

"After eight weeks of being able to just go back to my fundamentals and working on my game, spending hours and hours on the simple things, just my shots, working on my shapes and my technique as a whole, is something that I definitely needed," Labuschagne told reporters in Brisbane last week.

Loading Instagram content

It has been over 1,100 days since he last reached triple figures in a Test match back in 2023. Cowan believes these Tests could be a step in the right direction for Labuschagne.

"The greatest thing that you can have as a Test batsman is confidence. And confidence is only bred through performance," he said.

The youngest member of Australia's most recent Test team is Cameron Green. When the West Australian debuted in 2020, aged 21, he was touted as one of the best young talents in the country, but his recent form has some questioning his future in the side.

The now 27-year-old has played 37 Tests and has a batting average of 32.75 and a bowling average of 38.94, but Australian coach Andrew McDonald is resolute that Green remains a vital member of his side.

"We believe Cam Green is a very, very skilled player, and we believe, sometimes, his performances have been taken a little bit out of context," McDonald told SEN Radio.

"He's been contributing to this team, as have a lot of that top seven, in conditions that haven't been favourable to batters."

Cowan believes these two Tests present an opportunity for those out of form to find some form at a time when there is less pressure coming from other domestic players.

The last time Australia played a Test against Bangladesh was 2017, where Australia won the series 2-1. (Getty Images: /SOPA Images/LightRocket/Md Manik)

"They get first crack at it. And when there's no other cricket going on, there was a CA XI game that we'll come to, but there's no Shield cricket, there's no Aussie A tours, no-one's putting pressure on anyone," he said.

"It's a bit of a free swing. And in many respects, that should free the batters up to just go and play."

World.title: High school American footballer rattled by snake in helmet
World.content:
A high school American football player in the United States had every right to be rattled after finding a venomous snake inside his helmet during practice.

A team was going through its paces at Maumelle High school in Central Arkansas when a student felt unusual movement inside his headgear following warm-ups and brought his helmet to an assistant coach for inspection.

A slithering 2-foot (61cm) cottonmouth was discovered behind some padding.

The pit viper was so reluctant to exit the helmet that police officers had to pour water into it to force the snake out and into a bag.

Animal services technicians arrived a few minutes later, identified the snake as a deadly cottonmouth and took it to a wooded area far from the school.

Cottonmouths are the second-most-venomous snakes found in Arkansas.

Snake caught in bike chain bites woman The woman, in her 60s, was riding on a northern NSW rail trail when she ran over a two-metre snake that became trapped then bit her.

Animal services director Chris Davis said the player wore the helmet for nearly an hour and was fortunate he was not bitten.

"It was unreal," Davis said. "You had to kind of be there and take pictures to say this was real."

The player grabbed a different helmet and continued practice.

But the situation caused the head coach to reiterate to his team that players should examine their equipment carefully before using it, to check for insects or anything larger and more dangerous.

AP

World.title: 'Right to privacy': Scott speaks as Geelong concussion saga continues
World.content:
Geelong coach Chris Scott insists there has been no negativity around the playing group since Jake Kolodjashnij identified himself as the player at the centre of the Cats' concussion crisis.

Kolodjashnij, who is out of contract at season's end, faces an uncertain future after being ruled out of playing at any level this weekend.

The 31-year-old has played 11 AFL games this season, but was managed out of the team in round 19 and has since made one appearance in the VFL.

Geelong sits atop the VFL ladder and should make a deep run in the finals, potentially giving Kolodjashnij more opportunities to press his case for an unlikely new contract.

Chris Scott would not be drawn on the details of what's going on behind closed doors at Kardinia Park. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

The mental toll of the saga is unknown, with Scott simply saying Kolodjashnij had been supported by teammates and the club.

The dual premiership coach also refused to go into the exact reasons why Kolodjashnij had been ruled out for the club's matches against North Melbourne this weekend.

Kolodjashnij decided to name himself last Friday, a day after news broke of Geelong's controversial waiver for a previously unidentified player.

"I think any player deserves the right to privacy," Scott said.

"I understand that we are in a public game, and there's a quite savage desire to know certain things.

"I suspect the players are saying, 'Hey mate, if there is anything we can do …'

"In terms of the impact on our broader group, I haven't seen any negativity at all.

Jake Kolodjashnij (right) with brother Kade. Kade was forced into early retirement due to concussion issues. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

"I thought our players, as they have done for a long period of time, they just get on with the job.

"Difficult to compartmentalise sometimes, maybe this is a little more challenging than other times, but I'm still pretty confident we can do it.

"Because the situation is the status quo, I haven't felt the need to get an update [on Kolodjashnij].''

Geelong are facing a nervous wait after being issued with a belated "please explain'' for their handling of the secret concussion deal with Kolodjashnij.

The AFL has hired independent legal counsel to help decide on the case.

It was expected the league would wrap up its investigation yesterday, but the findings will likely not be released until early next week.

Kolodjashnij unavailable amid concussion saga Geelong confirms Jake Kolodjashnij will not be available for selection at VFL or AFL level this weekend as the spotlight continues to shine on the club over the controversial secret concussion waiver in his contract.

Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and former Cats president (now AFL Commission boss) Craig Drummond have been under fire since news broke of the controversial waiver.

"There's a part of me that would like to give an impassioned defence of certain people within our club, but I just don't think it would help at the moment," Scott said.

"Even if it is to our detriment, our responsibility, and especially my responsibility, is to respect his [Kolodjashnij's] privacy."

Kolodjashnij dealt with concussions in the 2024 season, but ultimately signed a two-year deal until the end of 2026.

Instead of receiving a definitive answer when forced to face the AFL concussion panel in 2024, Kolodjashnij was left in limbo about playing on or retiring.

His twin brother Kade, who played for the Gold Coast and Melbourne, prematurely retired in 2020 due to concussion.

Multiple AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern, and former number-one pick Paddy McCartin, have also been forced into retirement because of repeated concussions.

World.title: Everything you need to know as Australia hosts Bangladesh in the Top End
World.content:
Australia is hosting Bangladesh in a rare Test series this August, as winter cricket hits the Top End.

The two teams will play two Tests, the first of which gets underway in Darwin on August 13 at Marrara Stadium.

The second starts on August 22 in Mackay, where Harrup Park will become the 12th ground to host a men's Test match in Australia.

You can listen to live coverage of both Tests on the ABC Listen App, or follow the ABC Sport live blog.

'Nowhere to hide' or free swing?: ABC Cricket Podcast

It is the first time in 23 years that Bangladesh will tour Australia for a Test series.

Here's everything you need to know.

When does Australia play Bangladesh?

The first Test gets underway on Thursday, August 13, with the first session starting at 10am ACST in Darwin, NT.

That means the start time is 10:30am AEST (Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania), 10:00am in South Australia and the Northern Territory, and 8:30am in Western Australia.

The second Test starts on Saturday, August 22, with the first ball again set to be bowled 10:00am AEST in Mackay, Queensland.

That is 10am in Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania, 9:30am in South Australia and the Northern Territory, and 8am in Western Australia.

Each Test is scheduled for five days.

Where are the Tests being played?

Australia played South Africa at Marrara Stadium last year in a T20 international. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

August is not normally cricket season in Australia, but officials are taking advantage of the dry season in the north to take these matches to the tropics, with Darwin and Mackay hosting the Test matches.

Darwin's Marrara Oval will host just its third ever men's Test match and first since Sri Lanka visited in July 2004.

Australia have a 100 per cent winning record in Tests in Darwin, winning by an innings and 132 runs against Bangladesh in 2003, following that up with a 149-run victory against Sri Lanka the year after.

Australia has also played four ODIs in Darwin, all against Bangladesh and all resulting in emphatic victories.

In T20Is it's a slightly different story though, with South Africa sharing the spoils across two matches at the venue last year.

Mackay's Harrup Park has never hosted a men's Test match before and will become the 12th venue in Australia to do so.

Harrup Park in Mackay will become the 12th ground to host a men's Test match in Australia. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

The ground did host a youth Test match last year between Australia and India's under 19 sides, a low-scoring match won by India by seven wickets.

There have been three ODIs at the ground, two of them involving Australia. Again, South Africa were the opponents in 2025 and, again, the spoils were shared.

The only other ODI took place during the 1992 Cricket World Cup between India and Sri Lanka.

Given that Mackay averages 313.2 millimetres of rain in February — the wettest month on average across the year for the city — it's perhaps not a surprise that rain meant that the match was abandoned after just two balls were bowled.

That was even after a helicopter hovered above the pitch in an attempt to dry it out.

Australia's women have played three ODIs (in 2021) and two T20Is (in 2024) at the ground, winning all but one game.

Who is playing?

Pat Cummins returns for Australia's first Test of the season. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Mark Brake)

Australia has named a strong squad, with front-line bowlers Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all returning following their injury lay offs.

Such impressive bowling depth has seen Michael Neser miss out, the luckless Queenslander then suffering a hamstring injury in any case that will keep him out of contention.

It is, essentially, a full strength team, something Bangladesh skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto, is pretty impressed about.

"I personally liked the fact that they have chosen their full-strength team," he said earlier this month in an interview with ESPN Cricinfo.

"They are not taking us lightly. I think our team has earned this respect."

Najmul Hossain Shanto will lead Bangladesh in Australia. (Getty Images: Sameera Peiris)

Disappointingly for Bangladesh, they come into the series missing two key weapons in lightning-fast seamer Nahid Rana, who has been ruled out due to a left-side strain, and Shoriful Islam, who has a hurt hamstring.

Then, key spin bowler Taijul Islam suffered a blow to the hand in the warm up game and did not bowl at all in the second innings.

The 23-year-old Rana is one of the form bowlers in world cricket, capable of delivering the ball at speeds in excess of 150km/h. He has already taken 44 wickets in international cricket this year — the most by any bowler — at an average of 18.31.

On a positive note, Litton Das recovered from a calf injury he picked up during the home ODI series against Australia in June.

Batting is a problem for the tourists though — chief selector Habibul Bashar said the selection of 33-year-old lefty Soumya Sarkar was as a result of "a bit of desperation". Hardly a ringing endorsement for a man who has not played Test cricket since 2021.

Australia Squad Bangladesh Squad Pat Cummins (c) Najmul Hossain Shanto (c) Scott Boland Amite Hasan (wk) Alex Carey (wk) Ebadot Hossain Cameron Green Hasan Mahmud Josh Hazlewood Jaker Ali (wk) Travis Head Khaled Ahmed Josh Inglis (wk) Litton Das (wk) Marnus Labuschagne Mehidy Hasan Miraz Nathan Lyon Mominul Haque Steven Smith Musfik Hasan Mitchell Starc Mushfiqur Rahim (wk) Jake Weatherald Shadman Islam Beau Webster Soumya Sarkar Taijul Islam Tanzid Hasan Taskin Ahmed

Jake Weatherald, the first Northern Territorian to play a Test for Australia, was watching on in the crowd the last time the Australians played in Darwin.

He is a great chance to start on his home ground after a solid spell in the County Championship with Leicestershire, where he scored 483 runs at an average of 60.37, including scoring an unbeaten 104 against Glamorgan in Cardiff.

What form are Bangladesh in?

Bangladesh have only lost one of their last five Test matches. (Getty Images: Sameera Peiris)

Bangladesh come into this Test series off the back of a pretty decent run, having lost just one of their last five matches in the format.

Two thumping victories at home against Ireland in November 2025 were backed up by a hugely impressive 2-0 series victory against Pakistan in May this year.

That wasn't bad.

Now for the things that have been pretty poor.

A one off Test against Zimbabwe at the Harare Sports Club resulted in a calamitous defeat by an innings and 85 runs.

If that was bad, then the absolute thrashing the Cricket Australia XI delivered last week was even worse, the tourists bowled out for just 54 in their second dig as the CA XI won by an innings and 38 runs.

If it wasn't for Mehidy Hasan Miraz's unbeaten century in the first innings, rescuing his side from 6-110, who knows how bad the score would have looked as Corey Rocchiccioli took 6-83 in that first innings and Campbell Thompson took 8-25 in the second.

What is Bangladesh's record against Australia?

Jason Gillespie's stunning double century will go down in the annals as one of the best ever night watchman displays. (Getty Images: Hamish Blair)

Bangladesh have only ever played against Australia six times in their Test history — they've only played fewer Tests against Ireland (3) and Afghanistan (2) which, given Bangladesh have been a Test-playing nation since 2000, is a damning inditement on Australia's commitment to playing the minnows.

Somewhat surprisingly then, Bangladesh does have a Test victory against Australia to their name and, it was their most recent series in 2017.

Bangladesh claimed a stunning 20-run victory in Mirpur, with Shakib Al Hasan claiming player of the match honours after scoring a 133-ball 84 in the first innings and taking 5-85 with the ball in the final innings.

Australia got revenge in Chattogram, winning by seven wickets as Nathan Lyon took 7-94 and 6-60, while David Warner scored a brilliant, six-hour, 234-ball 123 in the first innings.

Australia's best ever batting performance in Chattogram though came 11 years before that, when night watchman Jason Gillespie scored a stunning unbeaten 201 to help Australia claim victory by an innings and 80 runs.

The first Test of that series in Fatullah had been won by the far more tense margin of three wickets, with Ricky Ponting's grinding 118 not out helping the Aussies over the line.

Bangladesh have never beaten Australia in Australia though, losing both their 2003 Tests by over an innings, in matches that took place in Darwin and Cairns.

Tech.title: How Google’s new Pixel 11 phones compare to last year’s models
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google just added four new phones to the Pixel family: the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. They’re slightly more expensive than their predecessors, but they come with some notable upgrades, including improved cameras and a new Tensor G6 chip that should deliver faster performance. The phones also have new photography tools, like Magic Capture, along with improvements to Gemini Intelligence, expanded Live Translate capabilities, and the ability to use Circle to Search directly through the camera.

To make deciding whether you’ll upgrade or hold onto your last-gen phone a little simpler, we’re focusing on comparing the specs of the 6.3-inch Pixel 11 and Pixel 10 models, as well as the 6.8-inch Pro XL models. If you’re curious about how the Pixel 11 Pro Fold compares to its predecessor (and to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 series foldables), we’ve got a spec comparison right here.

Before we get to the specs, here’s a breakdown of what’s new.

They’re more expensive, but you get more storage

The most obvious difference is that, like almost everything these days, they’re more expensive than before. The Pixel 11 starts at $899, $100 more than its predecessor, but Google has doubled the base storage to 256GB with 12GB of RAM. The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 — $100 more than the Pixel 10 Pro’s launch price — with the same 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, and is available with up to 1TB of storage and 16GB of RAM. Meanwhile, Google’s larger 6.8-inch Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 and offers the same storage and RAM configurations as the Pro.

Tensor G6 allows for even more AI features

Both the Pixel 11 and Pro phones run on Google’s new Tensor G6 chip, which the company claims should improve performance by up to 25 percent compared to its predecessor. The new chip also powers a host of AI upgrades, including improvements to Gemini Intelligence, which Google says can now pull more context from supported apps to proactively surface useful information. There are also new voice-to-text tools that remove filler words and clean up formatting, while writing assistance can use what’s on your screen to help draft, rewrite, and refine messages. Live Translate is also available on videos, podcasts, and voice messages, and Circle to Search now works directly through the camera, letting you identify objects, translate text, or search your surroundings without snapping a photo first.

The cameras get some notable upgrades inside and out

There are a number of camera improvements, too, along with new photography and video features. On the hardware side, the Pixel 11 has a slimmer camera bar that sits flush when paired with one of Google’s phone cases. It can also zoom in farther than its predecessor, reaching up to 30x for photos, while the Pixel 11 Pro series gets an updated 1/1.3-inch 50-megapixel sensor for its main camera and a redesigned telephoto sensor that Google says captures 32 percent more light. The Pro can also zoom up to 120x and features a 42-megapixel selfie camera. The Pro should be quicker at shooting in the dark, too, with Google claiming its Instant Night Sight can capture photos up to 4.5 times faster.

Google has made several software improvements as well. The new Magic Capture mode in the camera app automatically captures photos and videos to make them ready to share with a tap. Camera Looks let you create custom styles for photos, while the Pixel 11 Pro series can record stabilized video at up to 8K using Pro Stable Video with Video Boost. A new Creator Suite also features tools for trimming and rearranging clips, using a teleprompter while recording, and improving speech clarity, and it automatically saves clips to a designated project album.

How the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 compare

Those are some of the biggest changes, but they’re far from the only differences between the two lineups. For example, both the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro offer an Extreme Charging Mode that prioritizes charging over other tasks for a faster boost when you’re short on time. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL also gets HiLight, colored LEDs around the camera flash that can alert you to things, like calls when your phone is face down or when Gemini is activated.

For a closer look at those changes and everything else that separates the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro from their predecessors, we’ve broken down the specs side by side below.

Tech.title: ICE wants to give agents electrified gloves that shock people into compliance
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is aiming to spend up to $20 million on equipping officers and agents with specialized gloves that deliver painful electric shocks. These plans were outlined in a notice published by the Department of Homeland Security on Monday, with an unspecified quantity of the devices set to be delivered by March 2027.

The electrified handwear outlined in the contract is the CTG 5 GLOVE (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter), which manufacturer Compliant Technologies refers to as a CD3 (Conductive Distraction and De-escalation) device. Compliant Technologies describes it as “a great, humane, low-optics, de-escalation solution” that is “usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds.”

These are the gloves in question, which insidiously just look like a regular pair of protective gloves instead of something a comic book supervillain would engineer. Image: Compliant Technologies

The shock feature can be activated in a second using a switch located on the glove, which delivers a maximum voltage of up to 380V upon skin contact — closer to a dog’s shock collar than a taser device. Still, this “inhibits/ distracts the subject from performing coordinated muscle movement” according to the glove’s user guide. The same guide includes several warnings: don’t use more than one pair on a single individual, don’t shock people for more than 15 seconds, and don’t use it against high-risk populations such as children, or people who are elderly, pregnant, or disabled.

Because the CD3 gloves are not immediately identifiable as a weapon, Compliant Technologies describes them as an “invisible partner” that can be used to enhance “established tactics, techniques and procedures,” and calls them “The New Protocol in Peace Keeping.” Similar gloves from the same company have already been used by select police departments and jails in recent years, and two corrections officers were charged in 2022 for beating and shocking an inmate in two separate attacks.

ICE has demonstrated it can wield power with little oversight or accountability, fueled by an administration that encourages rough tactics. It has shown up at people’s doors to intimidate them, used mass surveillance, and killed people in broad daylight. The agency’s new shocking gloves will just be a new way to hurt people.

The Associated Press reports that the Department of Homeland Security is working on a response to its press inquiries, but offered “no immediate comment” on the purchase plans. In a statement to the publication, Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, questioned why the devices would be necessary for civil immigration enforcement:

“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do. Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”

Tech.title: Amazon gets out of the MMO game
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon is fully stepping back from MMOs. After saying last year that it would be halting “a significant amount” of its work on first-party AAA games, “specifically around MMOs,” Amazon will be handing over live operations of Throne and Liberty and Lost Ark in the West to other companies, according to announcements on Wednesday. Throne and Liberty will be taken over by FirstSpark Games and NC in Q4 2026. Lost Ark will be run by Smilegate starting in early 2027.

When Amazon announced the broader strategy shift in October, the developers of a third MMO, New World: Aeternum, announced plans to stop offering new content updates. As of January, you can’t buy that game anymore, and it will be taken offline on January 31st, 2027.

Amazon’s current gaming strategy focuses more on its Luna cloud gaming service, party games you can play on a TV with your phone (including ones with AI-powered Snoop Dogg and Arnold Schwarzenegger characters), and games that tie into other franchises Amazon is working on, like James Bond and Tomb Raider. Amazon’s gaming boss spelled it all out for me in a recent interview.

Tech.title: Guitar company D’Addario admits that AI music was used in a promotional video
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After weeks of controversy and speculation, music company D’Addario has admitted that AI, specifically Suno, was used as part of a recent promotional video. For nearly two weeks, the company has denied the allegations, even as evidence piled up against it. It offered various explanations, from low-quality exports, to combinations of plugins like Autotune introducing digital noise, and the use of AI-assisted mastering tools from LANDR and Logic. But now the company has edited its original Instagram post denying the use of generative AI to say it was wrong.

In a lengthy update to its post from July 29th (embedded at the bottom), it said:

We got this wrong. We’ve completed a full review and confirmed that Suno Studio was used to regenerate the original track. We shared inaccurate information, and we’re truly sorry … We do not support AI-generated music, and our process will reflect that going forward. We’ll require our employees and creative partners to disclose any use of generative AI, and we’ll more closely review everything we put into the world.

The post also apologizes for heavy-handed comment moderation, which saw posts from critics deleted and those users blocked. Rather than issue a new statement, it appears the company simply edited its original post five days ago, ten days after it was originally posted.

The original video was a demo for a new set of strings designed for extended-range guitars and low tunings. People immediately flagged the recording as suspicious. Things only got worse when D’Addario posted a clip of what it said were the Logic recording sessions of the demo track in question. But there were some very noticeable melodic and rhythmic differences between what people heard in the finished track and the Logic session.

Guitarist and YouTuber Rhett Shull managed to get his hands on the original Logic files directly from D’Addario, and it actually only added more fuel to the fire. Even in his rather generous assessment, Shull concluded that Suno was probably used at some point in the process, most likely to regenerate an original recording.

D’Addario has now admitted that Suno Studio was used to regenerate the track. This is just the latest AI controversy to shake the guitar world following the Fender CEO’s comments comparing bandmates to analog AI.

Tech.title: Google aims for influencers with the Pixel 11 Creator Suite
Tech.content:
Google knows creators are a big audience. The occupation is growing fast, and landing some influential names could be a major turning point for the Pixel’s market share. This year, Google is building features directly into its new Pixel lineup that it says can help creators record, organize, edit, and publish content faster and more efficiently than they could on other devices.
