Creator Suite is a new mode built into the Pixel 11’s camera app. The suite comes with features like a teleprompter, vocal enhancer, external microphone levels, and social media frame guides, which Google thinks will entice users who want to start building channels and have limited resources.

“ We really wanted to do something for those folks who are creating on their phones to make it easier to do that, make it faster to publish, fewer retakes, easier organization, and just streamline that workflow,” Isaac Reynolds, who leads the Pixel camera team, tells The Verge.

Reynolds says there is a massive gap between the top and bottom of the creator market, where the biggest creators have teams and resources, but the “hundreds of thousands of creators” in the bottom of the market need more accessible ways to make content.

“ They’re striving to put out content weekly or daily, even when they have full-time jobs,” Reynolds says. “They’ve got money coming in, it’s very enticing, but it’s not the replacement for their work yet.”

A frame guide with a cutout where the buttons show up on TikTok.

The arrival of TikTok has fundamentally reshaped what it means to be an influencer or a content creator, and the barrier to entry to do that work is lower than ever; all you need to do is film a selfie video. Over the last five or so years, the creator industry has both professionalized and de-professionalized: Influencers are signed to talent agencies and retain professional management, but there’s also been an explosion of cheap and fast content that is not tied to a specific personality — all that matters is whether it’s being served up to audiences. AI slop is everywhere. Follower count is increasingly irrelevant, and making content for the internet is, in theory, an attainable job for anyone, including people with other full-time jobs. Google recognizes that and wants those legions of people to use its phone.

Google has tried to court this demographic before, at least indirectly: Last year, it tapped Alex Cooper, host of the popular celebrity interview podcast Call Her Daddy, to make Google ads and post selfies on Instagram with the Pixel (she also promoted photo editing features at Made By Google last year). The partnership touted how Google’s ecosystem would help Cooper’s business as a content creator — scripting videos, shooting content, and keeping her team organized. Google now wants to reach the individuals who are pumping out content by themselves with just a phone.

Photography by David Imel / The Verge

Tech.title: The 7 biggest announcements of Google’s Pixel 11 launch
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is hosting a Pixel launch event on Wednesday night where it will show off its latest lineup of devices. But you don’t have to wait until then for all the news; we were able to check out the devices ahead of the event and take a look at everything Google’s unveiling, including the latest Pixel phones, new health features on the Pixel Watch 5, and more.

Google will be livestreaming the event on Wednesday at 6PM ET / 3PM PT. But if you aren’t able to watch along yourself, you can catch up on all of the highlights from Wednesday’s Pixel launch below.

One of the new Pixel 11 colors is a particularly hot hibiscus pink. Photo: David Imel / The Verge

Google refreshed its line of Pixel phones, starting with the Pixel 11. The design didn’t change drastically compared to the Pixel 10, although it now comes in a few new colors: a lilac-like frost, hibiscus pink, pistachio green, and obsidian black. It runs on Google’s new Tensor G6 chip, which Google claims offers 25 percent faster web browsing and 15 percent faster app loading. Google also says its battery lasts over 30 hours and supports 25 percent faster wireless charging than the Pixel 10.

The Pixel 11 also features an upgraded camera and a camera bump that’s over 40 percent thinner than the Pixel 10’s. It includes 48MP wide, 13MP ultrawide, and 10.8MP 5x telephoto lenses on the back and a 10.5MP selfie camera on the front. Google says the 48MP wide lens has 56 percent more light sensitivity and the 5x telephoto lens supports up to 30x Super Zoom.

Unfortunately, the Pixel 11 also got a $100 price bump — it now starts at $899, but the base configuration has 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, rather than the 128GB of storage in the Pixel 10’s starting configuration. It launches on August 20th.

The HiLight LED can be used for Gemini or incoming calls. Photo: David Imel / The Verge

Google’s Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL include a new feature in the camera bar called HiLight, which is an LED indicator light for things like Gemini interactions and incoming calls from favorite contacts. Google says the little LED will get more capabilities down the line, like signaling message notifications from frequent contacts.

The Pixel 11 Pro also features an upgraded display that maxes out at 3,600 nits. Inside, it has Google’s Tensor G6 chip like the base Pixel 11. The camera includes a new 48MP telephoto lens with up to 120x Pro Zoom and a new 50MP wide lens, along with a 48MP ultrawide lens and a 42MP selfie camera. According to Google, it offers over 30 hours of battery life and over 29 percent faster wireless charging compared to the Pixel 10 Pro / Pro XL.

The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 with 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, while the Pro XL starts at $1,299 with the same specs. The 512GB and 1TB storage options include 16GB of RAM. The Pro and Pro XL are both available in four colors: canyon, fog, olive, and matte obsidian.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold got a camera upgrade with a 48MP wide lens. Photo: David Imel / The Verge

Google says the Pixel 11 Pro Fold features the thinnest bezels ever on a Fold and claims it’s three times as durable as the Pixel 10 Pro Fold, with IP68 water and dust resistance and a back material that’s “designed to be nearly impossible to crack.”

The Fold’s displays are 20 percent brighter than last year’s model and the inner display goes up to 3,600 nits of brightness like the Pixel 11 Pro / Pro XL. It also runs on Google’s Tensor G6 chip and offers up to 24 hours of battery life. The camera includes a new 48MP wide lens plus a 10.5MP ultrawide lens and a 10.8MP telephoto lens with up to 30x Super Zoom.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs $100 more than last year’s model, starting at $1,899 for a base configuration with 256GB of storage and 16GB of RAM, and comes in two color options: olive and black.

Camera app updates include some new creator features like a teleprompter. Photo: David Imel / The Verge

In addition to hardware upgrades, Google’s also introducing some new features for taking photos and videos across its new lineup of phones. The Camera app has a new capture mode called Magic Capture that can pull photos and clips out of video recordings.

There are also Camera Looks, which offer customizable, stylized photo presets that change how your phone processes the photo, rather than simply applying a filter. The various Looks include styles like Minimal, Editorial, and “Digi,” which mimics digital cameras. The Pixel 11 Pro also has a new Pro Stable Video feature Google says can record at up to 8K.

A new Creator tab in the Camera app has a “Creator Suite” with tools for trimming and reordering videos, an onscreen teleprompter, and improved Speech Enhancement.

The Pixel Watch 5 looks identical to the Watch 4. Photo: David Imel / The Verge

The new Pixel Watch 5 might look essentially the same as the previous version, but it includes some major new software features. Breathing Emergency Detection, a follow-up to last year’s Loss of Pulse feature, can trigger an emergency call if the watch detects a significant, sustained drop in blood oxygen saturation (SpO2). The Pixel Watch 5 can also track nightly sleep breathing quality and sum up the data in monthly reports. Starting in September, Google’s also introducing Blood Pressure Trends and Insulin Resistance Trends.

The Pixel Watch 5 has some new workout features as well, like AI-generated strength training plans and the option to track reps directly from your watch. Google claims it includes the “most accurate GPS route tracking for exercise, outperforming Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro.”

Unfortunately, this year’s Pixel Watch is a little pricier — it got a $50 price bump and now starts at $399. It’s available in two sizes, 45mm and 41mm, and four colors: black, white, olive green, and pink. There’s also a Steph Curry special edition that costs $579 and launches a bit later, on September 3rd.

The Pixel Tag resembles an oblong AirTag, and has the same price. Photo: David Imel / The Verge

Google’s taking on Apple’s AirTag with the Pixel Tag, its own item tracker, launching on November 11th for $29 individually or $99 for a pack of four. It’s oblong rather than round, measuring 1.1 inches by 1.8 inches (the AirTag is 1.26 inches across). The tracker is IP67 water and dust resistant and Google says its replaceable CR2032 coin cell battery lasts over a year.

The two-year-old Buds Pro 2 now come in a new olive green colorway. Photo by Andru Marino / The Verge

Google is releasing the two-year-old Pixel Buds Pro 2 in a new olive green color on August 12th that matches the olive Pixel 11 Pro and Pro Fold. In September, Google’s also rolling out a firmware update for the Buds Pro 2 that’s supposed to improve the earbuds’ active noise cancellation.

Correction, August 12th: The Pixel Watch 5 section now includes an image of the Pixel Watch 5. It previously showed the Pixel Watch 4, which looks the same.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel 11 series pairs a little new hardware with a lot of new software
Tech.content:
is a technology reporter who has been covering the industry since 2007. He co-hosts the Waveform podcast with MKBHD. A former engineer, he now specializes in topics like computational photography and social media protocols.

When I first picked up the Pixel 11 Pro this week, it was clear to me that this was one of those refinement years — at least when it comes to hardware. Aesthetically, the phones are as beautiful as ever, with Google’s signature camera bar and bright, colorful backing glass. There are small updates, like a single piece of glass covering the camera bar and the all-new HiLight ambient LED on the Pros. But this year, the Pixel is all about quality of life and software improvements.

After weeks of teasers, Google has finally formally announced the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. The phones are all shipping next week, on August 20th, and Google is holding a splashy event the evening of August 12th to show off the devices. Ahead of that, we had a chance to take a first look at everything that’s coming up.

Pixel 11

The standard Pixel 11 gets some bold colors this year.

Let’s start with the bad news up front: All of these phones are $100 more expensive than last year’s. Google has killed off the 128GB base storage option this year, which means the Pixel 11 now starts at $899 for a 256GB model. All storage tiers still come with 12GB of RAM, but the higher entry price is no doubt driven by RAMageddon, which has been increasing costs across the industry.

If you can look past the price, you’ll find a refined version of last year’s phone that looks and feels a bit more premium. The camera bar is now made of a singular piece of glass and is over 40 percent thinner. If you use it with one of Google’s cases, the bar will become completely flush. (This gives you three different camera bar thickness options on the Pixel line now, which only get thicker the more premium you go.)

The camera bump difference between the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro.

The cameras have been upgraded, too. On the Pixel 11, the 48MP wide is quoted with 56 percent more light gathering capability from its new 1/1.56-inch sensor, and the 5x telephoto lens can now digitally zoom up to 30x, which Google says is enabled by the new image signal processor in the Tensor G6 chipset. And considering the new Tensor G6 chip is said to be up to 20 percent more efficient, Google is quoting up to 30-plus hours of battery life across the lineup.

Perhaps the most interesting update to me is the new Camera Looks feature. You can think of this similarly to the film recipes on Fujifilm cameras, presenting users with stylized presets that can be customized to their liking.

Editorial Camera Look. Minimal Camera Look.

What makes Camera Looks so interesting, though, is instead of just being a filter on top of the preprocessed Pixel photo, the phone will process the photo completely differently at the sensor level depending on which settings you choose, potentially using less frame stacking and sharpening to deliver the photo you actually want. During my briefing at least, this really delivered. The Natural mode does an amazing job of lowering the sharpness and contrast and making the photos look much more true to life, and I’m excited to take it for a proper spin later. If you want to learn more about this, check out my dedicated article where I spoke with Pixel camera lead Isaac Reynolds.

Another new feature inside the camera is Magic Capture. This is a camera mode alongside the photo and video modes that creates a sort of hybrid mashup of the two, where the phone will automatically pick out short clips and images you can share. During my hands-on time this feature didn’t work great, only giving me one small clip and one photo from a roughly 15-second recording, but I believe it’s meant for longer clips at things like kids’ birthday parties. We’ll have to test this in the field once we have more time with the device.

Magic Capture. Creator Suite.

Google is also adding a new Creator Suite inside the camera, which gives you access to tools like social media framing guides, speech enhancement, a teleprompter, and automatic folder structures for video. I was surprised to see this so deeply integrated into the camera itself, and it’s clear Google is going after a new audience and hoping to make the Pixel the best phone for small creators.

The phones also all feature Qi2.2 — an upgrade from Qi2 last year. Google says this offers 25 percent faster wireless charging of up to 25W, an upgrade from the 15W max the Pixel 10 offered. However, many users reported seeing a maximum wireless charge rate of only 5W with the Pixel 10 when using older chargers, so hopefully the problem is fixed this year.

The Pixel 11 will come in purple, green, black, and an extremely hot magenta.

Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL

The Pixel 11 Pro in blue.

The 11 Pro and Pro XL are where things get a little more interesting this year. Like the standard Pixel 11, they start at 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM (down from 16GB last year), which starts at $1,099. If you’re a power user, you can still get 16GB of RAM if you buy the 512GB or 1TB models.

You’re definitely getting more with the Pro models this year, though. The display on the Pixel 11 Pro gets up to a super bright 3,600 nits, which Google says is the brightest display ever on a smartphone. This isn’t a massive difference from the 3,300-nit peak brightness from last year, but it’s something for your money.

The Pixel 11 Pro beside a Pixel Watch 5. The new camera bar is all glass.

The main camera sensor on the Pixel 11 Pro has been improved, with a new 50MP model that Google says uses less power and should perform better in the 1x-to-5x zoom range. There’s also a new 48MP telephoto lens with a larger 1/1.95-inch sensor that delivers a quoted 30 percent improvement in light sensitivity. And just like the standard Pixel 11, the 11 Pro has a further zoom range, now extending up to 120x, which Google says is enabled by the ISP in Tensor G6.

On the Pro phones, Google has also substantially sped up Night Sight, offering up to 4.5x faster low-light image capture, though Google tells me on average it’s about 3x faster than last year. This is still a pretty substantial improvement, and Reynolds told me the idea was to optimize Night Sight for handheld capture. “You can still capture for up to four minutes if you want all the light,” he tells me, “but it’s really optimized for those awkward moments where you have to tell someone to hold still for a little too long.”

The HiLight LED replaces the old temperature sensor.

The flashiest feature (pun intended) of the new Pro phones is the HiLight feature. Pixel 11 Pro and Pro Fold phones now feature an RGB LED ring where the temperature sensor used to be on the right side of the camera bar. When you’re talking to Gemini, the LED will glow blue as it listens and responds to you. Separately, you can set favorite contacts to glow when they call you through the default Phone app or WhatsApp. Google is marketing the feature as a way to be more present in your everyday life, but it doesn’t feel particularly useful to me yet considering its use is so limited. Google says more functionality is coming in the future, but right now, this doesn’t feel like a reason to buy the phone.

The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL will come in olive, light blue, and a striking orange-ish “canyon” color, all with glossy side rails. There’s also a black option, which this year has matte side rails, unlike all the other Pro devices.

Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold in olive.

Finally, there’s the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Google is calling it the most durable Pixel Fold yet, with a new composite back material that Google says is nearly impossible to crack. This, alongside a thicker inner ultra-thin glass display, contributes to Google’s “3x more durable” claim compared to last year.

The inner bezels have also been reduced, making it Google’s thinnest Fold bezels ever, and the peak brightness matches the Pixel 11 Pro at 3,600 nits. The 11 Pro Fold is also inheriting the new 48MP main sensor from the Pixel 11 for a quoted 56 percent improved light sensitivity compared to last year, and it gets Qi2.2 for up to 20 percent faster wireless charging.

The 11 Pro Fold starts at 16GB of RAM standard with 256GB of storage, comes in olive and black, and starts at $1,899 — also a $100 price jump over last year.

Photography by David Imel / The Verge

Tech.title: Uber Freight reportedly investigating after hacking group claims data breach
Tech.content:
A hacking and extortion gang has taken credit for a cyberattack and data breach at Uber Freight, the ride-sharing giant’s logistics subsidiary.

A spokesperson for Uber Freight told Reuters, which first reported the incident, that there was no effect on its business operations and that its systems were running normally (The company did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.)

The shipping company is the latest victim in a spate of hacks in recent weeks conducted by the Helix hacking group, which has targeted transportation companies, financial giants, and private equity firms throughout the year. The hackers are known for targeting companies and exfiltrating large amounts of data from their cloud environments, which they then threaten to publish if the victim companies do not pay a ransom.

In a post on its data leak site, which it uses to host the stolen files, the Helix hackers claim to have taken mailboxes, cloud storage drives, files relating to accounts payable and dispatch documents from Uber Freight.

Some of the files seen by TechCrunch appear to show email correspondence between Uber Freight and several of its customers. TechCrunch could not immediately verify the authenticity of the files, which appeared to be dated around mid-June.

Uber Freight has not yet said if it received any correspondence from the hackers, or if it paid the hackers a ransom.

Google said earlier this week that the Helix hacking group is part of a wider umbrella collective of hackers that it tracks as UNC6671. The gang relies on social engineering tactics, such as voice phishing, a tactic that involves calling up IT helpdesks and requesting the reset of employee passwords. Security researchers have long warned that these attacks, while crude and rudimentary, are highly effective at tricking humans into granting access to sensitive systems.

In its blog post, Google said a review of the gang’s bitcoin wallets shows it has made at least $10.6 million in ransom payments between January and May this year.

Tech.title: Mesh, Automattic’s CRM for everyone, comes to Android
Tech.content:
Mesh, the relationship manager and personal CRM acquired by WordPress.com’s parent company, Automattic, last year, is now available to users on Android devices. The software allows users to privately visualize and keep track of the people in their personal and professional networks, add notes to people’s contact information, and be reminded when to reach out.

On Android, the company customized Mesh’s app to work with key platform features, like split-screen and pop-up views. This allows users to access Mesh while working in other apps, like messages or email. It also supports keyboard shortcuts for foldables and tablets, in-app search, home screen widgets (with Material You colors that match your Android’s wallpaper), and real-time sync across devices.

Image Credits:Mesh

The company’s broader plans for Mesh could eventually see it tied more closely to Automattic’s all-in-one messaging app, Beeper, which offers a way to connect with people across platforms, including through WhatsApp, Instagram, Signal, Messenger, X, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord, Google Messages, and more.

Already, Mesh and Beeper interoperate to some extent, as Mesh users can draft a text to someone in Beeper or click deep links in the app to visit a Mesh user’s profile. In time, the company wants to add additional AI features that will make users of both products more productive in terms of managing their personal relationships.

“We’re thinking a lot about how can AI help you be a better friend and have better work and personal relationships?,” Mesh co-founder Zachary Hamed told TechCrunch in an interview earlier this spring. “We have users who have ten-, twenty-, or fifty-thousand connections across multiple social media apps, across their work products. It’s an impossible task to think and be conscientious with you, with each of those people, by yourself,” he noted.

Image Credits:Mesh

Today, Mesh’s Nexus AI is in early access, offering a way to use AI to navigate your network. That means users can ask questions like who they know at a particular company or who lives in a certain city, or who has expertise in a particular topic. The company is also experimenting with using AI technology to provide a voice-based, hands-free experience and an improved business card scanning feature.

Importantly, personal information stored in Mesh isn’t shared or used for ad targeting, the company says, as the product is supported by subscriptions. (It’s free for up to 1,000 contacts, then has higher tiers for unlimited contacts and other features.)

In time, Mesh may consider a bundled subscription with Beeper or other Automattic products, but has nothing to announce on that front at this time.

Currently, the majority of Mesh’s customers, or around 70%, are using the app for some type of business purpose. Mesh co-founder Matthew Achariam says Mesh’s sweet spot is executives running bigger teams or those who have a tight network to stay in touch with. However, the company still thinks about the consumer use case, he notes.

“The beauty of [serving business users] is that the same things they’re using apply to every individual consumer. So every feature that we think about has to apply to both,” he says.

Mesh (formerly Clay) for Android will roll out to Google Play for phones, tablets, and foldables as a free download with in-app purchases.

Tech.title: Why Stream ring-maker Sandbar says the future of AI wearables is voice
Tech.content:
Loading the player…

AI notetaking hardware has taken off over the past couple of years, with credit-card-sized devices, pendants, pins, and even transcribing earbuds all promising to capture your meetings and turn them into summaries and action items. Now, a whole wave of wearables — rings especially — are betting people want to capture stray thoughts and ideas the same way.

One of the companies chasing that bet is Sandbar, the startup behind the private voice ring Stream, which has raised $36 million to date, including a $23 million Series A led by Adjacent and Kindred Ventures.

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Sandbar co-founder and CEO Mina Fahmi about why he thinks so many voice hardware devices before Stream struggled to break through, and why he’s betting that keeping the human firmly in control is what it’ll take to get wearable tech right.

Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify and all the casts. You also can follow Equity on X and Threads, at @EquityPod.

Tech.title: Tesla wants to build a $10B solar factory in Texas
Tech.content:
In Brief

Tesla intends to build a massive solar panel factory 45 minutes southwest of Houston, according to documents filed with the state of Texas.

The new factory, called Project Crystal Sun, could cost as much as $10.1 billion. Tesla has applied for tax incentives to partially offset the cost, saying that it is exploring other sites “across multiple U.S. states.” The factory would create about 9,700 full-time jobs, Tesla said.

Without incentives, Tesla’s accountants estimated that the property tax liability for the project would be about $1.1 billion over 37 years.

The project aims to break ground this year and be completed by 2028, and Tesla said the first solar panels would roll off the line in 2029. The company hasn’t indicated whether the panels would be destined for terrestrial installations or satellites. However, Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who also runs SpaceX, is famously bullish on orbital data centers.

In the filings, Tesla did not publicly disclose the factory’s annual output, though it has said that it plans to build 100 gigawatts worth of manufacturing capacity in the U.S. by 2028.

Tech.title: Form Energy raises $750M to build more 100-hour batteries for the grid
Tech.content:
Battery startup Form Energy said on Wednesday that it has raised $750 million to expand its manufacturing capacity in West Virginia, the latest sign that the AI data center building boom is fueling investment in energy storage.

The U.S. installed 9.7 gigawatt-hours of energy storage in the first three months of this year, up 32% from 2025. Most of those batteries can discharge for a few hours at most, but Form Energy’s iron-air batteries can deliver power for up to 100 hours. Long-duration energy storage is particularly desirable because it can help bridge the power supply gap in renewable power generation, which is expected to account for more than 90% of new generating capacity in the U.S. this year.

Form’s unique battery chemistry helps it store massive amounts of electricity for less by relying on iron instead of pricier minerals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel. Inside a Form battery, iron is oxidized and reduced as it is discharged and charged — that is, the battery turns iron into rust when it discharges and reverses the process when it charges, turning rust back into iron.

The approach has helped Form land some big customers. Google is building a new data center in Minnesota that will be partially powered by a massive, 30-gigawatt-hour Form battery that cost the tech company about $1 billion. Crusoe said in March that it would buy 12 gigawatt-hours of batteries from Form. Utility Xcel Energy is also a customer, as is FuturEnergy Ireland.

Some 80% of Form’s materials come from the U.S., while the balance comes from Europe and Asia — notably not China. Chinese companies dominate both the battery supply chain and battery manufacturing, and both the Biden and Trump administrations have sought to decrease U.S. reliance on China for batteries.

The company’s domestic-focused supply chain has helped it land big new customers as U.S. electricity demand rises for the first time in decades. Data centers are largely responsible for the uptick; they are expected to quadruple their electricity use in the U.S. by 2035, consuming about 20% of all electricity generated in the country.

The startup currently has a backlog of commercial projects worth about 80 gigawatt-hours of energy storage, the Wall Street Journal reported, up fourfold from earlier this year.

The Series G round was led by T. Rowe Price with participation from Sequoia Capital, Janus Henderson, Franklin Templeton, PEAK6 Investments, Prelude Ventures, Engine Ventures, TPG Rise Climate, Capricorn’s Technology Impact Funds, Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna, Gigascale Capital, Coatue, Energy Impact Partners, NGP, GE Vernova, Blindspot Ventures, and M&G Catalyst Fund.

Tech.title: Lovable confirms new $13.3B valuation, raises another $400M
Tech.content:
Europe’s favorite vibe-coding startup Lovable has confirmed previously reported whispers that it was raising another mega round at a $13.3 billion valuation. Lovable said on Wednesday that it has raised $400 million in a Series C round led by Menlo Ventures and the Scaleup Europe Fund, with more than a dozen other investors participating.

This new funding comes after Lovable hit $500 million in annualized run rate revenue in June, the startup told TechCrunch. Its previous round, announced in December, brought in $330 million at a $6.6 billion valuation and was also led by Menlo Ventures, with CapitalG as co-lead.

As the startup has grown — it now says it hosts 60 million projects that attract 900 million monthly visitors — so has its backend needs and sophistication, the company says. Lovable, for instance, offers its own in-house trained AI model, as well as the usual frontier model options. In June, it signed a multiyear deal with Google Cloud, a fivefold increase in usage. Lovable has also backed other European startups, such as Danish startup Atech, which is building vibe-coding software that designs tech hardware.

Note: one of Lovable’s new Series C investors is Regent, the investment firm that also owns TechCrunch.

Tech.title: Facebook officially rolls out its standalone Creator Studio app with AI tools for creators
Tech.content:
Facebook announced on Wednesday that it’s rolling out a standalone Creator Studio app, an AI-powered app that gives creators personalized tips to grow their audiences and new tools to engage with their communities. The official iOS rollout comes a few weeks after Facebook began testing the app with select creators.

Facebook’s AI creator assistant is built into the new app to provide creators with personalized recommendations based on their content style, performance, audience engagement, and goals.

Creators often have to sift through charts and dashboards to understand their performance, but with the AI assistant, they can get quick answers to questions like “When should I post?” and “What are people saying in my comments?” Creators can also ask follow-up questions.

By giving creators access to the new Creator Studio app, Meta is looking to keep creators active on Facebook as it competes for their attention against rivals like TikTok and YouTube. The company may also be trying to reduce its reliance on third-party tools like ChatGPT when it comes to content ideas and analyzing performance.

Image Credits:Facebook /

The Creator Studio app includes several new features, including an AI-powered comment tool that surfaces the most important comments and drafts replies in the creator’s own tone. Creators can edit and approve the suggested replies before posting them, according to Facebook.

Additionally, when creators open up the app each day, they’ll see a feed of daily priorities, including reviewing their latest post’s performance, tracking progress toward their goals, and flagging comments that need a reply.

Creator Studio is available for all creators on iOS in the United States and Canada.

The new app isn’t Meta’s only recent launch; the company has been on something of a product spree in recent months. The tech giant recently released a standalone app for Facebook Groups called Forum that functions similarly to Reddit, an app called Instants that lets users share disappearing photos with Instagram friends, a vibe-coded gaming app called Pocket, and an AI storytelling app called StoryKit that creates AI-generated children’s stories.

Tech.title: How a $250 million acquisition collapsed into allegations of fraud and forged signatures
Tech.content:
When VideoVerse announced its acquisition in September 2025, it felt like a victory for startups across India. VideoVerse was a simple clipping service, but after years of startup incubators and pitching clients, the company had pulled off a $250 million exit.

The acquirer was Minute Media, an international sports publisher split between New York and Tel Aviv, with plans to scale VideoVerse’s clipping software beyond its Indian niche and into the lucrative world of international sports.

Less than a year after the announcement, the deal has unraveled.

Investors are still waiting for their share of the $250 million windfall, and founder Vinayak Shrivastav is now at the center of multiple legal cases. Even the acquirer, Minute Media, seems to be backing away. In May, the company said it was terminating its contract with VideoVerse, underscoring that the two had continued operating as separate legal entities even after the acquisition closed.

Reached by TechCrunch, a Minute Media representative said that “after, among other things, significant discrepancies were discovered in VideoVerse’s representations, Minute Media decided to terminate its engagement with the company.”

If the allegations are true, this was more than just a deal that fell through. Across multiple legal filings, creditors and investors paint a picture of a serially untruthful CEO, who used the guise of a successful business to accumulate cash-generating debts and side deals until the pretense became untenable. The result is an alarming reminder of the limits of due diligence and how much the business of startups still relies on trust.

The sheer volume of legal cases shows that trust is now in short supply. Bluestone Capital, which backed VideoVerse in its 2023 round, is now suing the company for fraud, alleging that the startup violated its investment terms and refused to pay out proceeds from the acquisition. In a separate suit, a creditor is seeking to recover $64 million from a loan that Shrivastav took out shortly after the acquisition closed.

The same complaint alleges that Shrivastav committed fraud during the acquisition itself, claiming he “used fraudulent merger documents that did not reflect the business terms on which Mr. Shrivastav and Minute Media had agreed to induce Clippings’ shareholders to approve the merger.”

Even VideoVerse executives have begun lobbing accusations. The company’s COO alleges in a separate case that Shrivastav forged his signature on loan and share-repurchase agreements, extracting tens of millions of dollars from the company, in the wake of the Minute Media deal.

The Business of Clipping

While not a household name, VideoVerse became a key player in the billion-dollar clipping industry, providing automated tools for editing long-form broadcasts into the shorter clips that travel well on social platforms.

Its flagship product, Magnifi, is an AI-powered tool that can automatically identify key players and moments. Using the software, clients could easily generate packages of every three-point shot in a basketball game, for instance. Backed by an extensive human support team, the platform attracted high-profile clients like the Indian Premier League, FIFA+ and Nippon TV.

It is a lucrative niche, and one in which Minute Media had hoped to expand to the U.S. market before VideoVerse’s internal problems surfaced.

Even across the multiple cases against Shrivastav, there are conflicting claims and inconsistencies, as investors struggle to make sense of the current state of the company. What is clear is that tens of millions of dollars are missing, and there are already disputes about where the money went and how much is owed to whom.

In October, Shrivastav approached the investment firm Lingotto, arranging a $55 million structured loan — supposedly to satisfy an earlier creditor. With the Minute Media merger already public at more than four times that amount, it appeared to be a safe bet. The financing was even backed by statements from the creditor and Minute Media’s own CEO. According to a court filing from Lingotto, $53 million was transferred to an account controlled by Clippings on October 1, backed by a standard repayment schedule.

But Lingotto now says critical documents provided by Shrivastav were forged. Minute Media’s CEO never signed the documents, the lawsuit alleges, and screenshots purporting to show internal bank balances were also fabricated.

According to the terms of the loan, Lingotto was owed a $4 million payment on March 31, but it never arrived. When the investment firm called in the full amount of the loan with interest, it discovered a long list of people waiting to be paid by VideoVerse. A separate loan from Bluestone Capital had gone into settlement a few months prior, with similarly overdue payments. By the end of April, Shrivastav was out as CEO.

The following months have produced a web of overlapping court claims, as Minute Media, Lingotto, and Bluestone each seek restitution in Delaware Chancery Court. A separate claim from former COO Sabya Das alleges a more complex tangle of fraud involving secondary sales and a confidential high-interest loan.

Shrivastav did not respond to multiple attempts to contact him for this story. His most recent listed address, which appears in Das’s complaint, is on the Palm Jumeirah islands in Dubai.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel Watch 5 Can Now Detect Breathing Emergencies
Tech.content:
Google's first smartwatch debuted just four years ago, and at the time, the company went to great lengths to stress the accuracy of the Pixel Watch's heart rate sensor. Even if Google was late to the wearable party compared to peers like Apple and Samsung, that focus on heart rate seems to be paying off with new features that are yet to be seen on competing products.

On Wednesday, Google introduced the latest generation of its smartwatch, the Pixel Watch 5 (alongside the Pixel 11 smartphone family). The hot new health feature? Breathing Emergency Detection. Similar to the first-of-its-kind Loss of Pulse Detection feature introduced on the Pixel Watch 3, this new capability can be triggered by a variety of factors, like drug toxicity, accidents, severe pneumonia, and choking.

“Using a combination of data from the advanced sensors, including a PPG, accelerometer, and barometer, we've designed an AI-based algorithm running on device to detect a persistent drop in oxygen saturation and then call Emergency Services for you and even share your location,” says Francis Hoe, a product manager on Google's Pixel Watch team.

This feature hasn't been cleared by the Food and Drug Administration, which is why it's not launching in the US at the moment; Google says it's working with regulators to expand availability. It will only be available in select markets in the European Union to start. Google also says it's not intended for people with preexisting respiratory conditions and isn't designed to diagnose or treat medical conditions.

Courtesy of Google

You also don't need a new Pixel Watch 5 to take advantage; Google's bringing this feature to the Pixel Watch 4 as well. And two other big new capabilities are also coming to older devices: blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. These are coming to the Google Health app and will be available for anyone with a Fitbit Air, Pixel Watch 3, Watch 4, or Watch 5 later this fall.

“It might have felt strange—why are we harping about heart rate accuracy so much—back then,” Sandeep Waraich, senior director of Wearables at Google, tells WIRED. “We kept investing in that, and now it's very improved, because all these large sensor models can detect these signatures, insulin resistance, blood pressure trends—but underneath, they need a really capable raw signal.”

Google is placing these features into a new umbrella category called Health Guardian, which includes existing features such as irregular rhythm notifications, high/low heart rate notifications, Loss of Pulse, and Sleep Breathing Quality. The idea is to put these capabilities in a place where users can easily see what they have turned on, similar to Google's Personal Safety app on Pixel phones, which shows features like Emergency SOS, Safety Check, and Car Crash Detection in one place.

Tech.title: 4 New Camera Tricks on Google’s Latest Pixel 11 Smartphones
Tech.content:
The new Pixel 11 Pro, announced today, can zoom up to 120X, though in addition to the digital stitching, it relies on AI-generated pixels to fill in some details. Reynolds says maybe having that capability is enough to get someone interested in, say, wildlife photography. After experimenting on their phone, they’d be ready to invest in a professional camera and a big zoom lens.

“There's a reason I work on low light and zoom every single year," he says. "Because no matter how much I do it, when I do the user study with thousands of respondents, people always want more."

Every year, Google debuts a new Pixel phone, and every year, there's a slew of new camera tricks—largely powered by software wizardry—to deliver better photos than ever before. Last year, there was the Pro Res Zoom, which bumped up digital zoom on the Pixel 10 Pro to 100X. Two years before that, Google introduced “Add Me,” which lets two people take a group photo together without asking a stranger to take the pic for them.

For the Pixel 11 series, Google has demonstrated a handful of upgrades that can drastically alter the look of your photos, and even take some of the work out of capturing photos. Here's a closer look at a few top new camera capabilities on the Pixel 11 series.

Magic Capture

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

So you want to capture a video of an important event—a concert of your favorite band, singing happy birthday to a loved one as a waiter brings a cake over, or your kid's recital. Too often, you see people holding their phone up during these milestones, trying to capture the moment, instead of being present. That's the problem Google's new Magic Capture feature is trying to solve.

Tech.title: Google Pixel 11 Series, Pixel Watch 5, Pixel Tag: Specs, Features, Price, Release Date
Tech.content:
Google is dialing things up to 11 this year with its Pixel phones. Ahead of its annual Made by Google event in New York City, the company unwrapped the Pixel 11 smartphone family—which includes the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold—alongside the Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch. There's also a new hardware addition: the Pixel Tag, which seems designed to be the AirTag of the Android world.

Here's everything you need to know about the hardware changes and software upgrades on Google’s latest devices. Preorders open today, and the phones and watches go on sale August 20.

The Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 starts with 256 GB of storage and comes in an eye-popping Hibiscus color. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

It was inevitable, but prices are up across the board for Google's Pixel 11 series. The Pixel 11 now starts at $899, and on the highest end of the spectrum, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is now $1,900. This means both devices got $100 price bumps. There's some good news: Google has bumped the base storage up to 256 GB on every device, a move matching Samsung's and Apple's latest handsets.

The Pixel 11 series is powered by Google's Tensor G6 chipset, which the company says is 20 percent more power efficient, 25 percent faster for browsing, and 15 percent faster when loading apps. Many of the camera improvements in the new devices are thanks to an improved imaging signal processor on the chip and a 50 percent more powerful tensor processing unit.

One big design change across the entire Pixel 11 series is on the oval camera bar on the back—it's now an all-glass surface, as opposed to a mix of metal and glass on its predecessors. Google says the camera bar on the Pixel 11 is more than 40 percent thinner, and when you pop on Google's case, the camera bar disappears and is completely flush. The Pixel 11 has the most striking color of the lot—Hibiscus—joined by more muted Pistachio, Frost, and Obsidian.

Tech.title: Honor’s Robot Phone Has a Gimbal-Powered Camera for Vloggers
Tech.content:
The gimbal-powered 200-megapixel camera isn't the only camera, either. It's joined by a 200-megapixel telephoto camera and a 50-megapixel ultrawide, not to mention the 50-megapixel selfie shooter. The gimbal has 4 degrees of freedom, and you can activate it in the camera app or by making a palm motion on the selfie camera. And since it can rotate 300 degrees, you can use it as a selfie camera too.

The phone is shockingly light at 248 grams (the aforementioned iPhone 17 Pro is 206 grams). I wholly expected the Robot Phone to be top-heavy, with all those camera components at the top and the massive 7,060-mAh silicon-carbon battery inside powering the whole system. But in fact it’s decently balanced.

A glass cover protects the gimbal camera, and you can slide it to the right when you're ready to activate the gimbal. Once the camera is out, you can manually control the gimbal for ultra-smooth video capture through the camera app, or use preset motions to give your clips a cinematic look. There's even voice control with natural language, so you can say “turn around for 5 seconds.”

The motorized stabilization in the camera makes action shots—which can typically look shaky on traditional smartphones—look amazingly smooth. There are tracking modes as well, such as a subject tracker that keeps the selected person in the frame even as they move around. You can imagine how helpful that can be for solo travelers vlogging their way through a trip.

Specs Honor Robot Phone Display 6.31-inch, 120 Hz, OLED Processor, RAM, and Storage Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, 12 or 16 GB RAM, 512 GB or 1 TB storage Cameras 200-MP gimbal main, 200-MP telephoto, 50-MP ultrawide, 50-MP selfie camera Battery and Charging 7,060 mAh, 120-watt wired, 50-watt wireless Size and Weight 151.43 x 72.86 x 9.59 mm, 248 grams Colors Silver, Gray Water Resistance IP54

Some of these features extend past content creation. For example, the subject-tracking mode works in video calls, meaning you can set the phone up on a table (Honor includes a case and a magnetic stand) and the camera can follow you around. I also took a group selfie, and instead of taking a normal picture, the gimbal took three photos—left, center, and right—and stitched them like a panorama for a wide shot of everyone. Quick and seamless.

There's a less effective and quite gimmicky integration with Honor's Yoyo virtual AI assistant, where the gimbal camera acts like an enigmatic robot with a pair of eyes on the phone's screen. Ask it to dance to music, and the gimbal camera will move to the beat. It can pretend to be happy or angry, making the appropriate movements to indicate its mood. The camera also serves as the AI's eyes; ask it to describe the scene in front of you, and it'll take a peek.

Tech.title: This Coin-Sized Device Can Hack a Boeing 737
Tech.content:
Even as the digital components of so many life-critical systems have proven susceptible to cybersabotage—cars, medical devices, even water utilities and power grids—the computer systems of airplanes have, thankfully, remained uniquely inaccessible to hackers. But one group of academic researchers has spent years testing a different, devious approach to aviation cybersecurity. Perhaps, they suggest, a plane could be hacked the same way that spies and saboteurs have targeted other high-value, offline computers: by surreptitiously gaining physical access to one and plugging in a device designed to silently run the attackers' malicious code.

Tomorrow at the Usenix Cybersecurity Conference, researchers from the University of California at San Diego and Oberlin College will present a hacking technique capable of commandeering the autopilot of a Boeing 737 to redirect its navigation or silently altering key values in the plane's takeoff and fuel calculations while spoofing the results on the pilot's screen—subtle changes the researchers say could potentially cause anything from runway overruns on takeoff to diversions to a different country's airspace to catastrophic crashes.

To carry out that hacking, they've built a roughly coin-sized, Wi-Fi-enabled prototype device that costs less than $100. In less than a minute, that hardware implant can be fitted into a port accessible via a hatch on the exterior of the plane, one that's routinely within reach of maintenance workers or other airport and airline staff between flights. Once it's in place, the device can send electrical signals on one of the 737's internal networks to spoof commands to sensitive computer systems that guide its autopilot and show the pilot variables like the plane's total weight and outside air temperature, which play a critical role in a 737's takeoff calculations.

The researchers' hacking device, next to a quarter for scale. Photograph Courtesy of UCSD

By proving the viability of that technique, the result of a process that stretched over more than a decade and entailed buying tens of thousands of dollars’ worth of plane components for testing, they hope to show that this sort of physical access hacking represents a practical threat in the hands of well-resourced saboteurs and a significant blind spot in aircraft security. Compared to the traditional threat of simply planting a bomb on a plane, they argue, it's also an approach that would offer an attacker more control, stealth, and deniability.

“If you could get 60 seconds with an airplane, what could you do?” asks Stefan Savage, one of the UCSD computer science professors who led the project, describing the question that first motivated their line of research. “Well, it turns out there’s a port that’s externally accessible. You can get to it with no special tools in about 15 seconds. And you can shove in a piece of electronics a little bigger than a quarter that lets you basically tell the autopilot what to do and lie to the pilot about changes to the flight plan.”

Tech.title: How to Select the Office Chair That’s Right For You
Tech.content:
I spent years taking office chairs for granted. But when I began working from home six years ago, I learned quickly that the right office chair is the difference between pain and no pain. I prefer “no pain.” Turns out the human body was not designed to sit in the same position for long hours at a time. An ergonomic office chair can mitigate the strain on your back from long hours of sitting and help you keep good posture.

But what’s the best office chair? The answer is not the same for everyone. (See WIRED’s guide to the Best Office Chairs to examine your options.) The highest-end chairs offer excellent adjustability for a wide range of heights and builds, but almost none will serve everyone—and some styles and builds tend to suit tall or short people better.

Here are the main questions and considerations when finding an office chair, in consultation with Kristianne Egbert, an ergonomist at workplace-injury company Briotix Health with two decades' experience in the field.

How Much Should You Spend on an Office Chair?

Top-end picks like the Herman Miller Aeron ($2,195)—a favorite of many WIRED reviewers over the years for its elegant design, wide-ranging adjustability, and breathable Pellicle mesh—can rival the price of a good mattress or sofa. The price buys beauty and comfort, sure, but also durability (and a 12-year warranty, in Herman Miller’s case).

Top-end ergonomic chairs are designed for people who expect to spend long hours in their chairs and at their desks. If you have the budget, WIRED’s favorite premium chair, the Steelcase Gesture ($1,510), is an investment meant to last for your entire working life—elegant and near-infinitely adjustable to your shape and frame.

Tech.title: Ego 1300 Electric Mower Review: Tame Your Lawn Without Gas
Tech.content:
My old 21-inch gas mower was a Toro that a friend of mine found for free at the side of the road. He gave it to me, I replaced the carburetor, and it fired right up. Score! It ran fine for over a year. And mowing 5 acres with a small gas mower at an hourly rate made my son a relatively wealthy 11-year-old. But then it died again. And again. And at some point, small engine repair isn't fun anymore.

While I was spending weekends cleaning carbs, tracking down air filters, and not mowing, the grass was growing. In northern Wisconsin, grass grows so fast I'm pretty sure you can see it happening if you take the time. A wet June ensured that by the time the Ego arrived for testing, the grass was well out of control, up to 10 inches in the lower, wetter areas of the property.

I figured it would make a good torture test for the Ego, but I'd still need to go in afterward to hack it back with my string trimmer. To my surprise, the Ego 1300 plowed right through almost all of it in a single pass.

For the first pass, I set the height to 4.5 inches, which is easy to do using the height adjustment lever. Unlike an alarming number of mower makers, Ego's height adjustment system is a thing of beauty. The height markings aren't arbitrary letters or symbols that require you to consult a manual to translate to inches. On the Ego, the height adjustment is plainly printed in inches. Imagine that. This lets you know that if you set it to 4.5 inches, your grass will be 4.5 inches high when you're done.

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

Starting at 4.5 inches and running in Turbo mode allowed the Ego, in a single pass, to cut just about anything I pointed it toward. There is one patch of grass, below an active seeping spring, that was long enough and wet enough that I had to make two passes to get a nice even cut. After that initial mow, I then went back over it a few days later at 3 inches to finally get the height back to what I could call normal. The second mow was, dare I say, incredibly easy. Even the lowest self-propelled speed was generally fast enough for me, though I did crank it up to about the middle to get up the steeper slopes (and then turned it off entirely going downhill).

Tech.title: The Job-Interview Tattoo Guy Everyone Got Mad at Finally Explains Himself
Tech.content:
Jordan Zietz wants to be clear: He has never, and will never, force anyone to tattoo his startup’s logo on their body.

The 24-year-old briefly became the internet’s most hated person after LemonLime, his AI-for-small-business startup, hosted a party following Y Combinator's Startup School in late July. In a LinkedIn post, Zietz wrote that he brought an “actual tattoo artist” to the party and “offered an instant interview to anyone who got a LemonLime tattoo.” Seven people, Zietz wrote, left with ink.

The backlash was quick. Zietz’s LinkedIn posts were flooded with angry comments calling him “disgusting” and “very unfair,” the perpetrator of a “textbook display of predatory corporate behavior, a gross abuse of power, and a profound violation of professional ethics.” A screenshot of his post went viral on X. One representative response read: “The job market cannot be this cooked that kids have to get permanent tattoos to get interviews.”

In an interview with WIRED on Tuesday, Zietz attempted to set the record straight.

He says that, despite what his original post suggested, no one permanently branded themselves with LemonLime’s corporate logo at the party. While there were predesigned tattoos of lemons and limes, attendees could pick any design. (At least one said she got a personal tattoo; she added that she was “not seeking a job.”) According to Zietz, he told everyone at the party that getting a tattoo—citrus-themed or otherwise—was not a job requirement. In fact, he says, any attendee who wanted an interview got one.

“A decent amount of people who got tattoos never wanted to even take us up on any offer to chat” about a job, Zietz says. “They just wanted to get a tattoo for free.”

Three of LemonLime’s five employees received LemonLime-themed flash tattoos, including Zietz and his cofounder, Daniela Muñoz. So did at least one person who didn’t work for the startup, according to Zietz.

On Monday, Zietz got his second tattoo in less than month: the actual LemonLime logo, on his other shoulder. It is one of many. He got his first ever tattoo on a first date, and his thigh tattoos include a dinosaur doodle and text that says “This Is The Correct Knee,” with an X underneath.

“I would never ask anyone to do something I would not do myself,” Zietz says, while emphasizing, again, that he is the only person, to his knowledge, with the actual logo tattooed on his body. He plans to release a glossy video of himself getting the tattoo on social media.

Though Zietz insists the tattoos weren’t a prerequisite for employment at his startup, you’d be forgiven for assuming that was the case, and the language of his LinkedIn post certainly made people think it was. After reading various angry comments and posts, he says he understands why people were uncomfortable with the power dynamic.

Still, part of the reason Zietz hired the tattoo artist was to identify candidates who would be a good cultural fit for LemonLime. Zietz says his original post was “half-and-half” earnest, serving as something of a test for cultural alignment. He didn’t want people to feel obligated to get tattoos. But he did want people to see the tattoo station and think that what LemonLime was doing was “out there.” Then he wanted them to make a judgement call: Did they love it or did they hate it?

If partygoers were turned off by the tattoo station, they probably wouldn’t be a good fit for the startup, he reasons. Sure!

Zietz is trying to hire people who appreciate what he calls his “eccentric” approach to life. When he was a student at Stanford, Zietz was suspended from his role as the university’s mascot, the Tree, after unfurling a banner that said “Stanford Hates Fun” during a football game. Prior to LemonLime, Zietz cofounded a social-media platform called Confetti, and part of the hiring process, Zietz wrote last year on LinkedIn, involved an interview while skydiving.

Tech.title: The Biggest Meteor Shower Peaks Tonight. Here’s How to Watch It Live
Tech.content:
The first-ever report of the Perseid meteor shower came nearly 2,000 years ago, and the spectacular space event has enthralled observers of the night sky ever since. Tonight, the shower will hit its 2026 peak, with 50 to 100 meteors firing per hour. If you can’t make it to a viewing site, NASA is hosting a livestream.

The Perseid meteor livestream starts at 9 p.m. PT tonight (Wednesday, Aug. 12) on YouTube. NASA will broadcast real-time sky imagery from its Automated Lunar and Meteor Observatory at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Meteoroid experts from Marshall will host the livestream, which will include several guest speakers who will discuss the meteor shower, its history and other fun facts.

Perseids began its 2026 show on July 17, and it continues until Aug. 24, so if you’ve seen a meteor in the night sky here recently, there’s a good chance it was Perseids. The meteor shower peaks on the evening of Wednesday and into Thursday, when meteors will be coming at a rate of about one per minute.

NASA hasn’t announced how long the stream will last, but the stream’s name, Up All Night, suggests it’ll last for quite a while. It may be the best way for early birds to experience Perseids after waking up.

This Perseid fireball was seen over a lake in Ontario around dusk. “It was hot and muggy even after the sun went down, with lots of haze on the horizon but this Perseid was so bright it didn’t matter,” photographer Malcolm Park said. Spaceweather.com/Malcolm Park

A full schedule of live streams for NASA

NASA typically simulcasts its streams across its YouTube channel, Twitch channel and NASA Plus, which is often also streamed on Netflix. However, Wednesday is chock-full of interesting things to look at, including a solar eclipse and even a planet parade. It seems NASA’s strategy is to divide and conquer, so the Perseids stream is only appearing on YouTube.

The agency is also hosting a livestream for the solar eclipse on NASA Plus, Netflix, X, Amazon Prime and YouTube on Wednesday. The solar eclipse lasts all day and is visible to the northern third of the US. Those outside the path can watch the eclipse online, at least.

Tech.title: The $899 Pixel 11’s Longer 30x Zoom and New Camera Bar Design Are Impressive
Tech.content:
The new $899 Pixel 11, announced Wednesday ahead of the company’s Made by Google event, has a number of meaningful improvements, like a 30x zoom and faster wireless charging, while dancing around the $100 higher starting price than last year’s Pixel 10.

The Pixel 11 shares the same 6.3-inch screen size as the Pixel 10, shaves its camera bump and extends the camera’s digital zoom range, among a few other changes, such as an ever-so-slightly larger battery. While these iterative alterations don’t seem eye-catching, I appreciated a few of the Pixel 11’s redesigned features during my brief time trying them out.

Admittedly, some of my favorite improvements are to aesthetics. The slimmer camera bar is 40% thinner than the one on the Pixel 10, making it look like a slightly raised platform on the back of the phone. While it’s not flush, it is slim enough that using Google’s PixelSnap case helps the phone lie fully flat on a table.

While the Pixel 11 supports the same 30-watt wired charging as its predecessor, it now tops out at 25-watt Qi2 wireless charging, which should let it recharge faster than last year’s version. In my story exploring CNET Lab testing for the fastest-charging phones, the Pixel 10 (which only supports 15 watts) added only 27% in 30 minutes. The Pixel 11 has a baby battery bump in capacity to 4,985 mAh, up from the Pixel 10’s 4,970 mAh.

If you’re looking for areas of improvement, don’t look at the camera hardware, as the Pixel 11 has the same cameras as the Pixel 10. The upgrades lie, as they usually do with Google phones, in the software.

The Pixel 11 now features a 30x digital zoom, up from the 20x zoom on the Pixel 10. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Pixel 11 cameras

Lens Aperture Resolution Magnification Wide-angle f/1.7 48 megapixels 1x Ultrawide f/2.2 13 megapixels 0.6x Telephoto f/2.8 10.8 megapixels 5x Selfie f2.2 10.5 megapixels 1x

Software gives the Pixel 11’s digital zoom range a boost, now maxing out at 30x, up from last year’s 20x. During my hands-on time with the Pixel 11, I spent most of it experimenting with the improved zoom. I was impressed with how I could zoom straight into various plants in the demo room at 30x and the resulting image had sharp details — such as visible strands inside of a flower — with limited artifacting. Normally, I don’t bother with digital zoom because the resulting photos look like a pixelated mess. I still have to put the phone through more testing for my review

The Pixel 11 has Google’s new Tensor G6 processor and runs on Android 17, with a promised seven years of major OS and security updates. The Pixel 11 will also get the benefit of Google’s Pixel Feature drops that bring new functionality and refinements throughout the year between major Android overhauls.

The updated Android Switch works directly with iOS 26 for moving data from an iPhone to a Pixel phone. René Ramos/CNET Group

Google is also making it easier for iPhone owners to switch to the Pixel 11 with an update to its Android Switch app. I first tested this tool using the updated Samsung Smart Switch on the Galaxy Z Flip 8, and the Pixel 11’s process is similar: You launch it from the Pixel 11’s settings menu, the phone generates a QR code to scan with your iPhone and then you follow prompts on both devices to start the transfer.

But here’s where some of Google’s choices get messy. The barrier for entry is higher for potential Pixel buyers. Google did away with the $799 model with 128GB of storage. That means the Pixel 11 starts at $899 for 256GB, the same $899 price as last year’s 256GB Pixel 10. Even though this is a higher starting price, Google isn’t alone in raising the price of entry: Other 2026 phones like Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8 and Motorola’s Razr received $100 price increases over last year’s models without any storage bump. The Pixel 11 also now comes in a 512GB model for $1,019, which undercuts the $1,100 512GB Galaxy S26.

The Google Pixel 11 comes in Obsidian, Frost, Pistachio and Hibiscus colors. Tara Brown/CNET

This sort of price comparison is important, as we continue to grapple with the overall rising cost of electronics during an ongoing RAM shortage. This situation affects the entire industry, Google said in a press briefing, and stated that the Pixel 11’s pricing reflects this new reality.

The Pixel 11 is now available for preorder in four colors: frost, pistachio, hibiscus and obsidian. I’m personally into the greener hue of the pistachio model, but the pinker hibiscus is a bolder look that I suspect plenty of people will like.

The phone goes on sale Aug. 20, the same day as the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL, Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Pixel Watch 5.

Tech.title: I Tested the Pixel 11 Pro’s Camera in Beautiful Paris
Tech.content:
The Pixel 11 Pro has a variety of upgrades for photographers. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The Pixel 11 Pro is Google’s latest flagship phone, and I got to take it on a photo walk through the colorful streets of mid-summer Paris. Très charmant! Alongside a suite of upgrades like its Tensor G6 processor and delightful new peachy color, there are a bunch of camera updates. And, as a photographer myself, I was keen to see what was up.

So it might seem that most of the camera hardware is the same. It’s the usual trio of wide, ultrawide and telephoto lenses all at the same resolutions as last year’s model. But Google says that the main image sensor is new and generally offers better quality. And the telephoto sensor is physically larger.

But honestly, one of my favorite new features is called Camera Looks, and it’s all about the software. Similar to Apple’s Photographic Styles, Camera Looks change the colors and exposure in your images to give them a more creative look than just taking clinically accurate photos.

Lovely tones and gentle contrast from the main camera with the ‘Vanilla’ Camera Look. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Great tones and spot-on exposure from the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And there’s no discernible color shift when you switch to the ultrawide lens. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I really like the looks, and I actually had them applied to the camera pretty much my whole day. You can also customize each look further, adding some warmth or adjusting the depth of shadows and even adding grain. Typically, I really like the grainy look you get from authentic analog film — it’s why I recently spent a fortune on a Leica M6 film camera — but I’ve gotta say, I don’t love the grain effect that the Pixel 11 Pro applies.

There’s a lot of grain in this picture. I know that because I specifically added loads to the scene when I shot it. I probably shouldn’t have. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

It looks very digital and not especially realistic. I shot all my photos in JPEG and in RAW, which bypasses Google’s processing, allowing me to do my own edits instead.

I’ve done this with a few shots, actually, as sometimes the Camera Looks can be a bit…much. The Black Tie effect is a very high-key black-and-white style that won’t suit every scene, but did play an absolute blinder when I got the phone low for this shot of this person carrying a plant.

It’s a lovely, punchy shot. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And I liked it for this portrait mode shot with the 5x telephoto lens.

The amount of bokeh in the background is perfect. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Though I definitely prefer the ones we did in color using the Editorial Camera Look.

I think the colors in the ‘Editorial’ look have worked well here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But generally, it was the “Vanilla” Look that I stuck with for most of the day.

A new feature for the phones is Magic Capture, which shoots a few seconds of video and uses AI to identify the still frame that best captures the moment, then saves that one for you.

Magic Capture really nailed the decisive moment here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I put it to use with a couple of skaters I found, and it was surprisingly effective. All I had to do was just film the action and not worry about capturing the best moment — the phone would do that for me.

I think the phone definitely highlighted the best shots for me, and while it kind of takes the skill out of nailing that decisive moment, that’s kind of the point. It’s not really for pro action photographers who know exactly when to hit the shutter; it’s more for parents who want to capture an awesome moment of their kid on their bike but don’t want to try again and again to get the shot they want.

While I initially liked the look I chose for this photo, I don’t like how blown out the sky is. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I do like the look that I created on the phone here. It’s definitely got that feel of a summer day, but I do think the sky has been blown out, arguably, a bit too much.

But because I also shot the image in RAW, I was able to do my own edit in Lightroom, and I was surprised at how much dynamic range the phone had really captured. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But again, I shot in raw too, so a few tweaks in Lightroom and I discovered that the phone definitely had captured a lot more dynamic range than the JPEG suggested, giving me much more scope to edit the image how I wanted.

And again, I found the shadows a bit too deep in the shot using the Camera Looks. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

So I made my own edit to the raw file in Lightroom, and I really like the look I achieved. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But otherwise, most of my images were straight out of the Pixel’s camera.

Taken with the 5x telephoto lens, I love how much background bokeh there is here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The 5x telephoto lens has been tweaked to let you focus closer, turning it into something of a macro lens. I put it to use on this shot of a padlock, and I love the shallow depth of field it produced.

But if you want to take things further, that zoom can now reach 120x magnification. That’s basically at the level of an actual telescope, though there’s an important thing to keep in mind. Once you go beyond 30x zoom, the phone uses generative AI to artificially recreate the details in your images, which is good or bad, depending on your perspective.

On the left is the raw file from the 120x zoom. It’s basically just a collection of pixels. On the right is the generative AI’s interpretation. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I shot this image of the French flag on a building that was so far away I could barely even see it. The results speak for themselves. The raw version of that shot (left) is basically just a handful of pixels, yet the AI has reconstructed it (right) with all kinds of new details.

But the problem for me is that those details aren’t real. Or at least, they might not be real. The camera is essentially seeing what’s in front of it and rebuilding that scene almost entirely using generative AI, meaning that what you’re seeing in the finished image is really more of an interpretation of what you saw.

But it’s up to you as to whether that matters. As a photographer, I don’t want generative AI anywhere near my images. I want to know that what I’ve captured in an image is actually what I saw, not simply an algorithm’s interpretation. You’ll have to draw your own ethical lines with tools like this.

Strong colors and excellent details from the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I love the dramatic, low-angle paired with the ultrawide lens, but I don’t love the strong grain effect applied. That’s my fault. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

A classic street photo, converted to black and white in Lightroom from the raw file. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Anyway, the afternoon rolled on, and I continued my walk with the phone, trying to indulge in some street-style photography along the way until I eventually came to an iconic spot overlooking the Eiffel Tower. I switched lenses and styles here, shooting quickly to capture some of the moments as they unfolded before me.

I think the teal of the sky is quite unnatural here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Although I think the tones work really well here, giving it a feel of a magazine fashion shoot. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I tried out what I think was the Editorial Camera Look (though it might have been called something else), and I think it goes a bit hard on the teal sky in some of these, though I do like how it looks sometimes.

It’s too early for me to give a real verdict on the cameras on the new Pixels. You’ll need to wait for my full review and for me to put them up against rivals like the iPhone 17 Pro or Galaxy S26 Ultra.

But I do really like a lot of the photos I took on this little photo walk. The overall image quality is solid, and while I’m somewhat morally opposed to the generative AI in the 120x zoom, I do think tools like Magic Capture can be genuinely helpful. I’m thrilled to see more creative shooting options with the Camera Looks tool.

Gotta love that peachy tone. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I also want to spend more time using it and do a better job of it myself — it’s really handy that the style settings you apply will remain. However, it also means that the heavy-handed grain I chose earlier in the day was still active in images I took later, and it’s…not great.

But we must all learn from our mistakes, even though experience has taught me that I never learn a damn thing.

Tech.title: The Pixel Watch 5 Makes One of My Favorite Watches Better, but More Expensive
Tech.content:
The Pixel Watch 5 is a refined version of its predecessor, which was already a favorite of mine. But its $50 price hike might be a tough sell when many of the new watch’s best features are coming to older models too.

I got to spend a few hours with the Pixel Watch 5 in a press briefing — just enough time to get an idea of how it’s changed from last year’s Pixel Watch 4. Walking into Google’s demo room was like stepping into a rainbow. Each station had its own vibe, matching the shades of the new lineup: the Pixel Watch 5, Pixel 11 and Fold phones, Pixel Buds and Pixel Tags. I saw stations in peach, lilac, olive, lime, black and my personal favorite, bright pink.

The parade of colors — especially the almost blindingly bright pink, which I couldn’t stop staring at — momentarily distracted me from the fact that, aside from new band options and a new metallic finish called pyrite (a gold-and-silver blend), the watch itself hadn’t changed in the slightest. At least on the outside.

Google’s Pixel Watch 5 starts at $399 and is available to preorder. It’ll be in stores starting Aug. 20.

Pixel Watch 5’s welcome, but familiar design

I love the minimalist, bezel-free circular display, with nothing interrupting the curved glass except the rotating crown and side button. It still comes in both 41-mm and 45-mm sizes, and the domed display makes it feel more like a statement piece than a tiny computer strapped to your wrist.

My biggest complaint also hasn’t changed. That beautiful curved glass isn’t especially forgiving if you’re accident-prone. I managed to scratch my Pixel Watch 4 when I took a tumble during a trail run in the first month of testing, and the Pixel Watch 5 has the same Gorilla Glass 5 protection and the same LTPO AMOLED display with 3,000 nits of peak brightness and 320ppi resolution.

Pixel Watch 5’s battery and processing power

Under the hood, the Pixel Watch 5 gets an updated Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated processor, which Google says boosts CPU performance by 12% (over the previous generation). Google also bumps RAM from 2GB to 3GB (a 50% increase) and doubles onboard storage from 32GB to 64GB.

The Watch 5 also has a slightly larger battery than its predecessor: 465 mAh versus 455 mAh on the 45mm model. In practice, though, this shouldn’t translate to a longer battery life. Google says the battery gains mostly offset new AI capabilities like offline Gemini, and you can expect anywhere from 30 to 40 hours of use with the always-on display enabled.

Pixel Watch 5’s offline Gemini

Gemini is still one of my favorite reasons to use a Pixel Watch, as it makes interacting with its small screen largely hands-free. Whether I’m checking train schedules while sprinting for the subway or asking for nearby coffee recommendations during a walk, talking to the watch is often faster than poking at a tiny touchscreen.

Raise-to-talk isn’t new, but the assistant can now handle more tasks offline, even when the watch is disconnected from your phone. That includes simple actions like starting a workout or setting a timer without relying on a data connection.

With Wear OS 7 (preloaded on Pixel Watch 5), Google is also positioning the watch as the hub for its growing wearable ecosystem. From your wrist, you’ll be able to manage Gemini-enabled earbuds, smart glasses and even Google’s new Pixel Tag trackers for objects like suitcases and keys.

Pixel Watch 5’s health and fitness features

While the Pixel Watch 5 uses the same GPS and health sensors as previous generations, Google says improvements to its machine learning algorithms significantly boost accuracy, not only on the Pixel Watch 5 but also on older supported Pixel Watches.

The watch has the same dual-band GPS system introduced on the Pixel Watch 4, but Google says it’s now even more accurate in dense urban environments where tall buildings often interfere with GPS signals.

Google even says that the Pixel Watch 5 outperforms the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fénix 8 Pro, which seems like a tall order considering these are dedicated sports watches that retail for twice the price. I obviously couldn’t verify these claims inside a demo room, but I’ll be putting it to the test for my review.

Likewise, I’ll need some time to test Google’s assertion that the Pixel Watch 5’s sleep and recovery metrics are now 15% more accurate than its predecessor.

Pixel Watch 5’s workout Builder

Workout Builder lets you create custom strength-training workouts on the Google Health app that sync directly to the watch, guiding you through each exercise, counting reps, timing rest periods and nudging you through your routine.

All Pixel Watch 5 owners get free access to Google’s library of exercise videos, ranging from bodyweight movements like planks to dumbbell and kettlebell exercises. You can even filter workouts based on the equipment you have available. Ranking your workout effort after the fact helps the watch learn your threshold and adjust your next workout accordingly to challenge you more (or less) to match your current level.
